PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Traceability From Specification to Tapeout Breaks
Silently

A specification change lands in one place while its consequences surface in another,
because no system the operator runs holds the requirement, its implementation and its proof
together.

The abstract promised one governed model of the design, from specification to tapeout, owned outright
by a fabless chip design company in Saudi Arabia and running on its own hardware. Ontologies for
semiconductor design are what that promise takes literally, and this chapter states the problem such a

model exists to solve: the trace a verification lead needs breaks silently between the tools that hold its
pieces, and nobody sees it break.

1.1 The Question, the Data and the Regimes

The question the operation needs answered is narrow and daily: when an interface requirement changes
on one block, which signals, checks, tests, coverage holes, open bugs and waivers does that change
touch, and which requirements in the affected area have no proof at all. Answering it requires data no
single system holds: specification sections and their revisions, requirement records with owners, the
blocks, interfaces and signals that implement them, the checks and tests that prove them, coverage
findings, bug records, waivers with justifications, and the revision history that binds the whole into a
sequence of defensible states. Each fact must carry the tool, file and revision it came from, or the answer
is an opinion. The regulatory ground is threefold. The kingdom's data protection law applies because the
model holds people's decisions, and an impact assessment under its access provisions runs before go
live. Export control applies to the compute itself, since the GPU class the design needs is a licensable
item for its destination and a license determination is a named checkpoint. Trade secret law governs the
record end to end, in the kingdom and wherever the design might travel, and the European directive
codifying protection of undisclosed know-how is the reference regime the industry designs against
(Europa 2016).

1.2 The Documented Cost

The cost of this problem has two documented faces. The first is the cost of the record leaving control: a
foundry and its engineers pleaded guilty in the United States to trade secret theft and paid a 60 million
dollar fine (Reuters 2020), a parallel Taiwanese proceeding fined the same company NT$100 million
(Bloomberg 2020), and final sentences were handed down years later to former employees of another
chipmaker in a separate leak (Focustaiwan 2026). Those cases are why design data cannot ride a hosted
model service, and why the join must be built inside the boundary rather than exported to whoever can
compute it. The second face is the cost of the join failing in place: escaped bugs found after tapeout
instead of in verification, waivers that expire without anyone noticing, and requirements that reach silicon
with no check ever having proved them. Regulators and funding bodies now write these expectations
down: the United States commerce department's protection guidebook ties semiconductor funding to
research security requirements, including access controls and provenance of technical data (NIST 2024).
An operator of this class is expected to know where its design record came from and who touched it.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is a fabless semiconductor company in Saudi Arabia: it designs silicon in vendor design tool
suites, verifies through simulation and formal tools, and hands tapeouts to an outside foundry whose
relationship stays its own. Its specifications run to hundreds of pages and keep changing, which is the
root of the traceability problem. The design reads five named source systems: the shared specification
drives, the requirements site, the version control system, the bug records and the vendor design tool

suites. Three roles are named in the loop: the verification lead who approves every check before it enters
the regression, the design engineers who confirm each extracted requirement before it is used, and a
senior verification expert who is the escalation path when the approval queue ages. The physical
environment is one place, a design office and the company's own server room on its own premises; there
is no fab floor, no cameras and no physical sensing, and the only location that matters is which block and
which project a record belongs to. The regulatory ground combines the kingdom's data protection law, the
export control determination on the GPU node, and trade secret regimes enforced by courts on three
continents against companies exactly this size.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every Tool Sees One Slice of the Chip

The specification drives, the requirements site, version control, the bug records and the
vendor tool suites each hold part of the design record, and the join verification needs exists in
none of them.

Chapter 1 stated the question and the documented cost of not answering it. This chapter shows why no
system the operator runs today can answer it: each of the five holds one slice of the record, and the join
verification needs exists in none of them, as Figure 2 sets side by side.

2.1 One Slice Per System

The shared specification drives hold the specification documents themselves, hundreds of pages revised
as files. They see section text, owning authors and the revision history of each document, and they miss
everything downstream: no file on a drive says which block implements a section, which signals carry an
interface, or which check proves a requirement. The requirements site holds the structured requirement
records with ids and owners. It sees the requirement text and its edit history, and it misses the
implementation, the proof, and the specification revision and page each requirement was extracted from,
so a requirement edited in the site silently diverges from the specification it came from. The version
control system holds the design as it is: RTL file paths, blocks, interfaces, signal lists, design revisions,
and the assertions the agents would draft. It sees structure and history, and it misses intent, because a
commit message carries no requirement linkage and nothing in the tree says what the design is for. The
bug records hold open bugs by block with severity and whether each was found in verification or after
tapeout. They see failures, and they miss the context that would classify one: whether a bug is a
coverage gap, a spec change nobody traced, or a waived check whose waiver expired. The vendor
design tool suites each run simulation, formal verification and coverage in their own formats. Each sees
its own runs and findings, and each misses the cross-vendor record; no tool's output cites a requirement
id, and the vendor-neutral layer that would join them does not exist on any vendor's roadmap, because it
is not any vendor's product.

      Figure 2. Five systems, each seeing one part of the answer. the question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them Sees Together

What no system sees is the whole argument: requirement to block to signal to check to test to coverage,
each fact carrying the tool, file and revision it came from, with bugs and waivers hanging off the same
trace. In practice the cost lands as manual work and late discovery. An interface change arrives and its
impact list is assembled by hand across drives, sites and tools, so blocks are missed and the misses
surface as escaped bugs found after tapeout, the most expensive kind. Requirements with no proof are
invisible until they fail. Waivers age past expiry with no owner alerted. The verification lead cannot answer
the daily question without days of cross-referencing, which is exactly the delay a change cycle cannot
absorb.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereignty and Vendor Neutrality Shape Everything
Downstream

Four goals, design data staying in Saudi Arabia on the company's own hardware, vendor
neutrality under the existing design tools, named approvals for every check, and a cheap first
gate, are each hard in semiconductors and shape every choice after them.

Chapter 2 showed the join failing across five systems that each see one slice. This chapter states the four
goals that shape every choice made after them, each hard in semiconductors for its own reason, and then

the scoping decisions and rejected alternatives those goals force.

3.1 Design Data Stays on the Company's Own Hardware

The first goal is sovereignty in the literal sense: specifications, designs and models stay in Saudi Arabia
on the company's own hardware, and nothing crosses outward. This is hard in semiconductors because
the data is the company's core intellectual property and the industry's record of losing it is a matter of
court records, from a 60 million dollar guilty plea (Reuters 2020) and a NT$100 million fine in a parallel
proceeding (Bloomberg 2020) to final criminal sentences for leaked process knowledge (Focustaiwan
2026). The practical consequence is that no hosted frontier model service is available at any price, and
the compute must be owned: one node of eight GPUs of the 141 GB high bandwidth memory class,
drawing roughly ten kilowatts that the company's own facilities team must bear, and licensable under
export controls, so the license determination is a named phase one checkpoint before any class is
quoted. Funding regimes elsewhere now write such controls into contract terms (NIST 2024), and the
operator's own constraint settles the question before it is argued.

3.2 Vendor Neutrality Under the Existing Design Tools

The second goal is that the model sits under the vendors' own tools and agents, so any of them can work
from it. This is hard because an EDA estate is a set of vendor suites, each with its own property
languages and formats, and a model bound to one vendor's syntax locks the operator into that vendor
and breaks the goal. The design therefore drafts tool-neutral assertions into the version-controlled source
and runs them in the existing regression, and the integration is the exposure of the ontology beneath the
vendors' tools rather than a connector into any one vendor's silo. Each vendor's license terms are
confirmed in discovery before its connector is built, because terms that restrict reading a vendor's outputs
into a company-owned model would change the design, not the ambition.

3.3 Named Approvals for Every Check

The third goal is that agents draft and people decide: an engineer confirms each extracted requirement
before it is used, and the verification lead approves every check before it enters the regression. This is
hard because the control is structural, not cosmetic. A misread specification propagates into
requirements, checks, coverage and impact lists, and the confirmation step is the only point where the
error is caught cheaply, so the engineer rejection rate is a monitored gate signal rather than a courtesy.
The bottleneck risk is equally real, since a single approver can age a queue: queue depth and ageing sit
on the observability stack, and escalation to the senior verification expert after five working days is the
designed relief.

3.4 A Cheap First Gate

The fourth goal is a first gate that can stop the work cheaply. This is hard in an industry where the
temptation is to model the whole chip at once. Phase one is one block and one revision cycle, with

baseline measures bound before any extension, and the simulated event that proves the design is
deliberately small: one interface requirement change on one block. If the model cannot carry that trace
end to end with citations, extension to the full chip would only scale the failure.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Three scoping decisions follow from the four goals, each buying something specific at a stated cost, and
Table 1 sets them out. Designs of this shape are still rare among industrial ontology examples precisely
because most stop at the document layer and never reach the proof, which is the trade these rows
refuse.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From Records to the Command Center

Systems of record sit below, one governed object model sits in the middle, and agents,
services and surfaces run above it, all inside the company's perimeter with no edge estate
and no hosted service.

Chapter 3 fixed the constraints: sovereign on the operator's own hardware, vendor neutral under the
existing design tools, an engineer confirming every extraction, and proof on one block before any chip-
wide extension. This chapter lays out the stack those constraints produce, because the practical question
behind ontologies for semiconductor design is not which component to buy but where each layer sits
relative to the systems of record, and the answer here is a deliberately plain shape: records below, one
governed model in the middle, agents and services above, with nothing outside the perimeter.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

The stack runs in three bands, and Figure 3 shows the layered whole with a count on every layer. Below
sit the five sources: the shared specification drives, the version control system, the requirements system
of record, the defect tracker and the vendor design tool suites, all read-only and all owned by the
operator. In the middle sits one object model of sixteen objects with typed links, held in Hyper Ontology
v0.9 (Semantics plus Kinetics), which is the only place in the estate where a requirement, the block that
implements it and the check that proves it are neighbors. Above it run eight services, three surfaces and
three agents, with GLM 5.3 serving every one of them. The pattern fits because the operator's problem is

a join failure, and the pattern puts the join in one place that the operator owns and that any vendor's tools
can read from beneath their own interfaces. It also fits the published landscape: most industrial ontology
examples in this sector concentrate on fab-floor data, and the integration shelf behind them holds
connectors for fab-floor systems with nothing for a fabless design estate, so this design builds its
connector per source rather than inheriting one. The inference arithmetic keeps the whole stack in one
room: GLM 5.3 carries a filed count of 753B parameters at FP8, one byte per parameter, so the weights
alone are 753 GB; a single node of eight 141 GB GPUs holds 1,128 GB, leaving 375 GB beside the
weights for KV cache and activations against the roughly 151 GB that the 1.2 planning factor reserves.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The shape a team carrying a similar brief can reuse is the order of the bands, not their contents. Read-

stamps provenance on every fact; one governed object model holds the vocabulary of the vertical; agents
draft above it, and a named person approves every draft before it becomes a write; every weight runs
self-hosted inside the operator's own perimeter. A team swaps the object vocabulary, since sixteen
objects chosen for a chip's life from specification to tapeout will not fit a mine or a fleet, and swaps the
source list and the model sizing to its own hardware. What it keeps, unchanged, are the three controls
that make the model trustworthy rather than merely fluent: the adapter-only door, the approval-only write
path, and the reconciliation run after every sync cycle. Those three are independent of industry, and they
are the part of this design worth copying first.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Sixteen Objects Turn Design Records Into One
Argument

Sixteen objects with typed links carry the lineage from requirement to block to signal to check
to test to coverage, so a query can traverse what a document store cannot.

Chapter 4 placed the object model at the center of the stack and put a count on every layer. This chapter
opens that center: the sixteen objects, the typed links between them, and the human approvals that stand
at the only points where the model is allowed to change.

5.1 Every Object and Its Typed Links

The model holds sixteen objects: the specification section, requirement, design block, interface, signal,
design assumption, verification check, test, coverage result, bug, waiver, design revision, engineer,
verification lead, expert lesson and foundry handoff. Each is anchored where its record already lives: the
specification section in the shared drives, the requirement in the requirements system of record, the
design block, interface, signal, verification check, test and design revision in the version control system,
the coverage result in the simulation and regression environment, the bug in the defect tracker, and the
expert lesson in a kept record of decisions and outcomes that the next decision reads. Figure 4 shows
every object and its typed links, with the verification check as the focal object, and Table 8 carries the
same register as object, anchor and links. The links are what a document store cannot hold. The
simulated event makes this concrete: one interface requirement changes on one block, and a query starts
at the changed requirement, walks back to the specification section and the design revision that produced
it, out through the linked verification checks that claim to prove it, on to the tests that run those checks
and the coverage result each test produced, across to the signals on the affected interface and the blocks
that implement them, and finally to the bugs already filed and the waivers that excuse anything still failing.

answer the two questions that decide a tapeout: which requirements have no proof at all, and which
impact lists were built from a revision the systems of record have since superseded.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives at exactly two points, both named in the requirement and both structural. When the
spec agent reads a new specification revision into requirements, an engineer confirms each one before it
is used anywhere, and the rejection rate is a monitored signal and a phase one gate rather than a
courtesy, because a misread requirement propagates into checks, coverage and impact lists. When the
check agent drafts a tool-neutral assertion into version control, the verification lead approves every one
before it enters the regression, and queue depth and ageing are watched on the observability stack with
an escalation path to the senior verification expert after five working days so one approver cannot
become the bottleneck. The hosting posture follows from what the objects hold. Everything runs on the
company's own hardware on its own premises in Saudi Arabia; identity is carried by Keycloak; there are
no external links, and nothing crosses outward, with Harbor's offline installer governing what comes in as
the artifact and model registry. The only write path into the regression is the approval-gated one through
version control. That posture is not stylistic: design data is the operator's core intellectual property, and
the sector's trade secret record includes criminal findings and a 60 million dollar fine in one case (Reuters
2020) and final Supreme Court sentences in another (Focustaiwan 2026), while research security
guidance for funded programs treats exactly this class of asset as requiring documented protection (NIST
2024). Need-to-know partitioning per project and block is enforced in the schema, mirroring the existing
tool permissions, with a PDPL Article 25 impact assessment before go live.

6.1 Five Sources, One Adapter Family

All five sources are operator-owned and read-only, and Figure 5 maps each one to its provenance class
and its adapter path. The shared specification drives hold the specification documents the spec agent
reads; a chip specification runs to hundreds of pages and keeps changing, so every read is versioned
against the drive's own state. The version control system is the system of record for blocks, interfaces,
signals and revisions, and it is also the destination of the assertions the check agent drafts, which keeps
the drafted checks inside the same review machinery as the design itself. The requirements system of
record is projected rather than replaced: the ontology reads it and holds the requirements as objects with
traceability links, but the operator's system remains authoritative. The defect tracker supplies open bugs
by block to the command center, and the escaped bugs found late become one of the baseline measures
bound in phase two, after the pilot proves the model. The vendor design tool suites are integrated by
exposure rather than connection: the model sits under the vendors' own tools and agents, so any of them
can work from it, which is what vendor neutrality means in practice. Phase one reads only the files and
repositories the operator already owns, fixed at intake, which keeps the first gate cheap.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

The adapter tier guarantees three things. First, provenance: every fact carries the tool, file and revision it
came from, which is what lets a requirement trace to what implements it and what proves it, and what lets
the conversational interface cite the record rather than assert from memory. Second, reconciliation: a
reconciliation job runs after every sync cycle, comparing the model against the systems of record, and
impact lists built from unreconciled revisions are automatically flagged stale and excluded from citations,
so a drifting model cannot silently mislead the verification lead. Third, legality: design tool and foundry
license terms can restrict reading a vendor's records or outputs into a company-owned model, so each
vendor's terms are confirmed in discovery before its connector is built, and phase one touches nothing
beyond the operator's own files. The write path is narrower still: the assertions the check agent drafts
enter version control only through the verification lead's approval, and no agent changes a design file or
the regression without it.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Ordering, delivery and replication are carried by Apache Kafka 4.3.x running in KRaft mode with three
dedicated controllers and a dynamic quorum, so the cluster tolerates a controller change without losing
the log. Ordering of revisions and approvals is carried by the backbone's own sequencing together with
the version control system's commit order, which is why the design needs no sensor time synchronization:
the only ordering that matters is which revision came before which approval. Events are held in a
replicated, replayable log, so a service that falls behind resynchronizes by replaying rather than by asking
the sources again, and buffering survives the gap between a sync cycle and the consumers that read it.
Service health is carried by the observability layer of Prometheus v3.15.0, Grafana v13.2.3 and Loki
v3.7.8, since no machine telemetry is in scope, and identity on site is carried by Keycloak. The one
boundary that exists, the artifact and model registry, is governed by Harbor with its offline installer:
updates and model artifacts come in through it, inspected, and nothing goes out. That asymmetry is the
design's answer to the sector's documented loss pattern, in which design secrets leaving a perimeter
ended in criminal convictions (Bloomberg 2020); here the perimeter is the operator's own, and there is no
outward path to guard or to leak through.

7.1 Three Tiers, One Room, One Node

The design has no edge estate, so its inference tiers are separated by function rather than by location,
and all of them run inside the company's premises on hardware the company owns. The central tier is
GLM 5.3, the 753B-parameter work surface model, served on vLLM from one node of eight GPUs of the
141 GB HBM class; it carries the spec agent that reads specification revisions, the check agent that drafts
tool-neutral assertions, and the natural language answers the verification lead asks for. The retrieval tier
is BGE-M3, which embeds specifications, requirements, checks and records so that every answer can
cite the record it came from; it is small enough to run on CPU or a modest GPU beside the serving node.
The document parsing tier is PaddleOCR-VL 1.6, which turns the hundreds of pages of a chip
specification into structured text at ingestion, and which also fits on a site GPU. Figure 6 sets the three
tiers side by side with what runs on each.

The memory arithmetic settles the central tier's size, and it is worth stating in full because it is the
difference between a plan and a wish. The model's filed parameter count is 753B, held at FP8 precision,
which at one byte per parameter is 753 GB of weights. Applying the frontier model GPU footprint sizing
rule used with vLLM and SGLang, a 1.2 planning factor for KV cache and activations brings the
requirement to 904 GB the GPUs must hold. One node of eight 141 GB GPUs provides 1,128 GB, which
holds the weights with room to spare: after the weights and the planning reserve, roughly 280 GB of KV
cache ceiling remains for concurrent engineers working at the same time. The node carries a load of
roughly ten kilowatts, which is a question for the company's facilities team rather than for this design, and
it is a 4A090 item for a D:4 destination, so a BIS license determination is named as a phase one
checkpoint before any class is quoted; until the node lands, the platform runs on the company's existing
hardware.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The latency budget in this design is shaped by the fact that its slowest loop is a person, not a machine.
No assertion enters the regression until the verification lead approves it, so the approval queue sets the
pace of the whole system, and queue depth and ageing are monitored on the observability stack with an
escalation path to the senior verification expert after five working days. The spec agent's reading is batch
work bounded by a revision cycle, not by seconds: a new specification revision arrives, the agent reads it,
and an engineer confirms each extracted requirement before it is used, which means the loop is
measured in working sessions rather than round trips. The interactive surface is the natural language
interface, where the verification lead asks a question and expects an answer with citations; because GLM
5.3, BGE-M3 and the object model all sit on the same premises network, that answer makes no external
hop, and its latency is owned entirely by the company's own room. Retrieval and embedding are the only
sub-second commitments, and they run beside the serving node precisely so that they never become the
bottleneck in front of it.

7.3 The Boundary and Its Failures

Nothing crosses the network boundary outward in any direction: designs, specifications and models stay
in the operator's environment on the company's own hardware, and there is no third party model service
to leak toward. That constraint is not paranoia but arithmetic of consequence, because design data is the
company's core intellectual property and the industry's record shows what its loss costs: a Taiwanese
court fined a foundry operator tens of millions of dollars over employees who stole memory-maker trade
secrets (Bloomberg 2020), the same operator paid a 60 million dollar fine in the United States for the theft
(Reuters 2020), and final sentences were upheld for former employees of another chipmaker in a
separate leak case (Focustaiwan 2026). Research security guidance under the United States CHIPS
program treats exactly this class of information as requiring protection controls (NIST 2024). Inbound, the
only door is the artifact and model registry, Harbor with its offline installer, which governs what comes in;
updates arrive as artifacts through that registry and never as live pulls from outside.

Each failure path has a named answer. If the link fails, nothing stops, because nothing depends on an
external link: the site is the perimeter, and the event backbone's own sequencing carries on locally. If
power fails, the roughly ten kilowatt node is the exposure, which is why it is an open question for the
facilities team and why the platform runs on existing company hardware until the node is in place. If the
update path fails, the registry holds the last good artifact set and the system keeps serving what it already
holds, with no silent substitution of a smaller GPU class while the BIS determination is pending.

Confirm every requirement before it is used. The spec agent is the entry point for everything
downstream, and the engineer who confirms each extraction is the control that keeps a misread from

citations keeps that authority earned.

APPENDIX A

What the Company's Own Inference Node Costs
Over Three Years
The paper is written for a fabless chip design company in Saudi Arabia, with one design office and the
company's own server room on its own premises (chapter 1, section 1.3). This appendix therefore
prices for Saudi Arabia, with the Saudi Electricity Company commercial tariff for power and the AWS
Middle East (UAE) region, me-central-1, as the rental reference. The design runs every model on
hardware the company owns, and its central tier is "one node of eight GPUs of the 141 GB HBM class"
serving GLM 5.3 on vLLM (chapter 7, section 7.1; Table 4, "GPU class"). The two other models need
no further hardware line: BGE-M3 runs "on CPU or a modest GPU inside the perimeter" at about 1.1
GB, and PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 runs at roughly 1.9 GB "on a site GPU" (Table 4; chapter 8, section 8.1);
the paper gives no count for that site GPU, and together the two models are about 3 GB, which the
node's own headroom or the company's existing hardware holds, so nothing is added for them rather
than a card guessed. The node is priced two ways: owned, from a reseller's published configured price
with support and power added, and rented, from the AWS price files for the nearest region that offers
the same card, on demand and on the two three year all upfront plans. Every input is dated and cited,
and the arithmetic is shown.

A.1 The Answer
Owning the node for three years costs about 569,000 US dollars, inside a range of 541,000 to
594,000. Renting the same eight H200 cards around the clock costs about 751,000 dollars on the
deepest three year commitment (an AWS EC2 Instance Savings Plan, all upfront, for p5en.48xlarge in
Middle East (UAE)), about 1.33 million dollars on the three year Compute Savings Plan, all upfront,
and about 2.00 million dollars on demand. Against the deepest commitment, ownership costs about
three quarters (569,203 / 750,535 = 0.76, and 0.72 to 0.79 across the range); against on demand, a
little over a quarter (569,203 / 1,996,103 = 0.29). No rented option can sit inside the Kingdom today:
AWS's Saudi region is scheduled to open by December 2026 (W.Media 2026) and its price files list no
Saudi region on the day read (AWS 2026a), and every rented option would carry specifications,
requirements and design records across the border, which the company's own constraint of no third
party model service and nothing crossing the boundary rules out (chapter 3; Table 2; Table 4,
"Ground"). Renting is therefore a price reference only. GLM 5.3 carries a bespoke license whose terms,
in the paper's words, "allow commercial use, fine tuning and redistribution" (chapter 8, section 8.1); no
price is asserted for it here. BGE-M3 (MIT) and PaddleOCR-VL 1.6 (Apache-2.0) carry no license line
(Table 4).

Why this hardware: the paper's sizing line is explicit, "753 GB of weights times the 1.2 planning factor is
904 GB against the node's 1,128 GB" (Table 4, "Frontier footprint sizing rule"), and Table 4 fixes the
class as "141 GB HBM class, one node of eight GPUs" (Table 4, "GPU class"), sized "from the model's

eight H200 cards carry the same 1,128 GB (AWS 2026c).
Two inconsistencies in the paper's own numbers, neither of which changes the node count or the price.
First, the weights are 753 GB in chapter 4, chapter 7 and Table 4, but "about 756 GB of weights at FP8
as published" in chapter 8, section 8.1 and "~756 GB" in chapter 11 (Table 6); this appendix uses Table

reserve, while 1,128 less 904 is 224 GB, and chapter 4 and chapter 11 give "375 GB beside the

A.3 What the Price Does Not Include
• An export license determination, which is a checkpoint, not a price. The paper names the node
  a 4A090 item for a D:4 destination and makes the BIS license determination a phase one checkpoint
  before any class is quoted (chapter 7, section 7.1; Table 4). Saudi Arabia sits in Country Groups D:3
  and D:4 (eCFR 2026a), and 15 CFR 742.6(a)(6)(iii), as it reads on the day, carries a license
  requirement for 4A090.a items (eCFR 2026b). The order date for the node is therefore set by that
  determination, and until it lands the platform runs on the company's existing hardware (chapter 7,
  section 7.1), which this appendix does not price.
• Everything the paper's scope boundary keeps out: design execution, EDA and foundry licenses,
  any hosted model service, training and historic migration (Table 2, "Scope boundary"). The vendor
  design tool suites, the simulation and formal tools and the foundry relationship are the company's
  own and carry no line here.
• The facilities work behind the ten kilowatts. The paper leaves the load, cooling and power path to
  the company's facilities team as an open question (chapter 7, sections 7.1 and 7.3; chapter 9,
  section 9.5); any electrical or cooling upgrade to the server room is sold by quotation once that
  question is settled.
• The servers for the rest of the stack: the event backbone, the object model store, the observability
  stack and the air gapped Harbor registry are chosen by class and not sized in the paper (chapter 4;
  chapter 7, section 7.3).
• People: the engineers who build and run the platform, the design engineers who confirm each
  extraction and the verification lead who approves each check, whom every option carries.
• Customs duty, 15 percent VAT, freight and installation on the hardware, which a written quote
  delivered to the Kingdom settles, and residual value at the end of three years.
• Double counted cover. The configured price already carries a three year depot warranty, so the
  support line may count some cover twice.
• A closed model token comparison, which is not printed because the paper states no token volume
  for the work surface.

title: Sovereign AI Architecture for a Grid Control Room in Saudi Arabia
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · ENERGY & UTILITIES · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

Sovereign AI Architecture for a Grid
Control Room in Saudi Arabia
Energy & Utilities Watch: One Living Picture of the Operation

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the leaders accountable for energy & utilities operations, their supervisors, and the data and platform engineers
who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

The Answer Already Exists in the Systems the Operation
Runs
A sovereign AI architecture for the control room of a national grid operator in Saudi Arabia: a knowledge
system on one governed ontology of substations, busbars, lines, transformers, breakers, protection
relays, alarms, events, switching programs, planned outages, procedures, shift logs, connected
customers and weather cells, each fact tied to its source system.

The design reads 10 source systems through 3 adapter families into one object model of 16 objects, runs
8 services over it and opens 4 surfaces to the people who decide, with 2 models placed where the data
is. A sovereign system of context for one regional control center: a governed grid ontology built from the
network model and the systems of record behind a one-way replicated boundary, four drafting agents for
alarm triage, switching programs, handover and the sequence of events, whose drafts control engineers
and supervisors confirm and approve, GLM 5.3 self hosted on one 141 GB class node in the operator's
own Kingdom data center, and a summer trial gated on frozen baselines from trip to first correct action.
Nothing is trained into weights, no control command is ever sent, and every fact, draft and approval
traces to its source system and a named person.

The paper covers the operation and the problem its systems cannot answer, the constraints, the stack,
the object model, ingestion, inference placement, the models and their licenses, the rollout and its proof,
ownership, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.

     Figure 1. Energy & Utilities Watch on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it
                                         computes, and the person who decides.

Contents
Each chapter is tagged for the reader it serves most directly: Executive, Team Lead, FDE, Reference.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

A Daily Question Goes Unanswered in the Systems That
Hold the Data

The operation holds every fact the question needs and no system answers it.

The abstract promised a sovereign AI architecture that turns data an operation already holds into answers
a named person can act on. This chapter states the question that system exists to answer, what
answering it costs today, and the operation that will live with it.

1.1 The Question, the Data It Requires and the Regimes It Must Satisfy

Every shift in a transmission control room asks one question in a hundred forms: what just happened on
the grid, what does it affect, and what must be done next within the rules. At its sharpest, when one 380
kilovolt line trips at summer peak, the question becomes a list with a clock on it: which protection operated
and in what order, which busbars and connected operators now sit de-energized, what maintenance is
already in progress on the affected apparatus, which procedure governs the switching that follows, and
who must approve each step. The data that answers it all exists: alarms, events and telemetry from the
SCADA and energy management systems, topology from the network model, outage windows from the
outage management system, load behind busbars from meter data, asset condition, relay settings, the
procedure library in Arabic and English, weather forecasts tied to the lines, the shift log, and the
contracted sensitivity of every connected operator. The regimes it must satisfy are just as fixed: the
operator's own rule that the operational network stays separated from everything else, national
cybersecurity and communications controls that grade that network into segmentation zones, the grid

code that governs outage planning, and a clear direction of international regulatory travel, from safety and
security guidance for AI in critical infrastructure (DHS 2024) to an initial risk assessment of AI in energy
infrastructure (Energy 2024) and a regulatory inquiry into utility AI use that begins by inventorying use
cases and internal controls (NY 2026).

1.2 The Documented Cost of the Problem

Today the list is assembled by hand, and the industry has documented what that costs. An independent
review of AI use in electricity networks, published by the UK government, was commissioned precisely
because networks were adopting AI in fragments, without a joined view of risk and benefit across their
operational systems (Service 2026). Researchers at a major energy company go further and argue that
introducing AI into major accident hazard operations without a systemic safety risk assessment creates
new accident risk rather than reducing it, because knowledge that lives in separate systems cannot be
reasoned over safely (DOI 2025). At the console the cost is concrete rather than abstract: minutes spent
finding what a joined query would return in seconds, adjacent work discovered by phone after switching
has begun, and a connected operator's interruption sensitivity learned only when that operator calls.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The scenario is a national grid operator in Saudi Arabia that runs the electricity transmission grid: the
substations, busbars, lines, transformers and breakers that carry bulk power across the Kingdom,
operated from control rooms at regional and national level. The first phase covers one regional control
center for one summer, the season when peak load and peak heat coincide and the proving event, one
380 kilovolt line tripping at summer peak, is a realistic day rather than a worst case. Four roles are in the
loop by name: the control engineer who confirms alarm triage, the shift supervisor who approves
switching drafts, the incoming supervisor who approves the handover, and the protection engineer who
receives the event analysis. The physical environment is the control center itself, a conditioned room
watching remote substations and corridors, and the regulatory ground is national cybersecurity and
communications controls together with the grid code. The design names ten source systems, three
adapter families, sixteen ontology objects, eight services, four surfaces, two models and four drafting
agents, arranged in three phases carrying eighteen items, every figure traceable to its source or marked
as an assumption.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System Sees One Slice of the Operation

Each system of record sees its own part of the answer and none sees the whole.

Chapter 1 named the question and every piece of data it requires. This chapter shows where that data
lives today and why no system of record can assemble the answer alone.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The SCADA and energy management systems are the backbone: they see every alarm, every event, the
telemetry stream and the network model that describes how substations, busbars, lines and breakers
connect, and they miss everything written down elsewhere, from procedure text and outage plans to
asset history and operator contracts. The outage management system sees planned outage windows, the
apparatus involved and the requesting parties, and misses the live state of the grid those windows sit
inside. The meter data management system sees load behind busbars and what connected operators
actually drew, and misses the topology that would explain it, along with alarms, procedures and outage
plans. The asset and maintenance system sees the condition of every substation, line, transformer and
breaker, and the maintenance already in progress nearby, and misses the grid as it stands right now. The
protection settings databases see relay models, settings revisions and the elements each relay protects,
and miss the operational context that would make a settings change meaningful. The procedure library
sees the operating procedures and switching instructions, in Arabic and English with their revisions, and
misses the state of the equipment they govern. Weather services see forecasts of temperature, wind and
dust tied to lines and load at summer peak, and miss anything operational at all.

2.2 What None of Them Sees Together

The trip question crosses every one of these systems at once: the alarm and its sequence of events
come from SCADA and EMS, the affected apparatus and its maintenance state from the asset system,
the relay behavior from the protection databases, the restoration steps from the procedure library, the
outage window from the outage plan, the load at risk from meter data, the thermal context from weather,
and the sensitivity of who sits behind the busbar from the connection records. Figure 2 sets these views
side by side and shows them converging on a question none can answer alone. In practice the control
engineer is the join, working from memory, phone calls and window switching while an alarm flood is still
arriving at summer peak; the handover is only as good as what the outgoing shift can recall; and the
event analysis waits until the protection engineer can gather the pieces by hand. The cost is the minutes
between the trip and the first correct action, and the adjacent work found too late.

    Figure 2. Seven systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Four Constraints Shape Everything Downstream

The goals, the scoping decisions and the exclusions were fixed before any component was
chosen.

Chapter 2 showed that the join failure, not any single system, is the problem. This chapter fixes the goals
and exclusions that every component choice in Part II had to satisfy, and records what was weighed and
set aside.

3.1 Inference Stays Sovereign

The first goal is that every token of reasoning runs on the operator's own hardware, in the operator's own
data center in the Kingdom, on open weights the operator can hold. This is hard in this industry because
the easy path is a managed service, and a managed service puts grid data and grid reasoning outside the
boundary the operator is required to keep. The design therefore places all inference centrally: no edge
compute, no field site serving, one frontier class model, GLM 5.3 at 753 billion parameters, served at FP8
precision where its weights occupy 753 gigabytes, held on a single node of eight GPUs of the 141
gigabyte class with the remainder left for the key value cache and activations.

3.2 The Boundary Is One Way and Read Only

The second goal is that the platform never sends a control command and never writes into a system of
record. SCADA and EMS networks are safety segregated, and the operational technology segmentation
zones, OTCC 2 to 4, together with the operator's own rule that the operational network stays separated,
make any direct platform path into the control network a compliance breach rather than a shortcut. The
design reads through a replicated historian or demilitarized zone feed into a separate AI platform zone,
and a hardware-enforced data diode remains the committed fallback where the segmentation review
demands demonstrably one-way flow, with forward error correction sized to the link because nothing can
be resent.

3.3 Every Decision Has a Named Owner

The third goal is that agents draft and people decide, always by name. The alarm triage agent's ranking is
confirmed by the control engineer, the switching draft by the shift supervisor, the handover by the
incoming supervisor, and the event analysis is prepared for the protection engineer. This is hard in a
control room because the temptation under pressure is to trust whichever answer arrives first, so the
design makes the approval a first-class object with its own status vocabulary, and keeps an immutable
record of every confirmed decision, which is also what regulators inventorying use cases and internal
controls expect to find (NY 2026).

3.4 The System Improves Without Training

The fourth goal is that memory improves every shift without training a model. Nothing is fine tuned,
trained or distilled into weights: agents improve through memory loops over confirmed decisions and
event analyzes, each run reading what was decided before it acts. This is hard because fine tuning is the
industry's reflex answer to improvement, but a moving model would invalidate the frozen baselines the
summer trial is gated on, and the license terms that let the operator hold its weights carry conditions that
a training pipeline would put under new scrutiny.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From the Systems of Record to the
Surfaces

Systems of record below, one object model in the middle, services and surfaces above.

Chapter 3 fixed the four constraints that shape everything downstream: data and weights stay inside the
operator's boundary, no control command is ever sent, every draft is confirmed or approved by a named
person, and a first gate can stop the work cheaply. This chapter lays out the stack that satisfies those
constraints, stage by stage.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

The design uses the layered shape that a sovereign AI architecture in critical infrastructure converges on:
systems of record below, one object model in the middle, applications and agents above. Below sit the
ten read-only sources the control room already trusts, among them SCADA and EMS, the outage
management system, the asset and maintenance system, the protection settings databases, the
procedures library and weather services. In the middle sits the grid ontology, sixteen objects joined by
typed links and seeded by the CIM export from the EMS network model rather than assembled from
documents. Above sit the eight services and four surfaces where the agents draft and the control
engineers and shift supervisors decide.

The pattern fits because the control room's real problem is a join problem. When one 380 kilovolt line trips
at summer peak, the question that matters spans the alarms, the network model, the outage plan, the
protection record and the procedures library, and no single system of record holds that join. The pattern
also fits the regulatory ground: safety and security guidance for critical infrastructure treats AI risk as
something to govern before use (DHS 2024), and an independent review of AI in electricity networks
found the binding constraint to be trustworthy data foundations under operator control (Service 2026).

4.4 A Reusable Pattern

The reusable shape is the whole vertical slice: a replicated, read-only boundary out of the operational
network; an adapter tier that owns every contract; one governed object model that joins the records;
drafting agents that propose and named people who dispose; and weights the operator holds in its own
data center. A team carrying a similar brief swaps the source systems, the object set and the model sized
to its own budget, and keeps the rest unchanged, because the parts worth keeping are the ones that
make a system safe to stand next to a control room: no write path into the systems of record, adapters
owning contracts, and every decision tracing to a person.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Sixteen Objects Turn Operational Data Into One
Argument

The object model is the join the systems never made.

Chapter 4 showed the stack's layers and what each is responsible for. This chapter opens the middle
layer, where the design's whole claim rests: sixteen objects, joined by typed links, that turn the systems'
separate records into one argument.

5.1 Sixteen Objects and the Links Between Them

The model holds sixteen objects in five kinds. Sites and assets: the Substation, the Transmission Line,
the Busbar, the transformer, the breaker and the relay, each anchored in the network model or the asset
system and each carrying the properties its system of record already holds, from thermal rating to settings
revision. Events: the Alarm, anchored in SCADA, and the Grid Event, anchored in EMS. Records: the
switching program, the Planned Outage and the shift log. Documents: the Operating Procedure, anchored
in the procedures library. Measures and people: the weather cell, the Connected Operator, the Control
Engineer and the Shift Supervisor.

The typed links are what make this more than a list. When the 380 kilovolt line trips, the triage reasoning
starts at the alarm, reaches the line it references, the substations at both ends, the busbars behind them,
the operators whose supply runs through those busbars, the relays that protect the line with their settings
revisions, the procedures that govern restoring it, and the shift logs where the last comparable event was
handled. A document store holds all of those facts as text and cannot walk them; the object model walks
them in one traversal, which is the difference between a search result and an argument. Figure 4 shows
every object and its typed links, with the alarm at the focal center, and Table 8 records, for every object,

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in the status vocabularies and the links to people. An alarm moves from Raised to
Acknowledged only under the control engineer's confirmation; a switching program moves from Drafted to
Approved only under the shift supervisor; a shift log is approved by the incoming supervisor, not the
outgoing one. Regulators are moving toward exactly this discipline, inventorying utility AI use cases and
their internal controls (NY 2026), and sector guidance on ethical AI treats named human accountability as
a condition of use, not a courtesy (OFGEM 2026).

The hosting posture follows the same line. Everything runs in the operator's own data center in the
Kingdom: the ontology, the memory, the weights and the surfaces. Identity is issued inside the boundary,
so no decision is attributable to an account the operator does not control. The one external input, weather
services, enters through the integration adapter as data on a schedule, never as a live call the model
makes on its own. The single write path anywhere in the design is the recorded confirmation or approval,
written into the object model and the memory service, and never into any system of record.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Nothing reaches the object model except through an adapter that owns its contract.

Chapter 5 described what the object model holds. This chapter describes how data gets into it: through
three adapter families and an event backbone, and by no other route.

6.1 Every Source and Its Provenance Class

Ten sources feed the platform, all read-only, all of operator provenance, meaning every fact they
contribute carries the name of the system it came from. SCADA and EMS is the backbone: alarms,
events, telemetry and the network model that seeds the ontology's topology, read through the replicated
boundary and never commanded. The outage management system supplies the planned outage requests
that trigger the switching program agent and the live outage plan its adjacent work checks read. Meter
data management contextualises load behind busbars and connected operators, and joins during the
summer under the phasing the intake set. The asset and maintenance system gives every substation,
line, transformer and breaker its asset context, including the maintenance already in progress nearby that
a switching draft must respect. Protection settings databases supply the relay context the event analysis
agent reasons from. The procedures library is the corpus every answer and every switching draft must
cite, in Arabic and English. Weather services tie forecast cells to lines and load at summer peak. The
remaining sources enter on the same contracts as the phasing allows. Figure 5 shows each named
system, its provenance class and its adapter path into the object model.

       Figure 5. The 10 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

Three adapter families own every contract. The telemetry adapter carries the replicated SCADA and EMS
series into the time series store. The integration adapter carries documents and records: outage plans,
protection settings, procedures, weather. The ERP adapter carries asset, maintenance and meter data
from the operator's enterprise systems. Together the tier guarantees four things. Schema and unit
checking, so alert logic lands on curated, unit-checked series rather than raw tags. One-way flow, so no
path exists from the platform back into the operational network. Provenance stamped on every fact at the
moment it lands, so any answer can be traced to its source system. Citation resolution and freshness
checks on every answer, so a draft that cites a superseded procedure or a stale feed is caught before a
person reads it. This discipline is the operational answer to the risk picture the US Department of Energy
drew in its initial assessment of AI in critical energy infrastructure (Energy 2024): the guardrail is
architectural, not procedural.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka carries everything between the adapters and the platform. Ordering is per partition, keyed
by point or asset, so any one telemetry point's series arrives in order even when the flood is wide.
Delivery is at least once with idempotent writes into the time series store, so a replayed record cannot
double count an alarm or an event. Buffering absorbs alarm floods, which arrive in bursts, and lets the
platform drain at its own pace rather than at the SCADA scan rate. Replication runs inside the platform
zone, so the loss of a broker node costs availability, not data. The retained log is also the replay
mechanism: the pre-summer phase validates the triage agent on the operators' own recorded floods by
feeding them back through the same backbone. Time is held by linuxptp with chrony, disciplined by a
GNSS PTP grandmaster with holdover, so alarms, events and telemetry from different systems can be

placed in one sequence of events, which is the evidence the event analysis agent drafts from and the
protection engineer reviews.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Inference Belongs Where the Data Is

Each tier runs what its data and its link can carry.

Chapter 6 followed every source through its adapter into the event backbone inside the AI platform zone.
This chapter decides where the models that read that backbone run, what each tier must hold in memory,
and what the placement owes the control room when the link, the power or the update path fails.

7.1 Two Central Tiers and a Deliberately Empty Edge

The design has two inference tiers and both are central: a frontier tier that carries GLM 5.3 for all four
drafting agents, the command center surface and ontology maintenance, and an embedding tier that
carries BGE-M3 for retrieval over procedures, records and past event analyzes. Both run in the operator's
own data center in the Kingdom, on the operator's own hardware. The absent edge tier is a decision
rather than an omission: the platform consumes replicated data instead of serving models at field sites,
and fast protection and dispatch decisions stay in the relays and remote terminal units where they have
always lived.

The memory arithmetic fixes the frontier tier. GLM 5.3 is filed at 753 billion parameters, and at FP8
precision one byte per parameter gives 753 GB of weights; multiplying by the 1.2 planning factor for KV
cache and activations gives 904 GB the GPUs must hold. One node of eight GPUs of the 141 GB class
gives 1,128 GB, which carries the weights with 375 GB left beside them, well above the 151 GB the
planning factor reserves. That spare capacity is the KV cache ceiling, the memory that holds each in-flight
request's context, and it is what buys concurrent served requests during an alarm flood. The embedding
tier is small by comparison: BGE-M3 at FP16 is about 1.1 GB of weights, running on the platform zone's
dual-socket x86 rack server class beside the ontology, streaming and retrieval services. Figure 6 sets the
two tiers side by side, with what runs on each and what crosses into them.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget is built on the control room's own rhythm rather than a single number, because the human
terms dominate it. In order, the terms are replication lag across the one-way boundary, then retrieval, then
generation, then the named person's confirmation. Replication lag bounds the alarm triage agent, which
must rank a flood while the flood is still unfolding, and the embedding tier's small footprint keeps the
retrieval term short. Generation is the longest machine term, and the design spends it where the work
tolerates it: an event analysis draft for the protection engineer can take the time a careful engineer would
take, and a handover draft is bounded by the end of shift window rather than by seconds. Stated as an
ordering, nothing the machine does may outrun the freshness of the replicated stream, and nothing the
machine does substitutes for the confirmation that closes the loop.

7.3 What Crosses the Boundary, and What Happens When It Fails

Everything that crosses the network boundary crosses in one direction: replicated SCADA telemetry and
alarms, EMS events and the network model, outage plans, asset and protection records, the procedure
library, meter data and weather forecasts flow into the AI platform zone, and nothing flows back. No agent
sends a control command, no agent issues a switching instruction without a named approval, and the
platform holds no write path of any kind into SCADA or EMS. The advisory placement is also the safety
argument: guidance for critical infrastructure owners treats an AI system that can act on physical plant as
a materially different risk from one that advises a named person (DHS 2024), and work on major accident
risk argues that AI placed inside safety-critical loops demands systemic assessment the advisory
placement avoids (DOI 2025).

Failure is designed for rather than hoped away. If the link fails, platform heartbeat and data freshness
signals mark every surface stale, and the control room keeps operating on SCADA and EMS directly

because the platform was never in the control path; the degraded-mode procedure is written down and
rehearsed before summer go-live. If power fails, the conditioned data center room restarts the services
and the event backbone replays what was buffered, so the platform resynchronizes rather than loses the
record. If the update path fails, models and artifacts move through the Harbor registry as staged, signed
images, and the platform keeps serving the last verified version until the path returns. A named owner
watches these signals, because the US Department of Energy's initial risk assessment on AI in critical
energy infrastructure stresses governance and accountability from the start rather than after an incident
(Energy 2024).

Every model was chosen against its license before its accuracy.

Chapter 7 fixed where inference runs and what each tier holds in memory. This chapter fixes which
models run there, and on what terms the operator can hold them, because the license decides the
ownership before the benchmark decides the accuracy. Figure 7 opens the chapter: the model stack, with

8.1 GLM 5.3 on Terms That Let the Operator Hold Its Weights

GLM 5.3 is the register's frontier model, filed at 753 billion parameters, with about 756 GB of weights at
FP8 as published and roughly 1.5 TB at BF16; the design serves it at FP8 on one node of eight 141 GB
class GPUs in the operator's own Kingdom data center. Its role spans the agentic work surface, ontology
maintenance and all four drafting agents: alarm triage on a flood, the switching draft on a planned outage
request, the handover draft at end of shift and the event analysis draft on a protection trip. Its license is
the GLM-5.3 bespoke license: commercial use, fine tuning and redistribution are allowed, with an
attribution notice to carry and a trigger that applies only where a group's revenue rises above 10 billion

US dollars from managed access services. Internal control-room use does not reach that trigger, and
procurement reads the license and confirms the group position in writing before contract. The model was
chosen first because it is the one frontier-class model in the register, and second because its license lets
the operator hold the weights itself; the design trains nothing into weights, so the fine-tuning right matters
as ownership rather than as a training plan. That ownership is what regulators are beginning to ask about:
one state commission has opened an inquiry into how utilities use AI, starting from an inventory of use
cases and internal controls (NY 2026), and the British energy regulator's guidance on ethical AI in the
sector asks operators to account for the systems that shape their decisions (OFGEM 2026). A stack
whose weights, memory and decision record sit inside the operator's boundary answers those questions
in one place.

8.2 BGE-M3 Under MIT for Arabic and English Retrieval

BGE-M3 is the register's embedding model, a multilingual retrieval model that indexes the procedure
library, switching instructions, records and past event analyzes in Arabic and English. Its footprint is about
2.27 GB at float32, about 1.1 GB at FP16 and about 0.6 GB at 8 bit; the design serves it at FP16 on the
platform zone's rack server class, where its retrieval latency sits inside the fast path of the budget Chapter
7 set out. Its MIT license lets the operator hold, run and redistribute it without obligation, which is why it
was chosen against the license before its accuracy was weighed. Its accuracy is still proven before trust:
retrieval recall over the operator's own Arabic procedures is evaluated as part of the frozen evaluation set
before summer go-live, because a cited answer that misses the right procedure is worse than no answer
at all.

The rollout carries 18 items across three phases, and requirement coverage stands at one requirement

workstreams and the gates between them. Phase one, the pre-summer build and replay, carries 15 items
across six workstreams: the grid ontology, boundary and integration, memory and retrieval, the agents
that draft, governance and approvals, and the sovereign platform. Its items include the ontology built from
the systems of record, the one-way boundary from the operational network, and telemetry ingestion on
curated series. Its exit gate is the switching program drafting agent, the workflow that chains a planned
outage request through topology, procedure citation, adjacent-work checks and supervisor approval end
to end on replayed records, before anything runs live. Phase two, summer live at one regional control
center, carries 2 items across boundary and integration and the summer trial: the phased integration of
the remaining source systems during the season, and live operation at one regional control center
through one summer. Phase three, extension to every control center, carries a single item, the extension
gates that decide whether the design spreads beyond the first center. No phase carries a duration; each
closes on evidence, not on a calendar.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

Every baseline is frozen before go-live, and the headline measure is the interval from trip to first correct
action, exercised against the design's simulated event: one 380 kilovolt transmission line tripping at
summer peak. Around the alarm triage agent the rollout measures alerts surfaced per shift against the
alert budget, confirmation time in the triage queue, and how often engineers take the disagreement path
rather than confirming a ranking they doubt. Around the drafting agents it measures citation resolution on
every answer, retrieval recall over the operator's own Arabic procedures, and adoption as a gate in its
own right: the share of drafts confirmed unchanged against the share edited or rejected. Replay validation
runs on the operators' own recorded alarm floods before go-live, so the first live flood is not the first test.
Platform heartbeat and data freshness signals run throughout. The measurement-first posture follows
published guidance for this infrastructure class: safety and security guidelines for owners and operators
(DHS 2024), an initial risk assessment on AI in critical energy infrastructure (Energy 2024), and an
independent review of AI use in electricity networks that asks for evidence before scale (Service 2026).

9.4 Lessons

Shadow the flags before anyone trusts them. The triage agent earns its place on replayed alarm
floods from the operator's own historians before any live shift sees a ranking, and adoption is measured
as a gate in its own right. Work on systemic safety risk argues that new failure paths appear at the joins
between human and machine judgement (DOI 2025), and replay is how those joins are inspected before
the summer rather than during it.

Ask the license question once, early. The sizing holds at one node of the 141 GB class precisely so the
export license determination is asked once, naming this end user, before the order is placed; a two-node
answer would ask the same question twice and double the exposure to timelines nobody controls.

Make disagreement faster than agreement. If disputing a doubtful ranking takes longer than confirming
it, engineers will confirm, and the summer will measure politeness instead of accuracy; the disagreement
path is therefore a first-class control whose usage is counted alongside confirmation time.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Four questions remain open, and settling each changes a parts list or a gate. Which self hosted time
series store carries the replicated SCADA and EMS series is chosen at design against the historian's
export format and scan rate, and settling it fixes the telemetry tier. Whether the segmentation review
demands the hardware diode in place of the replicated feed decides the boundary's components and its
forward error correction budget. Whether Arabic retrieval meets the recall bar on the operator's own
procedures decides whether the human check stage stays a permanent cost on every switching draft.
Whether feeder risk ranking and outage prediction clear the summer evidence decides the shape of the
extension gates in phase three.

The Intelligence Should Stay with the Operation That

What the design builds belongs to the operator.

Chapter 9 showed the gates at which the rollout earns each phase. This chapter states who holds what

10.1 What the Operator Owns

The object model is the operator's. Its 16 objects and typed links are a projection over the operator's own
systems of record, never a migration or a shadow copy that competes with them, and the vocabulary,
property lists and status sets are the operator's people's to extend and govern. The weights are the
operator's. GLM 5.3 runs self hosted on one 141 GB class node in the operator's own data center in the
Kingdom, under a license that allows commercial use, fine tuning and redistribution; the operator may
hold, patch and resynchronize the weights without asking anyone's permission, subject to the attribution
notice and the managed-service trigger above 10 billion US dollars of group revenue, which internal
control-room use does not touch. No fine-tune exists by design: memory improves every shift without
training a model, so there is no forked weight set to reconcile at any future date. The decision record is
the operator's. Every confirmed decision, draft and approval traces to its source system and a named
person, and the record is kept as memory the next decision reads; it is the operation's own history, not a
corpus held elsewhere. The boundary is the operator's. The one-way replicated path from the operational
network into the platform zone, with the hardware diode as the committed fallback where the
segmentation review demands demonstrable one-way flow, is a control the operator owns and can

demonstrate to its regulator. The design sits squarely in the family of sovereign AI reference architectures:
intelligence that stays inside the boundary of the operation that produced it.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja builds this shape as its offer. Adaptive Operations covers the sensing and detection of physical
behavior over the replicated telemetry streams and curated series; Decision Systems covers the rankings,
attributions and drafts that a named person decides; Hyper Ontology holds the governed object model
this design is built on; Hyper Pragma is the command center and the cited Arabic and English
conversational interface, the surface where the operator's people build and run their own agents; Hyper
Engram keeps the record of decisions and outcomes that each run reads before it acts; Sovereign
Infrastructure covers own hardware, open-weight licenses and in-country operation in the operator's own
Kingdom data center; and the design itself was produced on Praxis, the platform for designing physical AI
systems.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Four patterns were adopted. The CIM import from the network model seeds the ontology's topology rather
than assembling it from records; the replicated historian feed replaces any direct platform path into the
control network; memory loops replace fine tuning, because the ask itself demanded improvement without
training; and core sources first, with meter, asset and protection phased in during the season, protects the
summer window. Four were set aside with reasons. Two nodes of the 80 GB class were rejected because
they add an RDMA fabric to a footprint one 141 GB class node already holds; direct read-only links inside
the operational network were rejected as a compliance breach rather than a shortcut; fine tuning GLM 5.3

title: Physical AI System Design for Wafer Defect Inspection in the United States
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · SEMICONDUCTORS · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

Physical AI System Design for Wafer
Defect Inspection in the United States
Fab Defect Watch: Ontologies for Semiconductor Defect Classification at the Edge

Inside a high volume United States wafer fab, this system classifies defect images on sealed
edge units at the inspection tools, joins them to lots, tools and chambers in one governed fab
ontology, and drafts classifications, holds and dispositions that named engineers confirm and
approve.

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For fab yield directors, defect review engineers and yield engineers, and the data, platform and equipment engineers
who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

Ontologies for Semiconductor Defect Classification
Decide Yield
When a wafer map shows a ring signature, physical AI system design has to give a wafer fab in the
United States one answer: which chamber drifted, when it started, and which lots it touched before
anyone noticed. Ontologies for semiconductor defect classification are how the industry names the
missing piece, because no single system of record can walk from a defect image to a lot, a tool, a
chamber, a recipe and a control limit in one trace. The manufacturing execution system knows the lot and
the hold, the yield management system knows the signature, the inspection tools' own databases hold the
images, the equipment data collection system holds the chamber telemetry, and the statistical process
control system holds the limits, but the join that the question demands is done by engineers reading
screens, and the cost shows up as hours between excursion onset and hold.

The design runs wholly inside the fab boundary on the operator's own hardware. Sealed fanless edge
units next to the optical inspection and electron microscope review tools classify defect images as they
arrive on the CodeNinja on-device AI stack; one adapter family joins eight sources into one governed fab
ontology of sixteen objects, from wafer, lot and process step through tool, chamber, recipe, inspection
run, defect, defect class and wafer map signature to excursion, hold, corrective action and the three
approving roles; seven services and five surfaces carry three named agents, a classification agent
drafting on a review image, an excursion agent drafting a hold when a wafer map signature crosses a
control limit, and a disposition agent drafting release, rework or scrap for a held lot, each confirmed by a
defect review engineer, a yield engineer or a process owner; and the model register holds zero verified
weights, with reasoning intended for GLM 5.3 open weights self hosted inside the fab once a verified row
stands in the register.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure across five systems of record, the constraints
that sovereignty and the tools-first rule impose, the layered stack, the sixteen object model and its typed
links, ingestion through one adapter family, where inference runs and what happens when the link or the
update path fails, the honestly open model register, the two phase rollout with its item counts, gates and
the excursion to hold time it measures, who owns what the system produces, and it closes with how
Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.
