PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Ontologies for Semiconductor Defect Classification
Decide Yield

A drifting etch chamber prints its ring signature on wafer maps long before any single system
can name the chamber, the lots it touched or the hold that should follow.

The abstract promised a physical AI system design with defect images classified at the tool, one
governed model of the fab, and three named agents that draft while engineers decide. This chapter states
the question behind that promise, the documented cost of leaving it unanswered, and the operation the
design is written for.

1.1 The Question, the Data and the Regimes

Ontologies for semiconductor defect classification exist to answer one operational question: when a wafer
map signature crosses a control limit, which chamber is drifting, which lots has it touched since onset, and
what hold and disposition should follow. Ontologies for semiconductor defect classification answer it by
joining evidence the fab already holds, because the question spans five systems at once: review images
from the optical inspection and electron microscope tools, wafer maps and signatures from the yield
management system, chamber sensor traces from the equipment data collection system, control limits
from the statistical process control system, and lot genealogy from the manufacturing execution system.
The proving fault is precise: one etch chamber drifting and printing a ring signature on wafer maps, a
pattern the fab sees only after wafers have already carried it into later steps.

The answer must satisfy more than engineering. As a United States operator, the fab works under export
control law, where deemed export of fab technology and semiconductor manufacturing end-use controls
make even the nationality of a supporting engineer a compliance fact, and under the sector's own tool-
network cybersecurity and equipment communications standards, which govern how any unit is
onboarded to the tool network. Because the system advises decisions that touch product and safety, the
functional-safety treatment of AI systems (ISO 2024) and the consensus finding that machine learning
already runs across safety-critical applications (Nationalacademies 2025) set the frame for how much
autonomy is granted; where visual inspection AI serves regulated markets, its risk classification is settled
by rules of the kind the EU AI Act service desk and a 2025 compliance-pathways study describe (Europa
n.d.; KB 2025).

1.2 The Documented Cost of the Problem

The sector's record shows what failure costs. The U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board
investigated an equipment fracture and fatal hydrogen chloride release at a polysilicon producer in the
semiconductor supply chain (CSB 2020), and state regulators cited a major fab for a safety violation after
a man died on the job (ABC15 2024); both document that equipment and process failures in this industry
carry human consequences, not only yield consequences. The yield cost is quieter and compounds
hourly: between excursion onset and hold, a drifting chamber keeps printing on every wafer that passes
through it. That is why the design's headline measure is the time from excursion onset to hold, with a
nominal of four hours, breached above it, measured against etch chamber drift printing a ring signature.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is a high volume wafer fab in the United States, and phase one is confined to a single etch
module. Three roles hold the decisions, each by name: the defect review engineer confirms defect
classes on review images; the yield engineer approves holds when a wafer map signature crosses a
control limit; the process owner disposes of held lots as release, rework or scrap. The physical
environments are cleanroom bays housing the etch, inspection and review tools, review stations where
engineers read images, and an on-site server room on the fab's segmented tool network where the
reasoning model runs on the operator's own hardware, with no third party model service anywhere. The
counts are five named source systems, three named roles, one process module and one fab site, joined
through one integration adapter family into one governed object model.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every Fab System Sees One Slice of the Wafer

The manufacturing execution, yield management, defect, equipment data collection and
statistical process control systems each hold one true slice of the argument, and none of
them can join the slices without an engineer in the middle.

Chapter 1 stated the question and the scenario. This chapter shows why no single existing system can
answer it, by walking through what each of the five holds and what it cannot see.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The manufacturing execution system is the system of record for lots, routes, recipes, tool states and
holds, and every trace the design builds ends in a lot and a hold here; it knows a lot is stopped, but it
holds no defect image, no wafer map signature and no chamber telemetry, so it cannot say why anything
stopped. The yield management system holds the wafer maps, the signatures and the excursion records,
which makes it both the trigger the excursion agent listens to and the evidence store a trace reads from; it
cannot reach back through process steps to a chamber's running hours since its last maintenance. The
inspection tools' own defect databases produce the defect candidates and review images the edge units
classify, fresh evidence from the fab floor, yet around each image they hold neither the route the wafer
traveled nor the limits a signature must cross to become an excursion. The equipment data collection
system carries the chamber sensor telemetry and fault detection traces in which drift announces itself
first, but on its own a precursor cannot be tied to a lot, a wafer map or an image. The statistical process
control system holds the control limits a wafer map signature crossing triggers on and raises the flag
faithfully; it cannot trace the flag to a chamber, name the lots at risk or draft the hold that follows.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

What none of them see together is the argument itself: one chamber drifting, the lots it processed since
onset, the ring signature those lots now carry, the review images that show it, and the hold that should

follow, in one joined view. Figure 2 sets the five slices side by side and converges on that question. The
cost in practice is the engineer in the middle, because a yield engineer assembles the join by hand across
five systems while material keeps moving through the drifting chamber; the design measures that
assembly as time from excursion onset to hold, against a nominal of four hours, with the fault being etch
chamber drift printing a ring signature.

     Figure 2. Five systems, each seeing one part of the answer; the question needs all of them in one place at once.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereignty and the Tools-First Rule Shape Everything

Open weights on operator owned hardware inside the fab, tools read but never commanded,
memory instead of training, and export control screening of every supporting engineer
together fix the shape of every layer downstream.

The join failure is structural, so the constraints on any fix are structural too. This chapter states the four
goals that shape every layer downstream, then the scoping they force.

3.1 Open Weights on Hardware the Operator Owns

The first goal is sovereignty: reasoning runs on GLM 5.3 open weights, self hosted inside the fab on
hardware the operator owns, with no third party model service and no data leaving the boundary. This is
hard in semiconductors because the fab's own data is controlled technology, which makes any external
model path a compliance event rather than a procurement choice. The named model's 753 billion

parameters served at FP8 need a full node of the 141 GB HBM GPU class, eight GPUs per node, to
themselves; no language model is served at the tool, where the edge units' anomaly classifier runs on the
on-device stack's own runtime.

3.2 Tools First: Read, Never Command

The second goal is the tools-first rule: the design reads from the tool databases and never commands a
tool. This is hard because fab integration is contractual and tool by tool, negotiated over SECS/GEM,
GEM300 and EDA according to which revisions each etch-module tool implements, and because a
certified tool's state is safety-relevant. The rule runs through everything downstream: the gate for any hold
is the manufacturing execution system interface, never an agent, and a hold placed or released without a
recorded named approval is refused in code and audited per hold.

3.3 Memory Instead of Training

The third goal is memory instead of training: every confirmed class and every root cause becomes
memory the next decision reads, and nothing is trained into weights. This is hard because the sector
default is a classifier trained on labelled images, which locks the estate to one defect mix and becomes a
standing retraining burden as that mix shifts. Improvement compounds in the record rather than in the
weights, and any future trained classifier would be a different architecture, stated plainly.

3.4 Every Supporting Engineer Screened

The fourth goal is export control over people: access to fab technology by a supporting engineer who is a
non-US person can be a deemed export under section 734.13, so every supporting engineer is screened
before access is granted and the check is carried as a named approval. This is hard in an industry where
the relevant expertise is global and the technology is controlled precisely because of what it makes; it is
also the constraint most easily missed, because it binds the support team rather than the software.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

These goals force scope, and Table 1 records the three decisions that buy the phase one gate. Published
examples of physical AI system design that travel across sectors trade fab specific keys for reusability, so
this design scopes its model to the fab's own sixteen objects and proves the joins on one real week of
production data before phase one is judged, recording where the truth actually lives in each source.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From Records to Surfaces

Systems of record sit below untouched, one governed object model sits in the middle as a
projection over them, and the edge tier, the agents and the work surfaces sit above, each
with a named responsibility.

Chapter 3 set the four constraints and recorded what the design chose against. This chapter turns those
constraints into a stack: one fixed order of layers, from the fab's systems of record up to the surfaces
where engineers decide.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits This Fab

The architecture is a projection, not a replacement. The fab's systems of record sit below, untouched:
never replaced, never modified, never loaded, because fab integration is contractual and tool by tool over
SECS/GEM, GEM300 and EDA interfaces, and because onboarding anything onto the tool network is
governed by SEMI E187 and E188 network security standards. One governed object model sits in the
middle, a projection over those systems that joins their records without copying their truth. Above it sit the
edge units at the inspection and review tools, the three named agents, and the five work surfaces where
the defect review engineer, the yield engineer and the process owner decide.

This order fits because the fab's hardest integration fact is that its records cannot be touched, and its
hardest quality fact is that every decision must resolve to a lot, a tool and a named person. A projection
answers both: the systems of record keep every fact, the object model keeps the joins, and the layers
above only read and draft. Machine learning is already running across nearly every industrial sector,
including safety critical ones (Nationalacademies 2025), but it only helps here if it sits over records that
stay authoritative. Figure 3 shows the layered stack with its counts: eight sources, one adapter family,
sixteen objects, seven services and five surfaces.

              Figure 3. The layered stack: 8 sources, 1 adapter family, 16 objects, 7 services and 5 surfaces.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The shape a team can carry to any similar brief is the projection stack: sources of record untouched
below, one governed object model projected over them in the middle, sensing and drafting agents above,
and a named human as every gate. What a team swaps is the vocabulary and the doors: the sixteen
objects become their own nouns, the SECS/GEM, GEM300 and EDA interfaces become whatever their
sector's systems speak, and the FDC traces become their own telemetry. What they keep is the grammar:
nouns become objects, facts become properties, relationships become typed links, and no agent writes to
a system of record without a recorded approval.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Sixteen Objects Turn Fab Data Into One Argument

Sixteen objects and their typed links let one query walk from a defect image to a wafer, a lot,
a tool, a chamber and a hold, a walk no document store and no single system of record can
make.

Chapter 4 fixed the layers and named the stack's components. This chapter opens the middle layer: the
sixteen objects, their typed links, and the single walk that turns a defect image into an argument about a
chamber, a lot and a hold.

5.1 Sixteen Objects and the Links Between Them

The object model holds sixteen objects in six kinds: the materials wafer and lot; the events process step,
inspection run, defect and excursion; the assets tool and chamber; the records recipe, hold and corrective
action; the measure wafer map signature; and the record defect class, alongside the three actors defect
review engineer, yield engineer and process owner. Each is anchored in the system of record that owns
its truth: the wafer, lot, process step, tool, recipe and hold in the manufacturing execution system; the
chamber in the equipment data collection system; the inspection run and defect in the inspection tools'
own defect databases; the defect class, wafer map signature, excursion and corrective action in the yield
management system. Figure 4 draws every object and its typed links, with the wafer in navy as the object
the most links reach.

The links are what a document store cannot hold. One query can start at a defect image classified as a
pattern defect, walk to the wafer it was found on, to the wafer map signature carrying a ring pattern, to the
lot that wafer belongs to, back through the inspection run to the tool and the recipe it ran, to the chamber
inside that tool whose running hours since PM and FDC trace explain the drift, to the excursion the
signature triggered, to the hold the yield engineer approved, and to the corrective action that closes it.
Table 8, printed with this chapter, lists every object with its anchor and its typed links. This is the shared
core of industrial ontology examples in manufacturing: a defect argument that reaches every system of
record without any of them being asked to join anything.

5.2 Where the Human Loop Lives and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in the actors and in the approval properties every record carries: a hold records
who raised it and who approved it, a defect records which review engineer confirmed its class, and an
attempt to place or release a hold without a recorded named approval is refused in code and audited per
hold, because the gate is the manufacturing execution system interface, never the agent. Functional
safety and AI is an active standards question (ISO 2024), and AI based visual quality inspection carries its
own classification and compliance pathways (KB 2025), which is why every drafting agent ends at a
named person rather than at an action.

The hosting posture is sovereign end to end. All data stays inside the fab on the operator's own hardware,
with no third party model service and nothing crossing the fab perimeter; identity is held in Keycloak on
site; the edge units carry no internet path; and no write path leads back toward a system of record except
an approved hold or disposition through the manufacturing execution system interface.

5.3 One Object in Its Recorded Form

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

One adapter family over SECS/GEM, GEM300 and EDA interfaces carries every record into
the event backbone, so no source system is ever loaded, modified or replaced, and no join is
trusted until it is proven on a real week of production data.

Chapter 5 showed what the object model holds and how one walk crosses its links. This chapter covers
how records reach it: through one adapter family, never directly, and never with a join trusted before it is
proven.

6.1 Eight Sources, One Door Each

Eight sources feed the design. Five are named systems of record, all of the operator's own and all read
only: the manufacturing execution system, the system of record for lots, routes, recipes, tool states and
holds, where every trace ends in a lot and a hold; the yield management system, which holds wafer
maps, signatures and excursion records; the inspection tools' own defect databases, the source of defect
candidates and review images the edge units classify; the equipment data collection system, which
carries chamber sensor telemetry and FDC traces for drift precursors and excursion tracing; and the
statistical process control system, which holds the control limits a wafer map signature crossing triggers
on. The remaining sources are the tool interfaces and telemetry streams at the edge. Figure 5 maps each
named system, its provenance class and its adapter path into the backbone.

        Figure 5. The 8 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

One adapter family, the integration adapter, carries every record in, over SECS/GEM, GEM300 and EDA
interfaces decided by which revisions each etch module tool implements. The tier guarantees four things.
First, no source is ever loaded, modified or replaced: the adapters read, and nothing is written back
toward a system of record except an approved hold or disposition through the manufacturing execution
system interface. Second, every record carries its provenance and its timestamp, so any figure on any
surface can be traced to the system that holds its truth. Third, event logs are constructed in the pipeline
layer rather than trusted as they arrive, because source systems differ in what they call an event and
when they record it. Fourth, no join is trusted until it is proven: the adapters reconcile the source keys
across the systems on one real week of production data before phase one is judged, recording where the
truth actually lives, because an ontology that joins silently wrong keys is worse than four systems that do
not join at all.

6.3 The Event Backbone

The backbone is Apache Kafka with KRaft, and it answers four questions. Ordering: events are keyed per
wafer and per tool, so inspection runs, defect candidates and telemetry replay in the sequence they
happened. Delivery: adapters are at least once and idempotent, so a replayed event cannot double count
a defect or a confirmed class. Buffering: the backbone absorbs bursts when a review tool emits images
faster than the edge tier classifies them, and the edge units buffer locally when their uplink is briefly lost.
Replication: topics are replicated across brokers so the loss of a broker does not lose records, and the
artifact registry in Harbor keeps the edge tier's software resynchronizable without any internet path. Time
alignment across sensors and systems is held by Linuxptp against an Open Time Card grandmaster class
clock, so an FDC trace, an inspection run and a wafer map signature from the same excursion share one
clock. Nothing on the backbone crosses the fab perimeter.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Classification Runs at the Tool, Reasoning Inside

The anomaly classifier runs on sealed fanless units at the inspection tools with no internet
path, while reasoning waits on verified open weights self hosted inside the fab, and the
latency budget is set by images arriving, not by users waiting.

Chapter 6 followed every record from the fab's systems of record through the adapter tier into the object
model. This chapter follows the same data one step further, to where it is computed: which model runs on
a sealed unit at the inspection tool, which runs on the operator's own servers deeper inside the fab, and
what that split costs in latency and failure exposure.

7.1 Two Tiers, Each Placed for a Reason

The design has two inference tiers, and Figure 6 sets them side by side with what runs on each and what
crosses between them. The first tier is the tool itself. Sealed fanless units beside the optical inspection
and electron microscope review tools classify defect images as they arrive, on the CodeNinja on-device
AI stack runtime, using an unsupervised anomaly model fitted on this fab's own normal images, so a class
candidate exists before any image leaves the tool bay. The unit is an octa core edge SoC class with a 6
TOPS neural processing unit, commercial grade rated 0 to 80 C, in a fanless sealed smooth-wall
cleanroom enclosure with a power over Ethernet front end, because a fan sheds and moves particles.
The arithmetic that matters at this tier is load, not weights: the NPU load figures on the on-device shelf
were measured for detectors rather than an anomaly model, so a 60 percent headroom gate governs until
the real load is measured, and a saturated unit dropping images silently is the named failure mode behind
that gate.

The second tier is inside the fab, on the operator's own servers. The stack row that names GLM 5.3 calls
it a 753-billion-parameter model at FP8 precision and node class, which is exactly why no language
model is served at the tool. What the plan holds for this tier is the class and the rule: a 141 GB high
bandwidth memory GPU class with 8 GPUs per node, and the frontier model footprint sizing rule for vLLM
and SGLang serving. What it does not hold is the split between weights, usable memory and the KV
cache ceiling, because no verified model row stands in the register; those figures are derived only when
one does, and Chapter 8 explains why none does yet.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 Latency Runs From Image Arrival to Hold Approval

The budget has two ends, and neither is a person waiting on a chat reply. At the near end, classification
sits in the arrival path: the unit must keep pace with the inspection tool's own output, and the headroom
gate exists so that bursts of arrivals never queue behind a saturated unit. At the far end sits the rollout's
own measure, time from excursion onset to hold, with a nominal of 4.0 hours and a breach above it,
exercised by the simulated event of one etch chamber drifting and printing a ring signature on wafer
maps. Everything between, from the wafer map signature crossing a control limit, through the excursion
agent tracing it to a chamber, to the yield engineer approving the hold, must fit inside that figure. The
people in the loop pace the budget and guard it at once, and that is deliberate: how inspection AI is
classified is an active regulatory question, with published analyzes of risk classification and compliance
pathways for AI-based visual quality inspection (KB 2025), so every class candidate and every hold draft
ends with a named approver rather than acting alone.

7.3 What Crosses the Boundary, and What Fails When It Does

Nothing crosses the fab perimeter. Tool-to-server flows ride internal segmented conduits under the fab's
own cybersecurity program, no edge unit gets any internet path, and the event backbone, Apache Kafka
in KRaft mode, carries class candidates, defect records, wafer map signatures and heartbeats between
the tiers, with linuxptp and an Open Time Card grandmaster class keeping event order honest across
systems. Each failure mode is bounded. If the link fails, classification continues at the tool because the
classifier is local, and queued events move when the conduit returns, while the surfaces show the gap
honestly. If power fails, the unit drops with it, since power arrives on the same Ethernet front end, and the
edge unit heartbeat puts the drop on the health surface where someone sees it. If the update path fails,
nothing is pushed from outside, because there is no outside path: artifacts and model updates move

through Harbor, the air-gapped artifact and model registry, on the internal network, and a unit that misses
an update keeps running its last verified artifact until the path returns.

8.1 An Honest Register Holds One Intention and One Fitted Model

Figure 7 lays the model stack out, and its most important feature is an absence: the register holds no

lens brought in were each verified by a person on the date the entry carries and were not rechecked live
for this build, and that outstanding verification is the gate to commit, not a matter of preference. GLM 5.3
therefore stands as a named intention. The operator's own ask names it, reasoning on GLM 5.3 open
weights, self hosted inside the fab, acquired by a commercial buyer, and the work surface commits
frontier-class open weights self hosted for sovereignty, of GLM 5.3 or Kimi class. Behind the name stand
a role and a placement: reasoning for the three named agents and for the command center's
conversational interface that answers with citations, running on the operator's own servers inside the fab,
never at the tool, never as a third party model service. Behind it do not stand a filed parameter count,
precision, license terms or context window, so the footprint is unsized and no GPU count is derived; the
stack row that calls GLM 5.3 a 753-billion-parameter FP8 node-class model is the argument for where it
sits, not a committed figure. Committing the row means a live check on this build, filed together with the
parameter count, precision and license terms, and only then does the sizing rule fix the node count, the
weights against usable memory and the KV cache ceiling.

The second model in the stack is not a language model at all. The edge tier runs an unsupervised
anomaly model fitted on this fab's own normal images, served on the CodeNinja on-device AI stack
runtime at the tool. It was chosen against a defect classifier trained on labelled images, for two reasons
the design states plainly: System of context forbids a model trained for this operator, and a trained-
classifier estate becomes a standing retraining burden. Confirmed classes and root causes become
memory instead, and no weight is ever updated by them. Assurance cannot lean on mature certification
here, because the functional safety and AI standard is a technical report (ISO 2024), so the design's own
gates carry it: the phase one bench run measures the anomaly model on the fab's own images, and no
accuracy is quotable before that run.

An empty register is not a gap in the design; it is the design holding its own rule. The operator is buying
weights it will hold, so which weights is part of what is being bought, and a row that could not survive a
live check would be a costly line in the build.

9.1 Phases, Gates and Coverage

Phase One is the etch module phase: 17 items across six workstreams, namely approvals and security,

development board against this fab's own images before any accuracy figure is quoted, and only ranges

nothing open.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

The loop is judged on one measure: time from excursion onset to hold, in hours, with a nominal of 4.0 and
a breach when the measured time rises above it. The fault that exercises the measure is the design's
simulated event, one etch chamber drifting and printing a ring signature on wafer maps. The excursion
agent must trace that signature to a chamber through the equipment data collection traces, draft a hold,
and a yield engineer must approve it before the clock stops. Baselines and counting rules are agreed
before the first model is fitted, a discipline the sector's own precedents taught, and since neither
precedent published a false-call rate, the nuisance trend surface carries ranges with conditions rather
than a single figure. Machine learning already runs across nearly every safety-critical industry, which is
why these gates are agreed in advance and judged against recorded baselines rather than after the fact
(Nationalacademies 2025), and the hold refusal rule is anchored in code in the spirit of functional safety
guidance for AI systems (ISO 2024).

9.4 Lessons

Agree the baselines and counting rules before the first model ships. The sector's precedent builds
that skipped this step spent their first measured period arguing about what counted as a defect rather
than improving the model; this plan fixes the counting rules as a gate item, so the bench run measures
against a settled definition and the false-call question is asked with the same denominators throughout.
Design drift handling in from version one. The simulated event is a chamber drifting gradually and printing
a ring signature, not a step change, so the excursion path, the chamber telemetry precursors and the hold
drafting are exercised from the first version rather than retrofitted after a first excursion is missed. Fit the
classifier on this fab's own images. The pattern the history lens surfaced is that an image model learns
the fab, not the defect: a model fitted elsewhere inherits another fab's illumination, another tool's artifacts
and another process's nuisance population. The anomaly model is therefore fitted unsupervised on this
fab's own normal images, and no edge unit holds any internet path.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Three questions remain open, and each settles into a design change. The false-call rate: neither sector
precedent published one, and settling it would let the nuisance trend surface carry a single quotable
figure instead of ranges with conditions. The model register: no open-weight model survived this run's live
checks, so the reasoning weights the operator named are not yet sized under the register; settling it fixes
the fab's inference server, its GPU count under the 141 GB HBM rule and its license terms. The sovereign
obligation: the rule of no cloud and no third party model service is confirmed with the operator's own
compliance owner and bound to a named scope item before design freeze, and settling it removes the
last condition on the boundary the ownership chapter describes.

Chapter 9 set the gates that protect the build's integrity; this chapter states who holds what those gates
protect, which is the operator, on every axis that matters.

10.1 Who Owns What the Build Produces

The operator owns the object model. The 16 objects and their typed links are a projection over the
operator's own systems of record, never a shadow copy of them, and the crossing mappings that answer
questions no single system can are held with the ontology. Unlike most industrial ontology examples,

which live in a vendor's documentation, this one lives on the operator's own hardware and changes only
through its named owners. The operator owns the memory: every confirmed class and every confirmed
root cause is kept as decision memory that the next run reads before it acts, and because nothing is
trained or distilled into weights under system of context, there are no fine-tunes whose ownership could
ever be contested; the anomaly model is fitted unsupervised on the fab's own normal images and runs
where the fab runs. The operator owns the decision record: every hold carries who raised it and who
approved it, the approval-missing attempt is refused in code, and the audit trail per hold is the operator's
own evidence, produced by its own people acting under its own authority. The operator owns the
boundary: the whole build runs on the operator's own hardware inside the fab, nothing crosses the fab
perimeter, no managed cloud service and no third-party model service appears anywhere, and the
support team is screened under the EAR deemed export rule before any access is granted.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja designed this system on Praxis, its platform for designing physical AI systems, and the design
maps directly onto what CodeNinja builds: the governed object model of wafers, lots, tools, chambers,
excursions and holds is Hyper Ontology; the command center where the yield team works excursions,
holds, tool risk and agent drafts, and where the operator's own people can build further agents on models
they can change without losing what was built, is Hyper Pragma; the three named agents that draft
classifications, excursion traces and dispositions for a named engineer to confirm and approve are
Decision Systems; and the whole posture, open weights on hardware the operator owns inside its own
fab with no third-party model service, is Sovereign Infrastructure.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Fab Should Reason Over Its Own Records
One design holds the whole argument: classification at the tool on sealed fanless units, one governed
ontology joining eight sources into sixteen objects, three named agents that draft while named engineers
decide, memory of confirmed classes and root causes instead of retraining, and every byte staying inside
the fab boundary on hardware the operator owns, with the model register stating plainly that no weights
are committed until a verified row stands.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes an operation willing to name its systems of record and its
approvers before the first model is discussed, edge units rated for the floor environment rather than
adapted office hardware, an export control screen on every supporting engineer before access is granted,
and a first phase aimed at the riskiest assumption, classification quality on that fab's own images, rather
than the widest scope.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

System of context was adopted as the primary pattern, pinned by the FDE, because the requirement asks
exactly for its shape: a governed ontology tied to source systems that are never replaced, never modified
and never loaded, agents that draft while engineers decide, and memory that improves without training.
Its fixed grammar governs the whole build: nouns become objects, facts become properties, relationships
become typed links, and actions change them. No pattern was set aside; the reasoning trace records
none, and the design carries no orphaned architecture.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on equipment classes rather than named products wherever the shelf holds no
verified entry: the octa-core 6 TOPS NPU edge SoC class in fanless sealed cleanroom enclosures, the
Open Time Card grandmaster class for time synchronization, the 141 GB HBM GPU class for the fab's
inference server, and fab integration decided tool by tool over SECS/GEM, GEM300 and EDA according
to which revisions each etch-module tool implements. Two precedents were read in the sector, the
Seagate fab image defect build and the SK hynix virtual metrology build, and both shaped the phase
gates rather than decorating the prose. Everything shown in this chapter was recorded reading: the
citation counts and the gap in the model register are as recorded, and nothing is inferred.

say the footprint is unsized and no GPU count is derived until a verified model row stands. This
appendix prices the one node; if the verified row changes the footprint, the node count and every line
above scale with it.

A.3 What the Price Does Not Include
• The edge estate. One octa core 6 TOPS NPU SoC unit per inspection tool group, in a fanless
  sealed cleanroom enclosure (Table 2; Table 4). The paper gives no unit price and no count of tool
  groups for the etch module.
• Export control, which is a checkpoint, not a price. The node is bought and run inside the United
  States, so no export license is priced for it. The control the paper does name binds people: access to
  fab technology by a supporting engineer who is a non-US person can be a deemed export under 15
  CFR 734.13, so every supporting engineer is screened before access is granted (chapter 3, section
  3.4; Table 5). That screening is a named approval and carries no line here.
• Everything the paper's scope boundary keeps out: new cameras, writes to tool control systems,
  ERP or supply chain integration, AMHS or robotics control and historic data migration (Table 2, "Out
  of scope").
• The servers for the rest of the stack: the Apache Kafka backbone, the object model store,
  InfluxDB 3 Core, K3s, the observability stack, Keycloak and the air gapped Harbor registry are
  chosen by product but not sized in the paper (chapter 4; Table 7).
• People: the engineers who build and run the platform, and the defect review engineers, yield
  engineers and process owners who confirm and approve every draft, whom every option carries.
• Sales tax, freight and installation on the hardware, which a written quote settles, and residual
  value at the end of three years.
• Double counted cover. The configured price already carries a three year depot warranty, so the
  support line may count some cover twice.
• A closed model token comparison, which is not printed because the paper states no token volume
  for the work surface.

title: Industrial Data Ontology for a Water Utility in the United States
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · ENERGY & UTILITIES · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

Industrial Data Ontology for a Water
Utility in the United States
Plant Context Grid: Industrial Ontologies for the Night a Duty Pump Trips

A governed industrial data ontology that joins the historian, CMMS, GIS, laboratory and
permit records of a municipal water utility in the United States, drafts tag mappings, alarm
context and permit reports for named staff to decide, and reasons on open weights in the
utility's own server room.

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the operations superintendent and plant engineer accountable for the migration, the compliance manager who
signs the permit reports, and the data, security and platform engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

Industrial Ontologies Answer a Question Six Records
Keep Apart
An industrial data ontology exists to answer the question a municipal water utility in the United States
cannot answer today: when the duty pump at a station trips at two in the morning, which asset tripped,
what work is open on it, and what the permit requires of the zone it feeds. The answer lives in records that
never meet, because the historian holds the tag and the alarm, the maintenance system holds the asset
number and the work order, the mapping system holds the pipe and the zone, the laboratory system
holds the sample, and the permit files hold the limit, so answering means one person holding all of them
in mind while the operators who can are retiring in the middle of a control system migration. The operator
is a state and local critical infrastructure owner, which means the join must happen without data leaving
its boundary and without any write path toward the control network.

The design is one governed object model of 16 objects, from the plant, well and distribution zone down to
the tag, the alarm, the work order, the lab result and the permit limit, fed read-only from six sources
through three adapter families, with the segregated control network reached only through a historian
mirror behind a hardware data diode in a demilitarized zone. Seven services and four surfaces carry the
work: a tag mapping confirmation queue, an alarm context pack, a monthly permit report draft, and a
command center with a conversational interface that answers with citations. Three named agents propose
and named staff decide, and memory keeps every confirmed mapping and resolved alarm. Two models
run on the utility's own air-cooled server with two cards of the 48 GB PCIe class: gpt-oss-120b, 117 billion
parameters at MXFP4, about 61 GB of weights, which with the 1.2 planning factor for cache and
activations reaches 70.1 GB against the 96 GB the two cards hold, and an embedding model for retrieval
with citations. Phase one covers one plant and its distribution zone, gated on the utility's own four
baselines before the estate follows.

The paper covers the industry problem and the cost of the join failure, the constraints that shape
everything downstream, the layered stack and its 16 objects, the adapter tier and the event backbone,
where inference runs and why, the model register and the licenses that let the utility own its weights, the
three gated phases with their item counts and measurements, who owns the intelligence the design
builds, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design, so that every choice can be traced
to recorded reading.

 Figure 1. Plant Context Grid on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes,
                                             and the person who decides.

Contents
Each chapter is tagged for the reader it serves most directly: Executive, Team Lead, FDE, Reference.

         Abstract · Industrial Ontologies Answer a Question Six Records Keep Apart   Executive

  PA R T I · T H E P R O B L E M

 2       Every System of Record Sees One Slice of the Station                        Executive   Team Lead

  PA R T I I · T H E D E S I G N

 4       One Stack Runs From the Diode to the Surfaces                               Team Lead     FDE

 5       Sixteen Objects Turn Plant Data Into One Argument                           FDE

 6       Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly                      FDE

  PA R T I I I · T H E R O L L O U T

  PA R T I V · H O W I T WA S D E S I G N E D

         Conclusion · An Owned Ontology Compounds Through the Migration              Executive

 11      Praxis Recorded Every Choice This Design Stands On                          Team Lead     FDE

         Sources                                                                     Reference

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Industrial Ontologies Answer Questions Six Records
Keep Apart

A night pump trip is answered today by memory and phone calls, because the records that
hold the answer sit in six systems that only a retiring workforce bridges.

The abstract promised an industrial data ontology that turns six records into one governed model of a
water system. This chapter grounds that promise in the question the operation actually asks at two in the
morning, in the cost the industry already documents for leaving it unanswered, and in the scenario the
rest of the paper designs against.

1.1 What the Night Trip Asks

Industrial ontologies earn their place in this sector because the operational question is never held by one
system. When a duty pump at a station trips at night, the operation needs to know in a single view: which
tag tripped, which physical pump that tag belongs to, which zone the pump feeds, how long the
distribution reservoir covers zone demand, what the last work orders on that pump found, what the
vibration and motor current sensing recorded before the trip, and which sampling points and permit limits
sit on the affected zone. Published examples of an industrial data ontology in this sector tend to begin
from a data model; this design begins from that question, because the question is what forces the join.
Answering it requires live telemetry, the asset register, work order history, network geometry, laboratory
records, permit terms and condition data at the same moment, and each of those lives in a different
system. The regulatory regimes raise the stakes on every part of the answer: the operator holds drinking
water and discharge permits that require monthly reporting against named limits and averaging periods, it
carries state and local critical infrastructure obligations, and it must keep its control network segregated
from its enterprise systems, a direction state utility regulators have formalized in published cybersecurity
baselines for utilities (NARUC n.d.). A partial answer is therefore not only slow, it is not a compliant
answer.

1.2 What the Industry Already Documents

The cost of the split record shows up in two ways, one documented publicly and one that shows up inside
every operation of this class. The documented part is the scale of what goes unseen when records cannot
be joined: a control system cybersecurity expert counts more than 17 million control system cyber
incidents hidden in plain sight, and argues that such incidents are more plentiful and more impactful than
the sector generally recognizes (Energycentral 2022). Incidents of that volume are discovered,
investigated and reported through exactly the records this design joins, and when the historian, the
maintenance system, the map and the laboratory cannot be read together, the evidence that would
connect an anomaly to its cause stays scattered. The undocumented part is quieter: the operator's own
engineers describe resolving alarms by phoning the person who remembers which tag is which, and that
memory is walking out of the workforce through retirement. Both costs land on the same night shift.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is a municipal water utility in the United States, a state and local critical infrastructure owner
and operator. Phase one covers one plant and its distribution zone during the migration; the estate
beyond phase one holds further plants and zones that the design extends to only after its gates are met.
Within phase one the operation runs wells drawing from an aquifer, a distribution reservoir, stations of two

kinds (pump stations with duty and standby pumps, and lift stations with wet wells and force mains), a
pipe network of segments with break history, and a control layer of PLCs and RTUs connected by radio
and leased lines. Six sources feed the design, five of them named systems of record: the historian, the
CMMS, the GIS, the LIMS and the permit records, with condition telemetry as the sixth. Four named roles
are in the loop: the engineer who confirms tag mappings, the operator on shift who confirms alarm
context, the compliance manager who approves the monthly permit report draft, and the operations
superintendent who runs the command center. The physical environments are a treatment plant, remote
stations and wells exposed to weather and washdown, and a server room that must air-cool an inference
server on the operator's own premises. The regulatory ground is the drinking water and discharge permit
regime, national cybersecurity and communications controls, and state oversight of a critical infrastructure
owner. That scenario, those six sources and those four roles are the fixed facts the design answers to.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System of Record Sees One Slice of the Station

Each source system holds a true but partial view of the same pump, and none of them can
say which work order, which zone and which permit limit stand behind a single alarm.

Chapter 1 named the question and the regimes that make a partial answer noncompliant. This chapter
shows, system by system, why each existing record cannot answer it alone, and what that costs in
practice.

2.1 One Slice at a Time

The historian is the backbone: it holds every tag value, every alarm and the event history for the phase
one plant and its distribution zone, and it knows which PLC or RTU each point arrives over. It does not
know which asset number a tag belongs to, what work that asset has had, or where it sits on the map.
The CMMS holds the asset register and the full work order history, with findings written in free text: in the
CMMS the pump is an asset number with a repair trail. It sees nothing live and nothing geographic. The
GIS holds the network geometry and the asset points: in the GIS the same pump is a point on a map,
placed in its zone and pipe network, with material, diameter and break history on the segment beside it. It
holds no telemetry and no controller namespaces. The LIMS holds the sampling points and lab findings
with their permit limit comparisons: in the laboratory records the same station is a sampling location. It
cannot say which asset or which zone a sample reflects, or what work was under way when it was taken.
The permit records hold the limits, averaging periods and reporting due dates, but not whether current
data shows compliance or where each obligation physically binds. The condition sensing added by this
design reads vibration on pump and motor frames and motor current at the starter panels, but a vibration
signature explains nothing until it is joined to the asset, its work history and its tags. Figure 2 sets these

views side by side, and the pattern is uniform: each system is complete on its own axis and silent on
everyone else's.

      Figure 2. Six systems, each seeing one part of the answer; the question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them Sees Together

No system in the operation can walk the chain the night trip demands: from the alarm tag to the pump,
from the pump to the station and zone, from the zone to the reservoir and its time to drain at zone
demand, from the pump to its work orders and their findings, and from the zone to its sampling points, lab
findings and permit limits. That chain exists only in the heads of the engineer and the operator on shift,
which is why the current answer is a set of phone calls at two in the morning. The cost in practice
compounds quietly: alarms get acknowledged without context, mapping errors survive because nobody
can see a tag and its asset in one place, and every retirement narrows the human bridge. The migration
makes it urgent, because a tag namespace nobody can map is a tag nobody can cut over.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Read-Only Across the Boundary Shapes Everything
Downstream

Segregation from the control network, on-premises compute, draft-only agents and a
migration already under way define what every layer below is allowed to do.

Chapter 2 showed that each system holds a true but partial view and that no system holds the chain. This
chapter states the four goals that shape every layer below, why each is hard in this industry, and what the
design chose to buy and to refuse in meeting them.

3.1 The Control Network Stays Behind a Diode

The first goal is segregation: the ontology and its agents must read the control network through a
demilitarized zone feed and never send a control command. This is hard in this industry because the
utility sector is a named target of state-sponsored actors whose documented tactics include reaching
control systems through enterprise networks (CISA 2022), and because the sector's precedent for the
consequence is the Ukrainian outage, where attackers used stolen credentials to switch substations off
(CISA 2015). A DMZ feed held by firewall rules alone can be misconfigured into a write path; a hardware
data diode makes read-only a physical property of the link rather than a policy that survives an error. The
constraint this imposes is total: the platform holds no credentials in the control network and no write path
toward any system of record, so every action in the control domain stays with the people who own it.

3.2 The Weights Stay on the Operator's Own Servers

The second goal is on-premises compute: the reasoning model runs as self hosted open weights on the
utility's own servers, and no data leaves the operator's boundary. This is hard because a municipal server
room limits the hardware classes available: the design sizes gpt-oss-120b, with 117 billion parameters at
MXFP4 giving about 61 GB of weights, onto two cards of the 48 GB PCIe class in one air-cooled node, 96
GB total, where the 1.2 planning factor for KV cache and activations still fits. A larger GPU class would
force new power and cooling into a room that does not have them, and a hosted model would break the
residency requirement outright. The constraint is that serving capacity is fixed at what the room holds,
which the sizing respects.

3.3 Agents Propose and Named Staff Decide

The third goal is draft-only agents: the tag mapping agent proposes on a tag found during migration and
the engineer confirms; the alarm context agent assembles context on an alarm and the operator on shift
confirms; the compliance agent drafts monthly permit report data and the compliance manager approves.
This is hard because the sector's own pattern recommends writing work orders back into the CMMS, and
refusing that means every confirmed action passes through a person's hands, bounding throughput by
staff time. The design refuses the write-back deliberately: no agent sends a control command or changes
a work order or a permit report without a named approval, and the system improves through memory of
confirmed mappings and resolved alarms rather than through any change to weights.

3.4 The Migration Sets the Clock

The fourth goal is to serve a migration already under way, whose target historian is not yet selected. This
is hard because connectors designed against an interface that changes at cutover fail silently, and
because the operators who can resolve unmapped tags retire on their own schedule, not the program's.
The design answers with a dual tag namespace that holds legacy and new namespaces at once, typed
extractors re-confirmed against the chosen historian before cutover, a design-freeze checkpoint on the
historian selection, and mapping coverage as a live weekly signal against the glide path.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

The scoping decisions follow from those goals, and Table 1 states what each buys and what it costs. The
pattern across all three is the same: the design pays in operational effort and throughput to keep
segregation, residency and human authority absolute.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From the Diode to the Surfaces

From the one-way feed through the object model and the event backbone to the confirmation
queues and the command center, one stack carries every byte and every draft.

Chapter 3 pinned the constraints: the control network stays segregated, the systems of record stay in
place, every decision stays with a named person, and every model and every byte stays on the utility's
own premises. This chapter turns those constraints into a stack in which each layer owns one
responsibility and the control boundary is crossed once, by the one-way feed through the demilitarized
zone.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

The architecture is a projection, not a consolidation. The systems of record sit below, bound in place and
never replaced; one governed object model sits in the middle, holding the 16 objects that Chapter 5
opens up; and the applications and agents sit above it, reading from it and proposing into it but never
writing beneath it. Figure 3 shows the layers with their counts: six read-only sources, three adapter
families, 16 objects, seven services, four surfaces and two models, every one running on the utility's own
hardware inside its own server room.

The shape fits this operation for three reasons. The migration is in flight, so tag namespaces and the
target historian will change underneath the design, and a middle model carrying a dual namespace bridge
absorbs that change without touching any source. Segregation leaves exactly one boundary to defend,

the diode-hardened read into the demilitarized zone mirror, with every other layer on the office side of it.
And sovereignty makes the inference layer a pair of models on the utility's own two-card server rather
than a rented endpoint, so no layer in the stack makes an external call in the inference path.

4.2 The Stack Stage by Stage

Table 3 walks the stack stage by stage, naming what each stage is responsible for and how it discharges
it. The stages carry the whole journey of a byte: born in a system of record or on a sensor, admitted
through an adapter with provenance, resolved into the object model, reasoned over by the models, acted
on by the services, and met by a person on one of the four surfaces.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The shape a team can carry elsewhere is the read-only projection with a confirmation loop. Bind the
systems of record in place, cross the control boundary once through a hardware diode into a mirror,
project everything into one governed object model in which every fact carries its provenance, let agents
draft with evidence, let named people confirm, and keep the confirmations as memory the next run reads.
A team with a similar brief swaps the object set, the sources and the sensing channels for its own, and re-
sizes the server if its work surface model exceeds the 117 billion parameters filed here. What it keeps is
the part that carries the guarantees: the adapter tier with its provenance stamps, the single write path that

5.1 Sixteen Objects and Their Typed Links

The model holds five sites and places: the plant, the well, the distribution reservoir, the station in both of
its forms, the pumping station that feeds a zone and the lift station with its wet well and force main, and
the zone itself. It holds four physical assets: the pump, the pipe segment, the PLC and the RTU. It holds
one measure and one event: the tag, whose status vocabulary carries the migration, and the alarm. And it
holds four records that carry the regulatory argument: the work order, the sampling point, the lab result
and the permit limit. Figure 4 shows all sixteen and the typed links between them, and Table 8 prints each
object with the system it is anchored in and the links it carries.

The links are what make the model an argument rather than a filing system. When a station's duty pump
trips at night, one query walks the chain: the alarm is raised on a tag, the tag maps to a pump, the pump
runs at a station, the station feeds a zone, the zone draws on a reservoir whose recorded time to drain at
zone demand says how long the operator has, and the pump carries an open work order in the CMMS. A
document store could answer that only if every join had been anticipated and precomputed, and a
migration guarantees joins nobody anticipated; a graph answers it by walking links that exist because
every object was placed with its anchor. This is the test that separates a governed industrial ontology from
the industrial ontology examples that stop at a data model: the links are typed, every one is traversable in
either direction, and every fact along the walk carries the source system it came from.

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Three adapter families bring six read-only sources into the ontology with provenance,
ordering and buffering, and no path anywhere in the tier points back toward a system of

Chapter 5 described what the model holds. This chapter describes how data gets into it: six read-only
sources, three adapter families, and an event backbone that keeps order, delivery and buffering honest
while the migration continues around them.

6.1 Six Sources and Their Provenance Classes

Figure 5 sets the six sources and their adapter paths side by side. The first is the historian, the backbone
system of record for tag values, alarms and event history across the phase one plant and its distribution
zone; its provenance class is a control-network mirror, because it is read not from the control network but
from the historian mirror in the demilitarized zone, carried across a hardware-enforced data diode by Lidi,
which makes the read a physical one-way property. The diode is not caution. The attackers who took
down distribution in Ukraine reached their targets through compromised paths into the control
environment (CISA 2015), and state-sponsored actors continue to target the energy sector specifically
(CISA 2022), so a feed held by firewall rules alone sits one misconfiguration away from becoming a write.
The other operator records are the CMMS, holding the asset register and work order history that give
every tag an asset number; the GIS, holding the network geometry that places every asset in its zone; the
LIMS, holding the sampling points and lab findings; and the permit records, holding the drinking water and
discharge limits the compliance agent drafts against. The sixth source is the condition sensing:
permanent vibration sensing on pump and motor frames and motor current sensing at starter panels,
classed as design-installed, with reservoir level and station discharge pressure read from existing
instrumentation.

          Figure 5. The 6 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

Three families carry everything: the ops systems adapter for the historian mirror, the integration adapter
for the CMMS, GIS, LIMS and permit records, and the telemetry adapter for the sensing channels, all built
on the Open62541 OPC UA stack. The tier guarantees four things. Every fact enters stamped with its
source system, its extraction method and its timestamp, so no fact in the ontology is ever unattributed.
Every connector is a typed extractor holding read-only credentials, and no path anywhere in the tier
points back toward a system of record, let alone the control network. The dual namespace bridge holds
the legacy and new tag namespaces at once, so the migration's renaming is absorbed as data rather than
felt as an outage. And because the target historian is not yet selected, connectors are typed extractors re-
confirmed against the chosen historian before cutover, with a design-freeze checkpoint carried in the
phase plan.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Ordering, delivery and buffering are carried by Apache Kafka 4.4, self managed in KRaft mode. Events
are keyed by tag and asset identifier, so every partition preserves per-asset order even when the whole
phase one estate streams at once. Delivery is at least once with idempotent upserts into the object
model, so a replayed event corrects rather than duplicates. Buffering sits at the mirror, which is
documented to push no back pressure toward the source during an outage; the platform raises a
staleness alarm at 15 minutes, and the command center shows an explicit degraded mode while the
alarms themselves stand alone. Time is its own guarantee: linuxptp with chrony, fed by the OCP Time
Card grandmaster, puts the historian's alarm timestamps, the lab result dates and the work order dates on
one clock, which is what makes the event ordering mean anything at all.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Reasoning Stays on Premises on Two Air-Cooled Cards

All reasoning runs in the utility's own server room on two 48 GB cards, sized so the weights,
the key-value cache and the failure modes of the room itself all fit.

Chapter 6 ended with every source entering through an adapter and the control network staying behind a
one-way mirror. This chapter follows the data to where it is reasoned over, which is also the question
industrial ontologies eventually force: where does the reasoning run, and who owns the room it runs in.

7.1 All Reasoning Sits in One Tier

The design has one inference tier, the site tier: a single node in the utility's own server room. Nothing
computes at a station or a well, because nothing there needs it; the vibration and motor current sensing is
low-rate telemetry the existing radio and leased-line RTU network already carries to the historian, and the
anomaly work on those signals is CPU-class work that runs on the site server beside the reasoning
model. The placement honors the intake, which requires the open weights self hosted on the utility's own
servers on premises, and so rules out colocation and any hosted option.

The sizing is arithmetic rather than judgment. The reasoning model files 117B total parameters; at INT4,
0.5 bytes per parameter, that is 58.4 GB of weights the cards must hold, and the planning factor of 1.2 for
the key-value cache and activations, the scratch memory a serving engine needs to attend over its
context while generating, brings the requirement to 70.1 GB. Two cards of the 48 GB PCIe class in one
node give 96 GB of memory, about 88 GB of it usable, leaving roughly 38 GB beside the weights against
the about 12 GB the factor reserves. The model's own card confirms the fit from the other direction: a
60.8 GiB checkpoint, 65.2 GB of root safetensors, with the mixture of experts weights in MXFP4 at 4.25
bits and the remainder at 16 bit, about 61 GB of weights and about 4.8 GB of key-value cache, figures
that fit an 80 GB GPU and reach about 234 GB only if expanded to 16 bit. At 117B parameters the model
sits below the 300B frontier threshold, so one node of two cards is the whole cluster. Figure 6 places the
tiers: sensing at the stations, one crossing of the diode, and every model in the utility's own server room.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

Only one of the four surfaces carries a number, because only one needs one. The alarm context pack
must be ready within the attention of the operator on shift who acknowledges the alarm, and the
freshness bound the design commits to is the 15-minute staleness alarm on the DMZ historian mirror: if
the mirror falls more than 15 minutes behind the source, the command center says so instead of letting a
stale pack pass as current. The tag mapping queue is migration-paced, with the engineer's confirmation

treated as the deliberate slow loop rather than a bottleneck to fight. The monthly permit report draft is
calendar-paced batch work where minutes are irrelevant. The conversational interface is the interactive
surface, and its latency is dominated by retrieval over the hybrid dense plus lexical index rather than by
generation, which is why that index is kept small enough to serve on the same node.

7.3 The Boundary and Its Failure Paths

Only telemetry crosses the boundary: tag values, alarms and event history, read through the diode-
hardened DMZ mirror and never written back. The platform holds no credentials in the control network
and no write path toward any system of record, so segregation is a property of the architecture rather
than of a firewall rule. The posture is earned by the sector's threat record: the tactics published against
energy-sector operators (CISA 2022), the outage that began with credentials taken from a control
environment (CISA 2015), and the cybersecurity baselines drawn for utility distribution systems (NARUC
n.d.) all assume this separation.

Each failure path is designed rather than hoped away. If the link fails, the mirror buffers per its
documented behavior and pushes no back pressure toward the source, the 15-minute staleness alarm
fires, the command center drops into an explicit degraded mode, and the raw alarm list stands alone
throughout, so an operator is never deprived of alarms because a context pack is unavailable. If the
power or the cooling of the room fails, the two-card 48 GB PCIe class was chosen precisely because it
air-cools in a standard rack, the UPS carries a clean shutdown, and serving acceptance is gated on a
measured load run in the actual room, whose power, cooling and rack space are confirmed at design
rather than assumed. If the update path is the concern, the artifact and model registry is an offline Harbor
install: updates arrive as artifacts brought inside the boundary, never as live pulls from outside it, and a
design-freeze checkpoint on the historian selection keeps the connectors from being reworked twice.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

The rollout measures five things, and the four baselines the utility set before any extension are fed by all
of them. Tag mapping coverage runs as a live weekly signal expressed as the percent of tags confirmed,
tracked against the cutover glide path, so the retirement of operators who know which tag is which shows
up as a slope change rather than a surprise. Confirmed mappings are sampled in a monthly audit whose
error rate is logged, which is what keeps the confirmation queue from becoming a rubber stamp. The
demilitarized zone historian mirror carries a staleness alarm at fifteen minutes and an explicit degraded

pressure toward the control network. The monthly review names alarms that fired without a finding and
findings that arrived without an alarm, which is the honest measure of the condition sensing, since

Serving acceptance is gated on a measured load run on the inference server, and the night trip scenario,
one station's duty pump tripping after dark, is the rehearsal case: the question is whether the alarm
context pack arrives with the pump's condition data and its work order history attached, in the minutes the
operator on shift has to act.

9.4 Lessons the Design Holds To

Segregation should be a physical property, not a policy. Firewall rules are configuration, and
configuration drifts: the attack that cut power to a large number of Ukrainian operators reached control
networks through paths that were supposed to be closed (CISA 2015), the documented tactics of state-
sponsored actors against the energy sector work the same seams (CISA 2022), and control system
incidents across the sector are held to be far more plentiful than reported (Energycentral 2022). The diode
behind the demilitarized zone mirror makes the read one way as a matter of physics, because there is no
write path to misconfigure.

Memory has to outlive the people who confirm it. The scarcest data in a water utility is knowing which
tag is which, and it walks out of the building at retirement. Every confirmed mapping and resolved alarm is
kept and read again before the next proposal, so the system's knowledge compounds while the staff who
built it can still be asked why.

A draft with no write path is the safer design. The sector's own pattern of writing work orders back into
the CMMS creates a parallel queue that the pattern itself warns about. This design builds no queue at all:
the named approver acts in the system of record, and the agent's draft carries evidence rather than
authority.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Historian selection is open, and settling it would freeze the connector design and the dual namespace
bridge, which is why the phase plan carries a design-freeze checkpoint on that selection. The server
room's power, cooling and rack space are unconfirmed for the inference server, and settling them either
confirms the two-card 48 GB class or forces a different class before serving acceptance. Whether phase
one extends beyond the four named staff is an open extension decision, and settling it changes only the
identity layer's scope, not the ontology or the agents. Whether the estate of wells, stations, reservoirs and
pipe segments follows at all is settled by the four baselines themselves, which is the point of holding the
gates.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Four patterns were adopted. The diode behind the demilitarized zone mirror makes the read a physical
property, which a firewall rule alone cannot. The dual tag namespace bridge holds the legacy and new
namespaces at once, so the ontology answers queries across the cutover rather than on either side of it.
Draft-only surfaces with named approvers put every decision with a person whose name is on the record.
Memory instead of retraining improves the system through confirmed mappings and resolved alarms
without ever touching weights, which removes the training run from the plan entirely.

Four were set aside with reasons recorded. GLM 5.3 class was set aside because its maker sits on the
US Entity List and the buyer is United States critical infrastructure, so origin follows the regime. Firewall-
only segregation was set aside because rules drift and diodes do not. Write-back into the CMMS was set
aside because the parallel queue it creates is the failure the sector pattern itself warns about. Frontier-
class GPU nodes were set aside because 117B parameters sit below the 300B threshold, and two 48 GB
cards hold the weights with room to spare.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

APPENDIX A

What the Utility's Own Inference Server Costs Over
Three Years
The paper is written for a municipal water utility in the United States, with the inference server in the
utility's own server room on its own premises (chapter 1, section 1.3; chapter 7, section 7.1). This
appendix therefore prices for the United States, with the national average commercial electricity price
for power and the AWS US East region, us-east-1, as the rental reference. The design runs every
model on hardware the utility owns, and its one inference tier is "two cards of the 48 GB PCIe class in
one node", 96 GB in all, serving gpt-oss-120b on vLLM (chapter 7, section 7.1; Table 4, "Inference
hardware"). The embedding model needs no further hardware line: Nomic Embed Text v2 MoE is about
0.95 GB at fp16 and runs "on the same node" (chapter 8, section 8.1), and the anomaly work on the
condition signals is "CPU-class work that runs on the site server beside the reasoning model" (chapter
7, section 7.1), so nothing is added for either rather than a card guessed. The server is priced two
ways: owned, from a system builder's published starting price with two 48 GB PCIe cards, support and
power added, and rented, from the AWS price files for us-east-1, on demand and on the two three year
all upfront plans. Every input is dated and cited, and the arithmetic is shown.

A.1 The Answer
Owning the server for three years costs about 59,000 US dollars, inside a range of 57,000 to 61,000.
Renting the same card class around the clock costs about 104,000 dollars on the deepest three year
commitment (an AWS EC2 Instance Savings Plan, all upfront, for g6e.12xlarge in US East (us-east-1)),
about 130,000 dollars on the three year Compute Savings Plan, all upfront, and about 276,000
dollars on demand. Against the deepest commitment for the same card class, ownership costs a little
under three fifths (59,280 / 103,681 = 0.57, and 0.55 to 0.59 across the range); against on demand,
about a fifth (59,280 / 275,747 = 0.21). The comparison is not like for like in one respect: the smallest
AWS instance with two or more 48 GB L40S cards in one host, g6e.12xlarge, carries four of them
(AWS 2026c), twice what the design sizes, so the rented figure buys more memory than the design
needs.
The lowest priced rented instance that holds the 70.1 GB requirement on any card class is a different

parameter, that is 58.4 GB of weights", and "the planning factor of 1.2 ... brings the requirement to 70.1

Two inconsistencies in the paper's own numbers, neither of which changes the card count or the price.
First, the weights are 58.4 GB at INT4 in chapter 7, section 7.1 and chapter 11, section 11.4, but "about
61 GB of weights" at MXFP4 in the abstract, chapter 7, chapter 8 and Table 6; 61 GB times 1.2 is 73.2
GB, which the same 96 GB holds. Second, chapter 7 gives "roughly 38 GB beside the weights" against
about 88 GB usable, while 88 less 58.4 is 29.6 GB (96 less 58.4 is 37.6 GB, so the 38 GB figure
appears to use the raw 96 GB); the figure should name which total it uses before publication.

A.3 What the Price Does Not Include
• Everything the paper's scope boundary keeps out: the migration itself, historic data migration,
  estate wide end user training, hardware, GPUs and third party license fees, "all held by the operator
  or its separate modernisation program" (Table 2, "Scope boundary"). This appendix prices the server
  only as a reference for that operator held line.
• The room behind the server. The paper leaves the server room's power, cooling and rack space
  unconfirmed and gates serving acceptance on a measured load run in the actual room (chapter 7,
  section 7.3; chapter 9, sections 9.3 and 9.5); any electrical or cooling work is sold by quotation once
  that is settled.
• The rest of the stack: the hardware data diode and the historian mirror in the demilitarized zone, the
  OCP Time Card grandmaster, the condition sensing on pump and motor frames and at the starter
  panels, and any separate servers for the event backbone, the object model store, observability and
  the offline Harbor registry, which the paper names by class and does not size (chapter 4; Table 4).
• People: the engineers who build and run the platform, the engineer who confirms each tag mapping,
  the operator on shift who confirms each alarm context pack and the compliance manager who
  approves each permit report draft, whom every option carries.
• Sales tax, freight and installation on the hardware, which a written quote settles, and residual
  value at the end of three years.
• Double counted cover. The starting configuration already carries a three year parts warranty, so
  the support line may count some cover twice.
• A closed model token comparison, which is not printed because the paper states no token volume
  for the work surface.
