title: Industrial AI for an Open Pit Mine Haul Fleet in Saudi Arabia
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · MINING · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

Industrial AI for an Open Pit Mine Haul
Fleet in Saudi Arabia
Pit Fleet Watch: A Sovereign AI Reference Architecture for Mine Haul Fleets

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the mine superintendent, the maintenance planner and the dispatcher, and the reliability, data and platform
engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

A Failing Final Drive Leaves Evidence Long Before It
Fails
When a haul truck's final drive fails on the ramp, the question an open pit mine operator in Saudi Arabia
needs industrial AI to answer is which machine fails next and what the planner should do about it today,
and that question cannot be answered with the data as it stands: the alarm lives in the operator's own
telematics, the wear metals in the laboratory's oil findings, the payload history in the fleet management
and dispatch system, the rebuild hours in the maintenance management system and the ramp itself in the
mine plan, and no one of those systems can see the other four. Reference architectures for industrial AI
exist for exactly this condition, because the join has to happen somewhere, the data may not leave the
site, and the pit must keep working when the link to the city fails.

The design is a sovereign, offline-capable system for one pit: five sources of record joined through two
adapter families into a governed fleet ontology of sixteen objects, with seven services and five surfaces
serving a control room command center, and four models placed across three tiers: GLM 5.3, at 753
billion parameters served at FP8 on one node of eight 141 GB GPUs, runs reasoning and the
conversational interface on the site's own servers; Chronos-2 forecasts telemetry and oil trends and BGE-
M3 embeds evidence for cited answers on the same site tier; Grounding DINO open weights run on heat-

rated automotive-grade edge units on the trucks and at the shovel bucket camera, where vibration, motor
current and camera evidence is gathered even when coverage drops. Three named agents draft for
named people: a health agent on a new alarm, oil result or tyre reading for the maintenance planner, a
tooth loss agent on a shovel camera detection for the shovel operator, and a dispatch agent on a truck
pulled from service for the dispatcher, with every work order outcome feeding memory, never weights.
Phase one runs one pit's haul truck fleet, about 35 trucks and one 600 tonne class shovel, for six months
against the operation's own baselines of unplanned downtime, mean time between failures, tooth loss
events reaching the crusher and cost per tonne.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure across the five systems, the constraints and
the stack, the sixteen-object fleet ontology and how every source enters it through an adapter, the
placement of inference across edge and site tiers, the four models and the licenses that let the operator
hold their weights, the four phases with their eighteen items, gates and measured run, what the operator
owns at the end, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.

 Figure 1. Pit Fleet Watch on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes, and
                                               the person who decides.

Contents
Each chapter is tagged for the reader it serves most directly: Executive, Team Lead, FDE, Reference.

       Abstract · A Failing Final Drive Leaves Evidence Long Before It Fails                   Executive

  PA R T I · T H E P R O B L E M

         Conclusion · The Join, the Boundary and the Named Decision Are the Design    Executive

 11      How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design                           Team Lead     FDE

         Sources                                                                      Reference

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Industrial AI Reference Architectures Start at the Pit
Floor

Industrial AI reference architectures start at the pit floor because a final drive announces itself
through months of alarms, oil findings and payload strain spread across five systems that
never meet, inside a regulatory ground where data stays on site and the desert heat and dust
are working conditi

The abstract stated the counts; this chapter states the question they exist to answer. Sovereign industrial
AI reference architectures are usually argued from the data center inward, but for a haul fleet the
argument runs the other way: the evidence a failing final drive leaves behind is generated at the machine,

in heat and dust, under rules that keep data on site, and an architecture that cannot live with those
conditions never reaches the question at all.

1.1 The Question, the Data and the Regulatory Ground

The operation needs one question answered continuously: which component on which truck will fail next,
and can it be caught before the failure arrives on the ramp with a loaded truck on it. The data that
answers it lives in five systems of record: alarm codes and severity from the operator's telematics, wear
metals and viscosity trends from the oil laboratory, payload and cycle records from the fleet management
and dispatch system, work order outcomes and rebuild findings from the maintenance management
system, and the grade and ramp flag of every haul road segment from the mine plan. The regulatory
ground constrains the answer as much as the data does. Data and models stay on site on hardware the
operator controls; camera coverage of named operators requires a personal data protection impact
assessment before the first camera runs; and any mechanism that can stop a machine must stand on
functional safety guidance for autonomous and mixed mining systems (Gmggroup 2020). The design
satisfies all three regimes at once rather than trading among them.

1.2 The Documented Cost of Getting It Late

The cost of a late answer is documented publicly. A mines safety regulator published a significant incident
report into a collision between an autonomous haul truck and a manned water cart, in which machine
state and mixed traffic were not joined in time to prevent contact (WorkSafe 2025), and the same
regulator maintains a code of practice for safe mobile autonomous mining whose continuing revisions
record the problem as standing rather than exceptional (WorkSafe 2025b). At the industry level, member
companies of the International Council on Mining and Metals still report fatalities year on year in the
council's safety data, which is the floor under every ranking this design produces (ICMM n.d.). A final drive
failing on the ramp is rarely an injury event, but it is the same evidence arriving late, and it costs
unplanned downtime, a recovery on a grade and a rebuild bay filled without warning.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is an open pit mine operator in Saudi Arabia, with the pit worked by a contractor. The pit
works a haul fleet of about 35 trucks of the 100 tonne class against one electric rope shovel of the 600
tonne class, feeding a crusher that is protected by catching shovel teeth before they travel with the ore.
Four roles sit in the loop by name: the maintenance planner approves health drafts, the dispatcher
approves haul redrafts, the shovel operator confirms a missing tooth, and the mine superintendent owns
the command center and holds escalation authority. The physical environments are the pit floor, the ramp
segments of the haul road, the workshop rebuild bay and a site server room. Five named systems of
record hold the evidence and two adapter families bring it in, and one rule runs through all of it: no agent
stops a machine or changes a work order without a named approval, with the single exception of the
tooth loss stop, which follows the site safety procedure. Phase one covers one pit's haul fleet and the

shovel, runs for six months, and is measured against the operator's own baselines of unplanned
downtime, mean time between failures, tooth loss events reaching the crusher and cost per tonne.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Five Systems Hold Five Slices of One Truck

Each of the five systems of record sees one slice of the machine and misses the rest, so the
one question that matters, which component fails next, is answerable by none of them alone
and by no one of them together.

Chapter 1 stated the question and the ground it must be answered on. This chapter shows why none of
the five systems of record can answer it, by walking through what each one sees and what each one
misses; Figure 2 sets the five views side by side.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The fleet management and dispatch system sees the movement: every haul cycle with its truck, shovel
and dump point, cycle time, delay code and payload tonnes, and it holds the live model of the roads and
assignments. What it misses is everything inside the machine, because hours since a component's last
rebuild, the wear metals in its oil and the alarm history are not its business. The operator's telematics
sees the machine's own voice: alarm codes with severity and timestamps, and operating hours per unit,
and it misses what any alarm means in maintenance terms, holding no work order history, no rebuild
findings and no oil trend against which an alarm could be graded.

The maintenance management system sees the component's biography: serial numbers, rebuild counts
and shop findings, work orders and their outcomes. It misses the live conditions that produced the failure,
because payload strain, ramp grades and delay codes never reach it. The laboratory sees the
component's blood: wear metals, viscosity and the trend against baseline for each oil sample, and it
misses the machine's context, since a sample is flagged without knowing which truck carried it, what it
hauled or up which grade. The mine plan sees the ground itself: haul road segments with grade, length,
ramp flag and source revision, and it sees nothing live at all, because it is revised on planning time, not
operating time.

     Figure 2. Five systems, each seeing one part of the answer; the question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

What no system sees is the chain. The simulated event that drives this design is one truck's final drive:
months of rising wear metals sit in the laboratory's records, payload strain on ramp segments sits in the
fleet system's cycles, an escalating alarm sits in telematics, and the maintenance system holds a rebuild
history that says the component is past its mean time between failures. Each system holds one link and
none holds the chain, so the planner reads an alarm without the oil trend and the laboratory flags a
sample without knowing the truck works the ramp loaded, and the failure announces itself on the ramp
instead of in the workshop. That is the join failure, and it is the cost in practice.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereignty and Named Approvals Shape Every Layer

Sovereign data on the operator's own hardware, named people approving every action, heat
and dust that punish commodity equipment, and a pit that must keep working when the link to
the city fails together shape every choice downstream of this chapter.

Chapter 2 showed the join failure: five slices and no chain. This chapter turns that failure into the
constraints every layer downstream must satisfy, then records what the scope buys, what it costs and
what the design refused.

3.1 Data and Models Stay on Site

The first goal is sovereignty: every fact, every model and every ranking stays inside the boundary, on the
operator's own hardware in the site server room, with no egress and a hardware-enforced data diode as
the single outward path. This is hard in mining because the equipment makers' telematics often live in
vendor clouds whose data rights conflict with residency, and because most inference offerings in the field
assume a hosted service. The design answers with open weights under licenses that permit self-hosting,
and with on-machine edge reads as the fallback that keeps evidence on site when the cloud path is
closed.

3.2 Named People Approve Every Action

The second goal is accountability: agents draft and named people decide. This is hard because the pit is
worked by a contractor, which splits accountability between the contractor running the machines and the
operator owning the data and the deposit. Every approval surface therefore names its approver scope,
the maintenance planner for health drafts, the dispatcher for haul redrafts and the shovel operator for
tooth loss, and the write-back path into the fleet management system carries an audit trail the system's
owner accepts before the dispatch agent is built on it.

3.3 Heat and Dust Are Working Conditions

The third goal is survival: the equipment must work where the fleet works. Commodity edge hardware is
rated for offices, and the desert is not one; the automotive-grade system on chip variant is committed for
the cab and shovel mounts, enclosure thermal budgets are run against solar gain, cleaning intervals are
treated as a design parameter rather than a chore, and the handed over temperature grade is a
commissioning check because published ratings for the board conflict with the chip's.

3.4 The Pit Works When the Link Fails

The fourth goal is availability offline. Private spectrum on a light-licensed shared-access basis gives no
guaranteed channel, so the edge units buffer locally and send events and small crops rather than
continuous pixels, and the site servers keep answering when the link to the city drops. The safety loop
stays on the machine and the optimization loop in the control room, a separation the mining guidance on
autonomous systems states directly (Gmggroup 2020), and the reason the pit must tolerate link loss at all
is that production cannot wait on a city.

One Stack Runs From Systems of Record to Surfaces

The architecture places the five systems of record below, one governed fleet ontology in the
middle, and the services, agents and surfaces above, so that nothing is integrated around the
ontology and nothing bypasses the systems the operation already trusts.

Chapter 3 fixed the constraints: reasoning stays on site, no agent acts without a named approval, and the
systems of record stay exactly where they are. This chapter lays out the stack those constraints produce,
from the five systems the operation already trusts to the five surfaces where its people decide.

4.1 The Architectural Pattern and Why It Fits

The stack has three bands. Below sit the five systems of record: the fleet management and dispatch
system, the operator's own telematics, the maintenance management system, the laboratory and the
mine plan. In the middle sits one governed fleet ontology of sixteen objects, a projection over the five
rather than a migration of any of them. Above sit the seven services, the three agents that draft and the
five surfaces where the maintenance planner, the shovel operator, the dispatcher and the mine
superintendent decide. The pattern fits this operation because it binds the silos in place while giving every
agent one model to read, and because the safety loop stays on the machine, where the bucket camera
and its edge unit watch for a missing tooth, while the optimization loop runs in the site server room, a
separation the functional safety guidance for autonomous mining treats as foundational (Gmggroup
2020). Figure 3 shows the layers with their counts: five sources, two adapter families, sixteen objects, four
models across three inference tiers, seven services and five surfaces. Nothing is integrated around the
ontology, and nothing bypasses the systems of record: every read arrives through an adapter, and every
write returns through the owning system.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The reusable shape is the projection ontology with adapters as its one door, and it is the part of this
design that reads as a sovereign industrial AI reference architecture made concrete. A team carrying a
similar brief keeps four moves: bind the silos with a governed object model rather than a data lake; make
the adapter tier, not the ontology's readers, responsible for provenance; place detection where the safety
consequence is and ranking where the evidence joins; and write back only through the owning systems,
with an audit trail on every write. They would swap the object list, the sensing mix and the model sizes for
their own, and they would keep the rule that no fact enters ungoverned and no draft carries weight without
a named approval.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The three actors are objects in the model, not labels outside it. The maintenance planner approves health
rankings, the dispatcher approves haul redrafts, and the mine superintendent owns the command center
and holds the escalation authority. The work order's status vocabulary marks the boundary of the
machine's authority: a draft sits at "Drafted by agent" until a named person moves it to "Approved", and
every later state, from "In progress" to "Overdue", records a human decision. The hosting posture follows
from sovereignty. The ontology, the models and the memory run on the site servers in the mine's server
room, on hardware the operator controls; identity is served on site; the running system holds no external
links, and the one inbound path is the one-way data diode that carries artifact and model updates in. The
one write path out of the ontology returns through the owning systems, the fleet management system for
assignments and the maintenance system for work orders, each write carrying its audit trail.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Every Fact Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Every fact from the five named sources enters the ontology through one of two adapter
families, carrying its provenance class and its source system, so the join is governed at the
door rather than repaired after it.

Chapter 5 described what the object model holds. This chapter describes how facts reach it, and the
guarantees they arrive with.

6.1 Five Named Sources, One Provenance Class

Five systems feed the ontology, all of them the operator's own, and all read-only at the door. The fleet
management and dispatch system holds the live model of roads and assignments, and the health and
dispatch agents read cycles, payloads and delays from it. The operator's own telematics supplies alarms
and operating hours, while the edge units also read the truck bus on the machine so evidence keeps
flowing when coverage drops. The maintenance management system supplies the history and the work
order outcomes the rankings learn from, and receives approved work orders and rebuild records back.
The laboratory supplies the oil analysis, one of the five kinds of evidence that never meet today. The mine
plan supplies haul road segments, pits and benches, each carrying its source and revision so a ramp
event attributes to the right segment; the road network is safety-critical configuration, and its revision trail
is treated accordingly (Gmggroup 2020). Figure 5 sets the five systems, their provenance classes and
their adapter paths side by side. One survey item stays open in phase one: the telematics may live in
vendor clouds or carry data rights that conflict with the sovereign constraint, so an interface and data-
rights survey runs early, with on-machine edge reads as the fallback that keeps evidence on site.

          Figure 5. The 5 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

Two adapter families cover every entry. The integration adapter handles the vendor APIs, database reads
and scheduled file exports that reach the five named systems; the telemetry adapter handles the high-
rate signals from the truck bus and the edge units. Between them they guarantee four things: every fact
carries its source system, its provenance class and a synchronized timestamp; no source writes into the
ontology directly, so the join is governed at the door rather than repaired after it; replays are idempotent,
so a redelivered record updates rather than duplicates; and the write-back path runs only through the
owning systems, the fleet management system for assignments and the maintenance system for work
orders, each write carrying its audit trail.

6.3 The Event Backbone

The backbone is Apache Kafka 4.3.x in KRaft mode, on the site servers. Ordering is per partition, keyed
by machine, so one truck's events land in the order they happened, and delivery is at least once with
idempotent consumers on the far side. Buffering happens twice: at the edge, where units hold events and
small image crops locally while the private LTE link is down and forward them on recovery, and in the
backbone, whose retention covers a replay after a consumer failure. Replication runs across brokers on
site, and the time card grandmaster keeps sensors and systems synchronized so joins across the five
sources line up in time. Models and artifacts enter through the air-gapped registry over a hardware-
enforced data diode, one way, so the running system has no egress at all.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Forecasting Runs on the Truck, Reasoning on Site

Tooth detection runs on heat-rated edge units at the bucket and on the trucks, forecasting
and evidence retrieval run on the site servers, and GLM 5.3 reasoning runs on one node of
eight 141 GB GPUs in the site server room, with nothing that matters crossing the network
boundary when the link fails.

Chapter 6 showed how the five systems of record enter through two adapter families and land in one
governed object model. This chapter fixes where the four models run, because placement decides what
survives a failed link, a summer afternoon and a broken update path: on the machine, on the site servers,
or on the node that answers the superintendent.

7.1 Three Tiers and the Arithmetic That Sizes Them

The edge tier is the automotive-grade octa core SoC variant committed for the cab and shovel mounts,
and it exists because heat and abrasive dust are normal on this site rather than exceptions. It serves
Grounding DINO, the Swin-T open weights checkpoint at about 345 MB at 16 bit, through ONNX Runtime
under K3s, a footprint that fits in the SoC's memory with the video pipeline beside it and lets the enclosure
stay fanless, since a fan would pull dust through the board. The larger Swin-B checkpoint at about 467
MB at 16 bit is the fallback if evaluation on representative footage demands it, and the sizing still holds.
Tooth detection runs here because the pixels are here: the bucket camera produces continuous frames,
and the shared-access spectrum across the pit carries no guaranteed channel, so the design never
commits to sending continuous pixels anywhere. The split follows the mining safety guideline's own
discipline of keeping the safety loop on the machine and the optimization loop in the center (Gmggroup
2020).

The site tier is rack servers in the site server room, fed from the internal Harbor registry with no egress.
They run Chronos-2, about 0.48 GB at 32 bit as published and about 0.24 GB at 16 bit, thresholding
forecast residuals for anomaly across the telemetry of about 35 trucks and one shovel, and BGE-M3 at
about 1.1 GB at fp16 for evidence retrieval. Both are small against server memory, so the binding
constraint on this tier is not capacity but the rule that nothing leaves it.

The central tier is one node of eight 141 GB GPUs, roughly ten kilowatts, in the same server room,
holding GLM 5.3 for reasoning and the work surface. The arithmetic is exact: GLM 5.3 is filed at 753B
parameters, and at FP8, one byte per parameter, that is 753 GB of weights. A 1.2 planning factor
reserves another 151 GB for KV cache and activations, so the GPUs must hold 904 GB in total. Eight
GPUs of 141 GB give 1,128 GB, which leaves 375 GB beside the weights, more than twice the 151 GB
the planning factor reserves, so the KV cache ceiling holds with headroom for concurrent command
center sessions. Figure 6 sets the three tiers side by side with what runs on each and what crosses
between them.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget is ordered by consequence rather than by a single number, because each loop ends at a
different person. The shortest loop never leaves the machine: a frame is judged on the SoC beside the
camera, the in-cab alarm sounds, and the shovel operator confirms the tooth loss before the ore travels
toward the crusher; no step in that loop waits on the network, which is how a stop can be trusted when
the channel is shared and unguaranteed. The middle loop refreshes as evidence arrives: when an oil
result lands from the laboratory or a telematics alarm opens, the health agent's failure risk ranking is
recomputed on the site servers and waits in the planner's approval queue, and its deadline is the shift,
because the maintenance planner decides within it. The longest loop is conversational: the command
center asks, BGE-M3 retrieves the evidence across the ontology, GLM 5.3 answers with citations, and the
answer is only useful if it arrives while the mine superintendent is still looking at the machine in question.

7.3 The Boundary and Its Failures

What crosses the network boundary is events and small crops, never continuous pixels: the edge units
buffer locally and send detections, confirmed events and crops small enough for the shared channel. The
edge units also read the truck bus on the machine directly, so telematics evidence keeps flowing when
coverage drops and the operator's own telematics cannot be reached. When the link to the city fails, the
pit keeps working, which is the reason reasoning sits on site rather than in an in-country data center:
every ranking, draft and approval continues inside the boundary, in line with the fail-safe discipline the
autonomous mining codes require on link loss (WorkSafe 2025b). When power fails, the edge node and
its PoE switch sit on one UPS and NUT orders the clean shutdown, so the units resynchronize cleanly
when power returns rather than waking corrupted. When the update path is the failure in question, model
and container updates arrive through a hardware-enforced data diode running Lidi into the Harbor

registry: the registry cannot be written from outside, and the update path can never become an egress
path.

8.1 Four Models, Each Held Under Its Own Terms

GLM 5.3 is the reasoning tier, filed at 753B parameters: about 756 GB of weights at FP8 as published
and roughly 1.5 TB at BF16, which is why eight GPUs of the 141 GB class are sized before any KV cache
is counted. It runs in the site server room on the operator's own hardware as the agentic work surface and
ontology maintenance model, drafting the health, tooth loss and dispatch agents' outputs and answering
the command center with citations. Its license is the GLM-5.3 bespoke license, whose terms permit
commercial use, fine tuning and redistribution, and those terms are what let the operator hold the weights,

serve them with vLLM from the internal registry, and keep serving them whatever any external
relationship becomes.

Grounding DINO, the Swin-T open weights checkpoint at about 345 MB at 16 bit, detects the shovel
bucket, its teeth and the ground engaging tools per frame on the heat-rated edge units at the bucket
camera. Its Apache-2.0 license permits the operator to hold and serve the checkpoint inside the perimeter
and to relabel footage in CVAT toward a future retrain if evaluation on representative footage demands it,
even though phase one commits no fine tuning of any model. Chronos-2 is the forecasting model on the
site servers, about 0.48 GB at 32 bit as published and about 0.24 GB at 16 bit, doing zero-shot
forecasting with covariates and thresholding the residual for anomaly, so no model is tuned for this
operation. It was chosen over TimesFM 3.0 and Moirai 2.0, whose non-commercial terms cannot ship
inside the operator's boundary, and over Chronos-Bolt, because covariates and several co-evolving
channels matter here. BGE-M3 is the evidence retrieval embedding on the site servers, served at fp16 at
about 1.1 GB: its dense, sparse and multi-vector retrieval in a single pass, with an 8,192 token window
and an MIT license, keeps part numbers and alarm codes retrievable across records that mix Arabic and
English.

9.1 Four Phases Carry Eighteen Items Through Their Gates

The rollout is four phases carrying eighteen items, with their gates and requirement coverage shown in
Figure 8. Foundation carries five items across three workstreams, one model of the fleet, phase one
measurement, and sovereignty and approvals; its exit gate is the fleet ontology standing on the systems
of record, the sixteen objects anchored in the five named systems with evidence joins proven on live
records. The edge and site build carries six items across industrial AI at three layers and sovereignty and
approvals; its gate is the private LTE network working across the pit, on which every later capability
depends. The agents and command center phase carries six items across command center, memory and
named agents that draft; its gate is the tooth loss stop agent, the one capability that touches a machine
and therefore the one that must work first. The measured run carries a single item, the phase-one pilot
read against its gates, in the phase one measurement workstream.

Requirement coverage stands at two requirements covered in full, none partial and none open, as Figure
8 records. The order encodes dependency rather than convenience: no agent is built before the ontology
and the write-back paths are settled, and no ranking carries weight before the baseline it will be
measured against is reconstructed.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 1 0

The Intelligence Stays with the Operator That Produced
It

The object model, the memory of work order outcomes and the weights all sit on the
operator's own hardware inside its own boundary, so the intelligence the pit produces
compounds for the operator and for no one else.

Chapter 9 set the gates, the item counts and the measurements that decide whether the design earns
trust in the pit. This chapter settles the question that outlasts every gate: who owns what the system
becomes once the six-month run has done its work.

10.1 What the Operator Holds When Phase One Ends

The fleet object model is the operator's from the day it is built. Its 16 objects and their typed links are a
projection over the operator's five systems of record, not a copy held somewhere else: every haul truck,
component, oil sample and work order carries the system it came from, so the model can be rebuilt from
those sources at any time and cannot be held hostage by anyone who did not build it. The same holds for
the weights. GLM 5.3 runs under a license that permits commercial use, fine tuning and redistribution,
while Grounding DINO and Chronos-2 run under Apache-2.0 and BGE-M3 under MIT; each license lets
the operator hold and serve its copy inside the boundary without a vendor's continued permission, which
is the entire point of self hosting on site. In phase one nothing is fine tuned, because rankings improve
through memory of work order outcomes and planner decisions and never through weights; there is
therefore no fine-tune to own yet, and any future one belongs to the operator on the same license terms.

The decision record is the third asset. Every approved ranking, haul redraft and tooth loss confirmation is
kept with the named approver who decided it, and that record is the memory each later decision reads; it
lives on the site servers and does not leave them. The boundary is the fourth asset: the servers in the site
server room, the edge units on the trucks and at the shovel bucket, the private network across the pit, and

identity served on site. Updates arrive one way through the hardware-enforced data diode, so even the
update path cannot become an egress path, and the pit keeps working when the link to the city fails.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja builds exactly this shape, and this design maps onto its offer part by part. Adaptive Operations
covers the sensing, detection and forecasting of physical behavior: the vibration and current sensing on
engines, final drives and wheel motors, the bucket camera watching for missing teeth, and the zero-shot
forecasting of telemetry and oil trends that ranks failure risk. Decision Systems covers the ranking,
attribution and recommendations a named person decides: the health ranking the maintenance planner
approves, the haul redraft the dispatcher approves, the stop the shovel operator confirms. Hyper
Ontology holds the governed fleet model, the 16 objects and their typed links, as the operator's own
projection over its systems of record. Hyper Pragma is the work surface in the command center where the
operator's own people act on agent drafts and build their own agents inside the boundary. Hyper Engram
is the kept record of decisions and outcomes that the next decision reads; it never updates model
weights. Sovereign Infrastructure is the posture the whole design takes: the operator's own hardware,
open-weight licenses and operation inside the boundary with no egress. Praxis is the platform that
produced the design, and everything it produced sits with the operator that paid for it.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Join, the Boundary and the Named Decision Are the
Design
In one view, the design is a projection rather than a migration: a governed fleet ontology of sixteen objects
that binds five systems of record in place and ties every fact to the system it came from, heat-rated edge
units that read the truck bus and watch the bucket when the network drops, forecasting and retrieval on
site servers, GLM 5.3 reasoning on the operator's own eight GPUs, and three agents that only draft, while
the planner, the shovel operator and the dispatcher decide, with the outcome of every work order held in
memory so each ranking gets better without a single weight changing.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes an operation with several systems of record it cannot replace,
an environment that punishes commodity hardware, and a rule that named people decide: the objects,
the sources and the models are swapped for the operation's own, while the join, the adapter discipline,
the memory of outcomes, the offline fail-safe and the gates stay exactly as drawn, because those are the
parts that make the intelligence compound inside the boundary of the organization that produced it.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every design in the series is produced on Praxis, and this chapter lets a reader trace any
choice back to the recorded reading that justified it, from the ask and the assigned family to
the eight lenses and the patterns adopted and set aside.

Chapter 10 closed the ownership argument: the model, the memory, the weights and the boundary all
stay with the operator. This chapter turns the design on itself and shows how it was reasoned, so that any
choice in the preceding chapters can be traced back to recorded reading rather than to assertion. Every
design in this series is produced on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for designing physical AI systems, and
this chapter lets a reader trace any choice back to what justified it, as Figure 9 shows: the ask as it
arrived, the family and industry assigned, the records in the room, the eight lenses, and the patterns
adopted and set aside.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask arrived in the operator's own words: a governed fleet ontology joining fleet management,
telematics, maintenance and oil analysis; edge units on the trucks and at the shovel bucket camera; on-
site servers; a command center with cited answers; three named agents drafting for named people; and
reasoning on GLM 5.3 open weights self hosted on site, with one truck's final drive failing on the ramp as
the event the design must catch early. Praxis assigned the design to the physical AI family in the mining
industry, with the country fixed by the operator's own requirement. What was in the room was recorded:
tooling and recency records, case study records, a first principles mining brief, and hardware shelf entries
covering the edge compute, the site servers, the cameras and the GPU node. Every record is listed in the
design's register and available on request.

11.2 The Eight Lenses

Each lens read what it could see and returned what it returned. The first-principles lens supplied the spine
of the design, and the rules lens grounded the approval rule in recorded regulatory practice: the codes of

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Four patterns were adopted. Integrate through the fleet management system, never around it, so the
dispatch agent's approved redraft is written back to the owning system with an audit trail. Keep the safety
loop on the machine, so the tooth loss alarm sounds in the cab where the shovel operator stands.
Improve through memory rather than weights, so every work order outcome makes the next ranking
better without any fine tuning. Buffer at the edge on link loss, sending events and small crops rather than
continuous pixels, because a shared-access private network guarantees no channel. Four were set aside
with reasons. Trajectory forecasting was set aside because the fleet management system holds the live
model of roads and assignments. A new positioning layer for people and vehicles was set aside for the
same reason. Off the shelf GPU modules per station were set aside because a sealed enclosure in this
heat and dust needs the fanless automotive-grade SoC, not a heat path no enclosure can serve. Any
direct control path from an agent to a machine was set aside because the approval rule forbids it.

APPENDIX A

What the Operator's Own Reasoning Node Costs
Over Three Years
The paper is written for an open pit mine operator in Saudi Arabia, with a site server room at the pit
(chapter 1, section 1.3). This appendix therefore prices for Saudi Arabia, with the Saudi Electricity
Company industrial tariff for power and the AWS Middle East (UAE) region, me-central-1, as the rental
reference. The design runs every model on hardware the operator owns, and its central tier is "one
node of eight 141 GB GPUs, roughly ten kilowatts" serving GLM 5.3 on vLLM (chapter 7, section 7.1;
Table 4, "GPU node"). The three other models need no further hardware line here: Chronos-2 at about
0.24 GB and BGE-M3 at about 1.1 GB run on the site rack servers, and Grounding DINO at about 345
MB runs on the automotive grade SoC edge units (chapter 7, section 7.1; Table 4); the paper names
those servers and edge units by class only, with no count, no part and no sizing, so they are listed
under A.3 rather than a part guessed. The node is priced two ways: owned, from a reseller's published
configured price with support and power added, and rented, from the AWS price files for the nearest
region that offers the same card. Every input is dated and cited, and the arithmetic is shown.

A.1 The Answer
Owning the node for three years costs about 556,000 US dollars, inside a range of 528,000 to
580,000. Renting the same eight H200 cards around the clock on the cheapest three year commitment,

to 0.77 across the range). No rented option can sit inside the Kingdom today: AWS's Saudi region is
reported for launch in December 2026 (W.Media 2026) and its price files list no Saudi region on the day
read (AWS 2026a), and every rented option would carry fleet, telematics, oil and work order records

and redistribution" (chapter 8, section 8.1); no price is asserted for it here. Grounding DINO and

• An export license determination, which the paper does not name. A node of eight 141 GB HBM

  worldwide license requirement for 4A090.a items (eCFR 2026b), and Saudi Arabia sits in Country
  Groups D:3 and D:4 (eCFR 2026a). The order date for the node is therefore set by a BIS license
  determination, which should be a phase one checkpoint before the class is quoted; this appendix
  does not price it.
• The edge units and the site servers: the automotive grade octa core SoC units on the trucks and
  at the shovel, the bucket, ramp and rebuild bay cameras, the vibration and motor current sensing,
  and the rack servers for the forecasting, embedding, ontology, event backbone, Harbor registry and
  observability tiers, all named by class with no count or part in the paper (chapter 7, section 7.1; Table
  4).
• The private LTE network across the pit, the hardware enforced data diode, the UPS and the
  time grandmaster (chapter 6, section 6.3; chapter 7, section 7.3), and any radio or private network
  licence from the communications regulator.
• The facilities work behind the ten kilowatts: cooling and the power path in a site server room in
  desert heat and dust, and on site generation if the pit is not on the grid, which this appendix does not
  assume.
• Everything the paper's scope keeps out: autonomous haulage and machine control, plant and
  crusher control beyond the tooth loss stop, replacement of the systems of record, training or fine
  tuning of any model, and bulk historic migration (chapter 3, section 3.6).
• People: the engineers who build and run the platform and the maintenance planner, shovel
  operators, dispatchers and mine superintendent who approve every draft, whom every option
  carries.
• Customs duty, 15 percent VAT, freight and installation on the hardware, which a written quote
  delivered to the Kingdom settles, and residual value at the end of three years.
• Double counted cover. The configured price already carries a three year warranty, so the support
  line may count some cover twice.
• A closed model token comparison, which is not printed because the paper states no token volume
  for the reasoning tier.

title: Industrial Ontology Examples: A Port Equipment and Berth Object Model in Saudi Arabia
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · MARITIME & PORTS · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

Industrial Ontology Examples: A Port
Equipment and Berth Object Model in
Saudi Arabia
Maritime & Ports Watch: One Living Picture of the Operation

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the leaders accountable for maritime & ports operations, their supervisors, and the data and platform engineers
who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

The Answer Already Exists in the Systems the Operation
Runs
Berth productivity drops and nobody can say whether the cause was the crane's hydraulic fault, the yard
block that could not keep up, the vessel's stowage or the berth window the authority granted; this paper,
one of the industrial ontology examples in this series, is a port equipment and berth object model that lets
a container terminal operator in Saudi Arabia answer that question.

The design reads 9 source systems through 2 adapter families into one object model of 16 objects, runs
10 services over it and opens 4 surfaces to the people who decide, with 3 models placed where the data
is. A governed industrial ontology of the terminal's berths, equipment and moves, built from the operator's
eight named systems of record and kept current move by move, with three drafting agents (productivity,
equipment, commissioning) whose outputs managers confirm and which write back only through named
approvals. Reasoning runs on GLM 5.3 open weights self hosted by a container terminal operator in
Saudi Arabia on one 141 GB HBM class node, with a kept record of decisions and outcomes that the next
decision reads, memory improving every next trace without training.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

A Daily Question Goes Unanswered in the Systems That
Hold the Data

The operation holds every fact the question needs and no system answers it.

The abstract promised one of the industrial ontology examples in this series, a system that answers a
daily operational question from data the operation already holds. This chapter states that question exactly,
documents what its absence costs, and sets out the scenario the rest of the design answers.

1.1 The Question, the Data and the Regimes

When berth productivity drops on a working vessel call, the person accountable needs one ranked
answer drawn from four candidate causes: a crane fault such as a hydraulic failure, a yard block that
could not keep up, the vessel's stowage, or the berth window the authority granted. A terminal that can
rank those causes daily belongs to the family of industrial ontology examples: reasoning held in country,
on the operator's own hardware, projected over the systems of record rather than copied out of them. The
data the ranking requires already exists, but only as separate facts in separate systems: moves with their
seconds and equipment identity, fault codes with clearing times, yard occupancy and reshuffle ratios,
stowage plan references, window grants against actual arrivals, work orders with their berth plan effect,
and the commissioning status of newly installed cranes.

The regulatory regimes shape the design as much as the data does. Marine casualty investigation
standards require timely, evidence-based reconstruction of what equipment did and when (IMO 2008),

and a fatal injury at a port shows how such reconstruction depends on joining equipment behavior to the
sequence of operations (TAIC n.d.). Port facility security obligations put a named officer's approval on
anything touching the secured area. National cybersecurity and communications controls demand
auditable segmentation of operational technology. The kingdom's personal data protection law sets
transfer conditions, including its Article 29 assessment, before gang, incident and driver records reach
group ports. Export control rules attach to the accelerator class the reasoning runs on.

1.2 The Documented Cost

The cost of an unanswered attribution question is not one bad shift but a recurring one. Ports carry
national weight: ports deliver 95 per cent of the country's imports and exports, including much of its food,
fuel and materials, according to the ports safety code (Service 2025), so every unexplained fall in berth
productivity propagates into supply chains rather than stopping at the quay. The safety record compounds
the same failure, because accidents are documented to be underreported to vessel accident databases
(NIH 2011), and an incident register that cannot be joined to the equipment and the vessel call it involved
leaves every investigation to rebuild the same links by hand, under the timeliness the investigation code
expects (IMO 2008).

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is a container terminal operator in Saudi Arabia. It berths container ships against a quay
served by ship to shore cranes, moves boxes with yard cranes, straddle carriers and terminal tractors,
and hands them to road and rail at the gate. A terminal expansion under way lengthens the quay,
deepens the berths, adds ship to shore cranes and a new yard block, and raises capacity toward two and
a half million containers a year; by the operator's own assessment the expansion roughly doubles the
objects under management and adds a second builder's equipment carrying its own vocabulary. The
people in the loop are operations managers, engineering managers, maintenance planners, berth
planners, the port facility security officer and the authority's vessel traffic staff; the planners who know
which crane behaves how are few, and name reconciliation happens in meetings today. The physical
environments are the quayside in Gulf heat and salt air, the yard blocks, the terminal machine room, and
the road and rail gate. The operation runs eight named systems of record, counted roles spanning
operations, engineering, maintenance, planning, security and the authority, and counted places spanning
berths, yard blocks, the gate and the machine room, and the design in Part II stands on those counts.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System Sees One Slice of the Operation

Each system of record sees its own part of the answer and none sees the whole.

Chapter 1 stated the question and priced its absence. This chapter shows why none of the existing
systems can answer it: each sees one slice of the operation, and each names the same physical thing
differently.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The terminal operating system holds vessel calls, moves, stowage and yard inventory, which makes it the
productivity record, but it never sees the fault code that slowed the crane, the window the authority
actually granted, or the commissioning state of the newest machine. The vessel scheduling and berth
planning tool owns the berth plan, the quay length and the crane split, yet cannot see whether the crane it
assigned is under repair. The crane and equipment control systems own machine state and fault codes,
but not the move sequence around each fault or the yard pressure behind it. The maintenance
management system owns work orders and component history, but not what any work order did to berth
productivity. Equipment telematics carries fuel state, utilization and position, but cannot join a drift signal
to the call it affected. The port authority's vessel traffic and berth window data holds the granted window,
but nothing about performance inside it. The civil works and commissioning records hold the expansion's
objects and the builders' cited documents, but nothing about how those objects perform once handed
over. The safety incident register holds incidents, but not, on its own, the equipment component and the
vessel call each incident belongs to. Figure 2 sets these slices side by side.

    Figure 2. Eight systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

The question of Chapter 1 crosses all eight slices at once, and no system crosses even two. In practice
the cost is paid in meetings: managers resolve names by hand, because a crane is an asset in
maintenance, a resource in operations, a controller in automation and a line item in the commissioning
records. The few planners who know which crane behaves how become a single point of failure for the
whole operation, and the expansion doubles the object count while the second builder's vocabulary
reopens the reconciliation the first builder's equipment already needed, so the manual join gets harder at
exactly the moment productivity matters most.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Four Constraints Shape Everything Downstream

The goals, the scoping decisions and the exclusions were fixed before any component was
chosen.

Chapter 2 showed eight systems, each holding one slice and none able to join even two. This chapter
fixes the goals and exclusions that every component choice in Part II answers to.

3.1 The Systems of Record Stay in Place

The design sits beside the systems of record, never replacing them, never modifying them, never loading
their databases out. This is hardest exactly where it matters most: the terminal operating system is the
operational clock the design reads productivity from, and the crane and equipment control systems are
safety-rated, so writing to them is not a shortcut but a boundary breach. The expansion runs alongside
live operations, which removes any window in which systems could be swapped.

3.2 The Weights Stay in the Country

Open weight models run on the operator's own hardware inside the country, and nothing about cargo,
vessels or equipment leaves the network. The easy path in this industry is a hosted frontier API, which the
requirement forbids; the sovereign path carries real friction, because the accelerator class the reasoning
needs attracts an export license determination for the destination country, national cybersecurity controls
demand auditable segmentation of the operational technology zone, and the operator, not a vendor,
carries the hardware.

3.3 Named People Decide Every Write

Agents draft, managers confirm, and the single write path back to a system of record is an approved draft,
raising a work order under the confirmer's name or adjusting the berth plan through the planning tool. The
difficulty is behavioral rather than technical: approvals drift into rubber-stamping, and a false confirmation

poisons the memory the system improves on, so approval latency is instrumented and known-answer
probes are injected into the draft queue from the start of phase one.

3.4 Improvement Comes From Memory, Not Training

The system improves by reading a memory of confirmed outcomes before each run, never by updating
weights. This inverts the standard machine learning loop, whose natural answer is fine tuning, and it holds
because the requirement says the next call and the next crane must be modelled better without training a
model on the fly; the constraint also protects the boundary, since no training pipeline means no data ever
leaves for one.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Sixteen Objects Turn Operational Data Into One
Argument

The object model is the join the systems never made.

Chapter 4 ended the stack at the object model, the one layer every service reads and no source system
writes. This chapter opens that layer: what it holds, where people enter it, and the exact form one object
takes in the record.

5.1 Sixteen Objects and the Links Between Them

The model holds sixteen objects in six kinds: three sites (Berth, Quay Section, Yard Block), four assets
(Ship to Shore Crane, Yard Crane, Straddle Carrier, Equipment Component), five events (Vessel Call,
Berth Window, Fault, Move, Incident), two records (Work Order, Commissioning Record), one material
(Box) and one measure (Productivity Measure). Each object is anchored in exactly one system of record,
the system whose word on that object is final: the Berth in the vessel scheduling and berth planning tool,
the Move and the Box in the terminal operating system, the Fault in the crane and equipment control

systems, the Incident in the safety incident register. Table 8 sets out every object with its anchor and its
typed links. Anchoring is what keeps the model a projection over the systems of record rather than a
second copy of them: the ontology claims nothing the sources do not hold, and it never becomes the
place a record is kept.

The typed links are the join the systems never made. Move carries Box and names Equipment
Component; Productivity Measure names its Vessel Call; a Work Order records its berth plan effect
against both Berth and Berth Window; an Incident names its Equipment Component. A query can
therefore start at a berth's productivity measure, walk back through the vessel call to the individual moves
and the equipment that performed them, continue to the faults that equipment raised and the work orders
those faults produced, and end at the berth window the authority granted, all in one traversal. Figure 4
draws every object and every link. A document store holds each of these facts somewhere, but it cannot
answer the operator's question, whether the drop was the crane, the yard, the stowage or the window,
because that answer lives in the joins, and typed links are the one structure that carries them. The same
traversal is why the Incident object matters: maritime accidents are documented to be underreported to
official databases (NIH 2011), and an incident that joins to its equipment and its call in the same model as
the fault codes is an incident that can be found.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

People enter the model at the confirmation step. The three drafting agents, for productivity, equipment
and commissioning, propose; managers confirm; and the single write path out of the ontology is the
named approval: an approved work order lands in the maintenance management system under the
confirmer's name, and an approved berth plan adjustment lands in the planning tool. No agent dispatches
equipment, and no agent writes to a control system. The hosting posture follows the same line: the model
runs on the operator's own hardware inside the country, identity is issued on site so every confirmation
carries a person, the port authority feed is the one inbound external link, and a hardware data diode
carries fault logs out of the control zone one way. Nothing about cargo, vessels or equipment leaves the
network, the boundary that sovereign AI reference architectures in regulated industries draw.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Nothing reaches the object model except through an adapter that owns its contract.

Chapter 5 showed sixteen anchored objects with typed links between them. This chapter shows how data
reaches them: every source enters through an adapter that owns its contract, and nothing reaches the
object model directly.

6.1 Every Named Source and Its Provenance

Eight named source systems feed the model. The terminal operating system holds vessel calls, moves,
stowage and yard inventory, the productivity record the ontology is built on. The vessel scheduling and
berth planning tool owns the berth plan that approved drafts adjust. The crane and equipment control
systems own fault codes and machine state, read through a one-way path with no write back. The
maintenance management system owns work orders, and receives the ones approvals raise. Equipment
telematics is the drift signal the equipment agent triggers on. The port authority's vessel traffic and berth
window data supplies the granted window, one of the four ranked causes of a productivity drop. The civil
works and commissioning records hold the expansion's objects and the builders' cited documents. The
safety incident register feeds the Incident object, the record safety investigations are built on under the
international code for casualty investigation (IMO 2008). All eight carry first-party provenance, systems
the operator or its authority owns, named by role because their products are confirmed on site; all are
read except the single approved write back to work orders. Figure 5 maps each system, its provenance
class and its adapter path.

       Figure 5. The 9 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

Two adapter families cover the eight systems. The integration adapter serves the transactional sources,
the operating system, the planning tool, the maintenance system, the commissioning records and the
incident register, over APIs and read-only views built per system. The telemetry adapter serves the high-
rate sources, the control systems' fault logs and the equipment telematics, and carries the hardware data
diode that makes the control zone read-only in silicon rather than in policy. The tier guarantees five things:
each adapter owns its contract, so a source change breaks one adapter and not the model; every event is
stamped with its source, provenance class and read time; source names are resolved to governed object
identities, so the second builder's vocabulary maps rather than invents; events are buffered and replayed
when a link fails; and no adapter ever writes to a source except the approval path already described.

6.3 The Event Backbone

The backbone is Kafka 4.3.x in KRaft mode. Ordering is per key: move events are keyed by vessel call so
a call's moves arrive in sequence, and fault events are keyed by crane so a fault history reads true.
Delivery is at least once, made safe by idempotent upserts keyed on object identifiers, so a replayed
event converges on the same record instead of duplicating it. Brokers replicate, adapters buffer against
source outages, and the terminal's own network carries everything committed. Time is the quiet
dependency: operating system events, control system fault logs and telematics join on one clock
disciplined by Chrony and linuxptp under an OCP Time Card grandmaster, because a fault joined to the
wrong shift is worse than a fault not joined at all.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Inference Belongs Where the Data Is

Each tier runs what its data and its link can carry.

Chapter 6 described how every source enters through an adapter and never directly, and how the event
backbone carries each record to the object model in order. This chapter decides where the models that
read those records run, and why each tier of hardware carries only what its data and its link can support.

7.1 Three Tiers and the Arithmetic That Fixed Them

The committed design runs inference on three tiers, and the memory arithmetic of the frontier tier fixed
the whole placement. The central tier holds GLM 5.3, the frontier-class work surface model, on the
operator's own hardware in country: one node of eight GPUs of the 141 GB high bandwidth memory
class, which is 1,128 GB of usable memory. The model's filed parameter count is 753 billion, served at
FP8 precision, where each parameter occupies one byte, so the weights alone occupy 753 GB. The 1.2
planning factor reserves a further 151 GB for the KV cache, the per-conversation attention memory a
running model allocates, and for activations, so the node must hold 904 GB in total; it holds that with
margin, leaving 375 GB beside the bare weights. Serving runs on vLLM, and because the node is inside
the country and owned by the operator, no reasoning request crosses a border.

The terminal tier hosts GLM-5.3-Flash on a two-socket air-cooled server class in the terminal machine
room, reading the builders' commissioning documents and carrying retrieval volume so the frontier node
stays reserved for reasoning. The embedding tier runs BGE-M3 on the central node. A fourth tier is
offered, not committed: continuous crane sensing, which would add edge compute of the fanless, sealed,
sunshielded class rated for Gulf quayside heat, serving detection through OpenVINO, with a
development-board measurement as the gate before any unit is fixed. Figure 6 sets the four tiers side by
side, with what runs on each and what crosses between them.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget is set by the decision each output serves, not by a number quoted for a component. Move
events must join in stream order on the backbone, because a productivity argument assembled out of
order is wrong, not merely late. The productivity question itself is answered after the vessel call, on the
terminal operating system's own clock, because that is the clock the measure is defined against. Drift
signals from telematics must surface within the shift, so a superintendent can act while the crane is still
the problem of this shift rather than the next one's investigation. Commissioning document reading is
working-hours work, and conversational retrieval answers within a session. Nothing committed needs a
model to answer faster than a manager can read it, because agents draft and managers decide; the one
latency the ontology itself carries is event ordering, which time synchronization through Chrony with
linuxptp and the backbone's ordering guarantee hold.

7.3 The Boundary, and What Happens When It Fails

What crosses the network boundary crosses it inward, and only as a read. The crane and equipment
control systems are read through Lidi over a hardware data diode, so fault logs and machine state leave
the control zone and nothing can return: the control-zone segmentation required of operational
technology is satisfied by construction rather than by firewall policy that a misconfiguration could undo.
Nothing about cargo, vessels or equipment leaves the country, because the frontier node is the operator's
own hardware in country and no third party model service is called anywhere in the design.

The failure paths are each specified. When the link between the terminal and the central node drops, the
backbone buffers events and replays them in order on recovery, so the object model catches up rather
than gaps. When power fails, each tier restarts against its last committed offsets and time resynchronizes
through Chrony with linuxptp, so joins made after restart still line up by timestamp. When the update path

is the failure, model artifacts arrive through Harbor, the air-gapped artifact and model registry: they are
staged, verified and applied on the operator's schedule rather than pulled live from outside. The systems
of record are never the point of failure for the intelligence, because the intelligence writes to none of them,
and the one write path that exists goes through named approvals into the maintenance system and the
berth plan, never into the control zone.

Every model was chosen against its license before its accuracy.

Chapter 7 fixed where each tier runs and what each node must hold. This chapter turns to the models
themselves, and to the licenses that decide whether the operator can keep what it runs: a model the
operator cannot legally hold on its own hardware is not a sovereign choice, however accurate it is.

                               Figure 7. The three models, their placement, and the work each one does.

8.1 Three Models and the Terms That Bind Them

Figure 7 sets the model stack on one page: a frontier reasoning model on the central node, a multimodal
reader on the terminal tier, and an embedding model beside the reasoning model, each with its license
written under it. GLM 5.3 is the work surface model, the frontier-class reasoning tier where the drafting
agents work and the ontology is maintained. Its filed parameter count is 753 billion, served at FP8, where
each parameter occupies one byte: about 756 GB of weights as published, and roughly 1.5 TB if carried
at BF16, the two-byte precision, which is why the design serves it at FP8 on one node of eight 141 GB
GPUs with the KV cache ceiling Chapter 7 sets out. Its license is the GLM-5.3 bespoke license, whose
terms permit commercial use and redistribution with attribution, and whose model as a service trigger
governs offering the model as a service to others; it does not touch a terminal operator's internal use. The

operator names this model and forbids third party services, and this license is what lets the operator hold
the weights, host them in country and keep them.

GLM-5.3-Flash is the terminal tier reader: 320 billion total parameters with 18 billion active per token, a
mixture of experts shape that carries a large vocabulary of knowledge at a small serving cost, and
natively multimodal, so it reads scanned drawings and photographed pages of the builders'
commissioning records as well as text. It carries the MIT license, which permits use, copying, modification
and redistribution with the license text carried and carries no trigger of any kind, so the operator can hold
and redistribute the weights without a determination. Its work is deliberately volume work: reading
documents at the rate the expansion produces them, and leaving the frontier node to reasoning.

BGE-M3 is the embedding model, the piece that turns text into the vectors search runs on. It performs
dense, sparse and multi-vector retrieval in a single pass over an 8,192 token context, occupies about 1.1
GB at FP16 on the central node, and carries the MIT license. The sparse leg matters more than the size:
container numbers and fault codes are exact strings, and a purely dense vector blurs them, while the
sparse leg keeps them retrievable exactly.

8.2 The Model and Equipment Register

The license is the line of sovereign AI reference architectures most often left vague: which weights the
operator may hold, on what ground, under whose trigger. Table 4 closes that vagueness by registering not
only the three models but everything the design stands on: the GPU class and the sizing rule that fixed
the node count, the diode and the thermal camera legality line, the sensing the offered tier would add and
the telemetry signals the committed design already holds, the patterns the architecture rests on, and the
ground it all runs on. One entry deserves its emphasis stated plainly: the improvement path is a kept
record of decisions and outcomes, a memory of confirmed outcomes which the next trace reads before it
acts and which does not update model weights, so no license with a training or distribution trigger can
ever be tripped by the system getting better at its job.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 9

Shadow Mode Comes Before Any Flag Is Trusted

The rollout earns each phase at a gate the operator can read.

Chapter 8 settled which models run, where they run and under what licenses. This chapter sets out how
the build earns trust in stages, what each stage must prove before the next begins, and what the operator
should still be asking about.

9.1 Three Phases, Eighteen Items, Two Hard Gates

The rollout is shaped by the requirement's own phasing, and Figure 8 shows it whole: three phases, 18
items, two gates, and the register of 21 requirements read against the build at every gate. Phase 1 covers
two berths and carries 15 items across six workstreams: ontology and naming, agents and decisions,
approvals and compliance, command center, memory and improvement, and phase one exit. Its named
items include the port equipment and berth object model, the source system mappings and joins, and
name reconciliation across systems. Its exit gate is the commissioning agent for expansion objects: the
agent must draft commissioning records from the civil works and commissioning records for the new berth
sections and cranes, and a manager must confirm them, before anything widens. Phase 2 carries two
items across the offered sensing tier and terminal scale workstreams: the whole-terminal rollout and the
continuous crane sensing option. Its gate is that option itself, taken on phase-one evidence rather than
assumption, which is why the sensing tier is priced and quoted separately rather than built in. Phase 3
carries a single item, the group ports worked example, on the terminal scale workstream; the group's
other ports inherit the worked example only when the running terminal has proven it, and that inheritance
is the requirement's stated purpose, that the ontology becomes the worked example for the rest of the
ports in the group.

            Figure 8. The three phases and their gates, and coverage of the 21 requirements across them.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

The phase-one measurements are chosen so the gate reads evidence, not opinion. The object model is
proven on one week of production joins before any agent runs: berths, windows, cranes, faults, moves
and measures must join across the eight systems of record with every object resolved to one governed
name. Approval latency is instrumented from the start, because the confirmations are the training data of
the memory, and known-answer probes are injected into the draft queue so rubber-stamping shows up as

a number rather than a suspicion. Drift resolution is measured on the phase-one cranes at shift sensitivity,
which decides whether existing telematics can carry the equipment agent's trigger or the offered
continuous sensing tier is needed. Attribution is measured against confirmed outcomes: when a manager
confirms a ranked cause among the crane's fault, the yard block, the vessel's stowage and the granted
window, that confirmation is recorded and the next similar call must rank better. The incident join is
measured too, and the join rate matters beyond the terminal because underreporting of maritime
accidents to official databases is documented (NIH 2011), so a safety register that reaches equipment
and vessel calls through the ontology is itself a finding.

9.3 Failure Modes

Table 5 states what fails and what the design does about it, and every row is a live risk with a named
mitigation rather than a residual accepted in silence.

9.4 Lessons

Shadow the drafts before anyone signs them. The agents begin in shadow mode, drafting productivity
explanations, equipment health notes and commissioning summaries that managers read and correct
before any draft can raise a work order or adjust a berth plan, and the probes in the queue keep the
confirmation honest. Trust in a ranked cause is earned one confirmed explanation at a time, and the gate
trusts nothing that a named person has not confirmed. Govern the vocabulary centrally or the second
builder reopens the war. The expansion doubles the objects and adds a second builder's equipment with
its own names, and the design answers with one naming service that every new object passes through,

so the builder's terms are mapped to the governed vocabulary instead of accumulating beside it. Price the
connectors before promising the joins. The eight systems are named by role, not by product, and the join
quality of the whole ontology rests on interfaces that are confirmed in the first week of phase one, which
is why the system survey is an item with a gate behind it and not a formality.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Four questions remain open, and settling each changes something concrete. The system survey settles
the connector effort and with it the true cost of the join layer. The export license determination for the 141
GB GPU class settles the license path the hardware order follows, and names the importer of record. The
drift resolution measurement settles whether the offered continuous sensing tier moves from option to
commitment. The Article 29 assessment under the personal data protection law settles what, if anything,
may flow to the group's other ports in phase 3 beyond the worked example itself.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 1 0

The Intelligence Should Stay with the Operation That
Produced It

What the design builds belongs to the operator.

Chapter 9 showed how the build earns each phase at a gate the operator can read. This chapter settles
the quieter question behind the gates: who owns what the build produces.

10.1 The Model, the Weights and the Record Belong to the Operator

The object model is the operator's asset in the fullest sense: 16 objects, from Berth and Vessel Call
through Ship to Shore Crane, Fault, Move and Commissioning Record, each anchored in one named
system of record, linked by typed joins, and named through one governed vocabulary. Nothing in the
model is a shadow copy of a vendor's database; it is a projection over systems that stay in place, which
means it cannot be repossessed by any of them. The requirement asks that this model become the
worked example for the rest of the ports in the group, and that is a statement of ownership before it is a
statement of reuse. The weights are equally the operator's to hold: GLM 5.3 runs under its bespoke
license, whose commercial terms and attribution requirement permit self-hosted internal use without
touching its model as a service trigger, and GLM-5.3-Flash and BGE-M3 run under MIT, so the operator
holds every model it depends on, on its own hardware, in country. There are no fine-tunes to own, and
that is deliberate: improvement runs through the memory of confirmed outcomes, which records what
managers decided and never touches a weight. The decision record is the third asset: every approved
draft carries the confirmer's name, every raised work order is raised under that name in the maintenance
management system, and the accumulated memory of confirmed explanations stays inside the operator's
boundary as the corpus the next decision reads. The boundary itself is the fourth: a hardware data diode

enforces one-way egress from the control systems, nothing about customers' cargo leaves the country,
and the single write path into any system of record runs through a named approval.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja designed this system on Praxis, its platform for designing physical AI systems, and the design
maps directly onto what CodeNinja builds: Hyper Ontology holds the governed object model of berths,
equipment and moves; Hyper Pragma is the work surface where the operator's own people extend the
drafting agents in the command center; Decision Systems is the ranking and attribution layer that puts
four candidate causes in front of a named manager who decides; Adaptive Operations is the offered
sensing tier that would watch crane behavior continuously; and Sovereign Infrastructure is the posture the
whole design stands on, with open weights on the operator's own hardware inside the country and
hardware-enforced one-way egress from the control zone. The intelligence stays with the operation that
produced it, and the platform that produced the design is the reason it could be specified that way.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Pattern Repeats Wherever Systems of Record Do
Not Meet
Seen whole, the design is one object model over the systems a container terminal operator in Saudi
Arabia already runs, with inference placed where the data is and every decision left to a named person.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes the same four things: the named systems, an object model
anchored in them, a first gate that can stop the work cheaply, and the license posture that lets the
operator own what it learns.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every choice above traces back to something Praxis recorded reading.

Chapter 10 settled where the intelligence lives. This chapter opens the record behind it, so a reader can
trace any choice above back to what justified it. Every design in this series is produced on Praxis, the
design team platform for designing physical AI systems, and this chapter lets a reader audit the reasoning
rather than take it on faith. Figure 9 shows the ask as Praxis received it, the family and industry it
assigned, what it read, the eight lenses it read through, the patterns it adopted and set aside, and the
equipment classes the reasoning landed on.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask, in the operator's own words, was an industrial ontology of the terminal, owned by the operator,
filled from its systems of record, with open weight models on its own hardware in the country, and nothing
about customers' cargo leaving it. Praxis assigned the design to the Physical AI family and the Maritime
and Ports industry, a pin made by the forwarding design engineer on this project and read as reasoning
input rather than a matched conclusion. What Praxis read was the corpus shelf of each lens, and those
shelves are the corpus behind every lens that follows.

11.2 The Lenses

Table 6 records each lens, what it could see, how many items it cited, and what it contributed to the
design. All eight lenses returned a contribution on this project; none is shown as a gap.
