10.1 What the Operator Owns

The object model is a projection over the company's seven systems of record, never a shadow copy of
them: every object, property and typed link describes this company's lines, equipment, fuel lots and
people, and the governed model stays inside the company. It is not one of the industrial ontology
examples a vendor ships ready made; it is built from the company's own records and changes only
through the governed path. The weights are held under licenses that permit the company to keep them:
the work-surface model runs under a license allowing commercial use, fine tuning and redistribution, and
because the design never fine tunes, the weights the company holds are the weights it audited, while the
forecasting and embedding models run under Apache-2.0 and MIT. The decision record, every draft,
confirmation, rejection and operator action with the person who decided, belongs to the company, and so
does the memory that compounds from it. Public discussion of self-improvement centers on AI
development delegated to AI systems (Anthropic n.d.) and on that practice diffusing into the wider
corporate ecosystem (Stanford 2026); this design compounds instead through a kept record the company
can read, audit and export. The boundary is the company's control as well: the one-way transfer, the in-

country hosting on the company's own hardware, and the OT policy decision retained by the company's
security function.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja designed this system on Praxis, its platform for designing physical AI systems, and each
element of the design maps to a named part of its offer. The sensing, detection and forecasting of
physical behavior, from the shell hot spot and ring formation detections to the drift forecasting on the
streaming tag register, is Adaptive Operations. The governed object model over the seven systems of
record is Hyper Ontology. The command center, where the company's people build their own agents on
models they can change without losing what was built, is Hyper Pragma. The kept record of decisions and
outcomes that the next decision reads, which never updates model weights, is Hyper Engram. The own
hardware, the open-weight licenses and the in-country operation are Sovereign Infrastructure.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Pattern Repeats Wherever Systems of Record Do
Not Meet
Seen whole, the design is one object model over the systems a cement company in Saudi Arabia already
runs, with inference placed where the data is and every decision left to a named person.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes the same four things: the named systems, an object model
anchored in them, a first gate that can stop the work cheaply, and the license posture that lets the
company own what it learns.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every choice above traces back to something Praxis recorded reading.

Chapter 10 closed the ownership argument: the object model, the weights, the decision record and the
boundary all stay with the company. This chapter opens the design record itself, so the reader can audit
how each choice was made. Every design in this series is produced on Praxis, and this chapter lets a
reader trace any choice above back to the recorded reading that justified it. Figure 9 shows that path end
to end: the ask, the family and industry assigned, what it read, the eight lenses, the patterns adopted, and
the equipment classes the reasoning landed on.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask arrived as a requirement written in the company's voice: a self-improving AI system for cement
kiln control, owned by the company, open weight models on its own hardware in the country, reading its
systems of record, improving every shift from what operators confirm, without training a model on the fly
and with nothing about the plants leaving the country. Praxis assigned the family Physical AI and the
industry Heavy Industry and Construction; the family was selected by the FDE on the project as a pin
rather than a reasoned match, and the brief was still read as reasoning input. Praxis read the case study,
tooling, hardware, regulation, approach and history shelves the lenses drew on.

                        patterns adopted and set aside, and the equipment the design lands on.

11.2 The Lenses

Table 6 states what each lens could see, how many records it cited, and what it contributed to the design.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

One pattern was adopted as primary: the system of context pattern, pinned by the FDE as the sole
primary because the requirement asks for exactly its shape, a governed ontology where an upset and the
actions that cured it form one story, memory that compounds without training, and a command center that
answers with citations. Its rules held throughout: systems of record below, never replaced, never
modified, never loaded; the ontology as a projection with crossing mappings rather than a shadow copy;
one small grammar in which nouns become objects, facts become properties and relationships become

typed links; and the kinetic loop closing on the model so the line it describes stays living. Nothing was set
aside, and the record shows why: no competing pattern answered the requirement's combination of read-
only sources, human confirmation and compounding memory without training.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on three equipment classes: the 141 GB HBM GPU class that holds the work-
surface model's weights with room beside them for KV cache and activations; the node-count rule by
GPU class that sizes the frontier node from the model's filed parameters; and the one-way data transfer
class that enforces the boundary. Everything above those classes, the phases, the gate, the failure
modes and the open questions, traces to recorded reading through the lenses of Table 6. Everything
shown in this chapter was recorded reading, and nothing is inferred.

title: Sovereign AI Reference Architectures for Passenger Rail Fleet Maintenance in Saudi Arabia
text:
V E R T I C A L - D R I V E N A R C H I T E C T U R E S · R A I L & T R A N S P O R TAT I O N · D E S I G N E D W I T H P R A X I S · N O V E M B E R
2026

Sovereign AI Reference Architectures for
Passenger Rail Fleet Maintenance in
Saudi Arabia
Fleet Condition Command: Industrial AI in Rail Maintenance the Operator Owns

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the fleet technical director and head of maintenance, the depot, reliability and control room leads, and the
platform, data and integration engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

A Drifting Converter Should Be Swapped Before the
Desert Decides
Sovereign AI reference architectures for passenger rail fleet maintenance in Saudi Arabia come down to
one question this operation cannot answer today: which vehicle on the fleet is drifting toward failure, and
what should be done about it before the timetable sends it back onto a long desert route. The operator's
present estate cannot answer that question, because condition data arrives from the builder's platform in
the builder's words, the depot closes work orders in its own, and the two meet only in a meeting, so a
door fault seen on board three times this month is never joined to the work order that was closed last
month for the same door. A locomotive whose traction converter is drifting is scheduled by the timetable
rather than by its condition and fails in the desert; when a train is late, the control room and the depot
each tell a different story; and the maintenance-included terms of the new trainset contract will be
measured against availability figures the operation cannot compute cleanly today, a gap that matters
wherever railroad performance measurement is itself a regulated reporting requirement (ECFR n.d.).

The design reads ten named source systems, among them the builder's remote monitoring platform, the
on board diagnostic logs, the maintenance management system, the depot work orders, the timetable
and train running system, the track condition monitoring service, the spare parts stock system and the
passenger incident log, through two adapter families, an integration adapter and a telemetry adapter, into
a governed ontology of fourteen objects joined by typed links; six services, the fleet ontology, condition
watching, agents and memory, the command center, the sovereign platform and baseline and gates, carry
the work to four surfaces, the command center's condition view, the diagram swap approval surface, the
month-end availability pack and the fleet engineer's approval surface; the model register carries no
verified model row from this run, so the frontier-class open weights behind the conversational work
surface are open work to be verified live and then sized, and in phase one all compute runs centrally in
the operator's existing in-country data center, with GPU capacity of the 141 GB HBM class procured
against measured load and nothing about the trains leaving the operator's network.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure across the systems of record; the constraints,
the layered stack, the fourteen-object model, ingestion through adapters, the placement of inference
inside the sovereign boundary, and the model and license register; the two-phase rollout with its item
counts, gates, measurements and failure modes, and who owns what the design builds; and it closes with
the chapter showing how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design, so any choice can be traced to
the recorded reading that justified it.

   Figure 1. Fleet Condition Command on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it
                                       computes, and the person who decides.

Contents
Each chapter is tagged for the reader it serves most directly: Executive, Team Lead, FDE, Reference.

  PA R T I · T H E P R O B L E M

  PA R T I I · T H E D E S I G N

 4       One Stack Runs From Systems of Record to Surfaces                             Team Lead     FDE

 5       Fourteen Objects Turn Fleet Data Into One Argument                            FDE

 6       Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly                        FDE

 7       Reasoning Stays In-Country on Hardware the Operator Owns                      FDE

  PA R T I I I · T H E R O L L O U T

  PA R T I V · H O W I T WA S D E S I G N E D

         Conclusion · Sovereignty Is a Data Structure Before It Is a Data Center       Executive

 11      Praxis Recorded Every Choice This Design Stands On                            Team Lead     FDE

         Sources                                                                       Reference

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

A Sovereign AI Reference Architecture Starts with One
History

Condition data arrives in the builder's words, the depot works in its own, and a traction
converter that is drifting keeps being scheduled by the timetable until it fails in the desert.

The design comes down to one question this operation cannot answer today: is this trainset fit for the
diagram the timetable has just given it? The abstract promised a design that answers that question from
data the operation already holds, and this chapter shows why sovereign AI reference architectures have
to be earned here rather than bought: the question itself, the regimes it must satisfy, the documented cost
of leaving it unanswered, and the scenario that must answer it.

1.1 The Question the Operation Needs Answered

The operator's own framing of the ask is a sovereign reference architecture, owned outright, reading its
systems and the builders' platforms, with nothing about its trains leaving the country or reaching a foreign
model service. The working question beneath that ask is narrower and harder: for every trainset on every
diagram, is it fit to run tomorrow, and if not, which vehicle, which component by serial number, which
evidence, which depot slot and which spare part. Three joins sit inside that question, and none of them
can be made today. Has this fault been seen and closed before, on this same door, by this same depot. Is
this traction converter drifting toward a failure that its next diagram will take into the desert. And what
availability did the fleet actually attain last month, computed the way the new maintenance-included
contract will compute it, with every figure defensible by citation back to its source.

The data the question requires spans condition telemetry from the builder's platform, the raw diagnostic
logs behind it, faults with confirmed causes, work order closures, depot slots, diagrams, journeys and
actual times, track condition reports, spare parts stock and the passenger incident log. The regimes it
must satisfy are the Kingdom's Railway Law safety certificate articles and the regulator's change control,
under which introducing the platform is filed as a significance decision inside the safety management
system before any contract-facing output goes live; the national data protection law over the incident log's
personal data; national cybersecurity and communications controls over the platform itself; and the
CENELEC scope note that keeps an advisory, non-vital system outside the safety case while leaving it
inside the governance. Performance measurement is a legal obligation in comparable regimes elsewhere:
United States federal regulation makes service metrics reporting a requirement for railroads (ECFR n.d.),
and Britain's regulator monitors train service performance against regulated outputs (ORR n.d.).

1.2 The Documented Cost of the Problem

The cost in practice is concrete. A locomotive whose traction converter is drifting is scheduled by the
timetable rather than by its condition, and fails in the desert. A door fault seen on board three times in a
month is not joined to the work order that was closed last month for the same door, so the same part is
faulted, worked and faulted again. When a train is late, the control room and the depot each tell a different
story, and neither story carries the other's records. The measurement layer is contested even where it is
most mature: an industry subgroup reviewing the designated railroad operating metrics recommended
removing some of them, because members' varied experience showed the measures did not carry
uniform meaning (STB 2023), and rail safety researchers have proposed transparency and published
data as the very basis for measuring national railway safety (Illinois 2023). This operator is in a weaker

position than any of those regimes describe, because it is tendering for trainsets with maintenance
included, measured against availability figures it cannot compute cleanly today.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is a national passenger and freight railway running long-distance passenger trains over a
network of more than a thousand kilometers, with more trainsets on order to raise capacity. Its passenger
fleet runs push-pull trainsets of locomotives and coaches across long desert routes, with maintenance
depots at the ends of the line. Railways of this class monitor dozens of coaches and locomotives remotely
through the builder's digital platform and track condition through a vibration based monitoring service, and
the tender now under way is for ten more trainsets from a new builder, with maintenance included.

The people in the loop, by role, are the fleet engineer who judges condition cases and approves agent
drafts; the few engineers who can read a diagnostic log and know which faults to trust; the depot
supervisor who owns work orders and depot slots; the control room that owns the running story; and the
accountable owner of the availability figures. The physical environments are desert heat that sets the
enclosure thermal budget before any camera is chosen, long routes with intermittent connectivity from
moving assets, and depots at the line's ends; the offered depot tier adds cameras on one depot's
inspection road and siding overview, detecting locomotive, coach, trainset, converter bay, door and
wheelset. The counts the design carries are ten sources read through two adapter families into fourteen
objects, served by six services onto four surfaces, with the named systems of record walked through in
Chapter 2 and the regulatory ground as stated in 1.1.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System Sees One Slice of the Trainset

Each of the operator's systems of record holds a true slice of the fleet, and none of them can
hold the one history of a single door or a single serial-numbered converter.

Chapter 1 stated the question the operation needs answered and the scenario that must answer it. This
chapter walks the systems that operation already owns, one by one, and shows what each sees, what
each misses, and what none of them can see together.

2.1 What Each System Holds

The builder's remote monitoring platform sees the vehicles it built: their telemetry, their diagnostic events,
and their condition in the builder's own vocabulary. It misses the depot's work orders, the operator's
confirmed fault history, and every word the other builder will use when the new trainsets arrive. The on
board diagnostic logs hold the raw record behind each event, with timestamps and severity, but they miss
the meaning the builder's vocabulary carries and everything that happens off the vehicle. The

maintenance management system holds faults with confirmed causes, the engineers who confirmed
them, and component history by serial number, but it misses live condition and the diagram demanding
the vehicle tomorrow.

The depot work orders see closures, slots and a repeat flag, but not the events that preceded the work,
because those events live in the builder's words. The timetable and train running system owns diagrams,
journeys, scheduled and actual times, and delays with cause codes; it sees no condition fact at all, which
is exactly why a drifting converter keeps being scheduled by the timetable rather than by its health. The
track condition monitoring service reports on route assets from wayside vibration data but not on the
vehicles passing over them. The spare parts stock system knows part numbers, stock levels and
reservations, but not what a condition case needs until someone asks it. The passenger incident log
records incidents by trainset, date and category, carrying personal data under the national data protection
law, but not the technical cause behind any of them. Figure 2 sets these systems side by side.

   Figure 2. Eight systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

The one history of a single door requires the diagnostic events from the logs, the vocabulary mapping
from the builder's platform, the fault record from the maintenance system and the closure from the work
order, joined by vehicle and component and time; no single system holds even two of those pieces in the
same words. The traction converter question requires drift evidence joined to the vehicle's diagram, so
that a swap can be drafted before the desert run rather than after the failure. The availability question

requires delays from the running system joined to depot records and part availability, with each figure
citable to its source for the maintenance-included contract. The cost of the gap is the repeat fault that is
worked three times, the desert failure that a swap would have prevented, and the two different stories told
about one late train. The engineers who could join these records by hand are few, and the new builder's
arrival multiplies the vocabularies faster than headcount can follow.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereign Constraints Shape Everything Downstream

Sovereignty inside the operator's network, decisions left to named people, memory without
training, and no replacement of systems of record together fix every choice the design makes
after them.

Chapter 2 showed every system holding one true slice and none holding the one history. This chapter
fixes the four constraints that shape every choice made after them, then records what those choices cost
and what was set aside to keep them.

3.1 Nothing About the Trains Leaves the Country

The boundary is absolute: fleet and passenger data never leave the operator's network, models are open
weights on hardware the operator owns, and no third party model service is called. This is hard in this
industry because the primary condition source is a builder's platform whose license and data terms may
restrict reading, retaining or internally reusing diagnostic events, so the data terms are read and signed
before any event is retained, and the approvals register carries that as a gate. The passenger incident log
brings personal data under the national data protection law, so the data protection impact assessment
and minimization at ingestion complete before the first quarter. The work surface runs on frontier class
open weights self hosted for sovereignty, and the specific weights and the GPU count behind them
remain open work until a model stands verified in the register, which is why no footprint figure is stated
here.

3.2 Every Decision Belongs to a Named Person

Agents draft and people decide: each ConditionCase carries an approving engineer, and each AgentDraft
carries an approval state and a citation set an engineer can check. This is hard because rail safety
governance treats a new platform as a change requiring a significance decision under the safety
management system before any contract-facing output goes live, and a system that acted on trains rather
than advising people would fall inside the CENELEC safety case scope. The design stays advisory and
non-vital: it reads and drafts, and nothing it does touches train control.

3.3 The System Improves by Memory, Not by Training

Improvement is a kept record of decisions and outcomes, the memory of confirmed outcomes, which
each run reads before it acts and which does not update model weights. This is hard because fault
histories in a fleet of this size are small and precious, because the requirement itself states memory
without training a model on the fly, and because weights the operator holds must remain artifacts the
operator can inspect rather than opaque byproducts of a tuning process.

3.4 The Systems of Record Stand

The ontology is a projection over the builders' platforms and the operator's systems, never a migration:
systems of record are read, never replaced, never modified, never loaded. This is hard because two
builders' vocabularies must join with citations, and no packaged product reconciles them. The ontology
examples a team finds in other sectors tend to be schema copies of one system, and a copied schema
cannot carry the load bearing join here, which is the crossing between a builder's diagnostic code and the
operator's work order on a serial-numbered part.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Three scoping decisions follow directly from the constraints, and each buys something at a stated cost,
which Table 1 records. Phase one runs one route for one quarter against the operator's own baselines, so
the riskiest assumption is proven on real extracts before anything extends. Two adapter families carry
every source, so there is exactly one controlled entry path with provenance classes and per-source clock
offsets. All compute is central, in the operator's existing data center, so sovereignty holds by construction
in phase one.

Each major choice had a live alternative, and Table 2 records what was picked, what it beat and why. The

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From Systems of Record to Surfaces

Systems of record sit below untouched, one governed object model sits in the middle, and
the services and surfaces above it all run inside the operator's own in-country data center.

Chapter 3 fixed the constraints and recorded what each scoping decision buys and costs. This chapter
turns those constraints into the stack that carries them: what sits below, what sits in the middle, and what

runs above, all inside the operator's own in-country data center.

4.1 Three Layers in a Fixed Order

The architectural pattern, the layered shape that sovereign AI reference architectures in critical
infrastructure converge on, has three layers whose order never changes. Below sit the ten sources: the
builder remote monitoring platform, the on board diagnostic logs, the maintenance management system,
the depot work orders, the timetable and train running system, the track condition monitoring service, the
spare parts stock system and the passenger incident log, plus two depot camera feeds. They are read in
place, never replaced, never modified and never bulk loaded. In the middle sits one governed object
model of fourteen objects, a projection over those systems rather than a copy of their schemas. Above it
sit six services and four surfaces, where agents draft and named engineers decide. Figure 3 shows the
layers with these counts. The order fits this railway because the fleet's facts live in systems the operator
cannot rewrite: one builder's platform speaks its own vocabulary, a second builder arrives with the new
trainsets, and the question the operator asks, what is the one history of this door, cannot be answered by
copied schemas. It needs one model in which every fact carries the source that produced it.

          Figure 3. The layered stack: 10 sources, 2 adapter families, 14 objects, 6 services and 4 surfaces.

4.2 The Stack Stage by Stage

Table 3 walks the same stack stage by stage, from the sources to the surfaces, and names the
component at each stage. Two adapter families carry the sources in, integration adapters over the
builders' documented APIs and the operator's systems, and telemetry adapters for streams, each
stamping provenance, preserving source vocabulary and carrying per-source clock offsets. The object

model runs on Hyper Ontology v0.9, with Apache Kafka 4.4 in KRaft mode as the event backbone, a time
series store chosen as a class and sized only after phase one counts events per day, Frigate NVR for the
depot cameras, Harbor as the artifact and model registry, Prometheus 3.13 LTS with Grafana and Loki for
observability, and Keycloak for identity. Inference runs centrally in the operator's existing data center on a
GPU node of the 141 GB HBM class; the model register holds no verified entry on this run, so the on-site
language model layer is open work, chosen and sized when a verified model stands in the register. Table
7, printed by the platform from the plan, sets out the same stack as rows of Layer, Component, Choice
and Why, and should be read alongside Table 3.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The shape a team with a similar brief should carry away is the projection, not the objects. Three things
are kept regardless of industry: the fixed layer order, with systems of record untouched below and every
write confined to the model's own objects; adapters that stamp provenance and preserve each source's
own vocabulary and clock, so no source is silently translated on the way in; and the rule that every agent
draft carries citations into objects that a named person approves before anything changes. What a team
swaps is the middle and the edges: the fourteen objects become their own nouns, the two adapter
families become their own sources, and the 141 GB HBM class node becomes their own data center
capacity. The grammar survives the swap, because nouns become objects, facts become properties and
relationships become typed links in any domain, and that grammar is what makes the model queryable
across systems rather than a copy of them.

5.1 Fourteen Objects and Their Typed Links

6.1 Ten Sources, Every One a Read

Ten sources enter the design, and Figure 5 sets out each with its provenance class and its adapter path.
Eight are the operator's systems of record, all of provenance class operator and all read only: the builder
remote monitoring platform, the primary condition source arriving in the builder's words; the on board
diagnostic logs, the raw record behind the builder's events; the maintenance management system,
holding faults, confirmed causes and component history; the depot work orders, whose closures the
repeat-fault baseline counts against; the timetable and train running system, owning diagrams, journeys,
actual times and delays; the track condition monitoring service, whose vibration based reports complete
the route asset picture; the spare parts stock system, feeding part availability into each recommended
depot slot; and the passenger incident log, completing the Incident object under the national data
protection law. The remaining two sources are the depot camera feeds, the inspection road and the siding
overview, of depot provenance and serving as context for the offered tier. Every event that enters carries
its provenance class, so a claim made from builder data is distinguishable, permanently, from a claim
made from depot data.

      Figure 5. The 10 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

The adapter tier makes five guarantees. First, it is read only: the design writes to nothing it reads, and the
writes anywhere are confined to the model's own ConditionCase and AgentDraft objects. Second, source
vocabulary is preserved: a builder's diagnostic code enters as the builder wrote it, recorded in the source
vocabulary property of the DiagnosticEvent, and translation happens in the ontology where it can be cited
and audited rather than at the pipe where it cannot. Third, each source's clock offset is kept, because
every causal claim the model makes, that this fault followed that closure, depends on the builders' and the
depot's clocks agreeing, and a named time source is designed in with per-source offsets rather than

assumed. Fourth, connectivity from moving assets is intermittent, so the adapters buffer rather than block:
when a trainset's link drops on a desert route, events queue and flow on reconnection. Fifth, no packaged
integration product reconciles two builders' vocabularies, which is the ontology's whole point, so the
connectors are bespoke read paths over documented APIs and the operator's own systems.

6.3 The Event Backbone

The backbone is Apache Kafka 4.4 in KRaft mode, running inside the operator's in-country network.
Ordering is per source key, so events from one vehicle keep their sequence even when other vehicles
interleave. Delivery is at least once, with deduplication on event identity at ingest, so nothing is lost in a
reconnection and nothing is double counted in a repeat-fault baseline. Buffering is built into the same
path: queued events from a disconnected trainset resume in order, and the telemetry volume behind them
lands in a time series store chosen as a class and sized only after phase one counts events per day.
Replication stays inside the country, so the backbone itself respects the sovereign boundary, and Harbor
holds every artifact the system runs, so updates to the platform never require an external fetch. The result
is that ingestion can fail quietly, on a dropped link or a slow depot clock, and recover without any system
of record ever knowing the design exists.

7.1 One Inference Tier, in One Room

Phase one has a single inference tier: the operator's data center. Telemetry arrives through the builders'
documented APIs, so there is no on-vehicle serving and no edge serving to specify; the offered
continuous tier would be specified to the EN 50155 class for on-vehicle electronics if taken up later, but
phase one is route based as tendered and commits nothing on the vehicle. What the tier will hold is fixed
even though its size is not. The work surface runs frontier class open weights, self hosted for sovereignty,

on the 141 GB HBM class with eight GPUs per node, which gives about 1,038 GB of usable memory per
node. The arithmetic the register applies when a model row stands: the house's named candidate, GLM
5.3 at FP8, carries about 756 GB of weights, which fits one such node and leaves roughly 280 GB as the
KV cache ceiling, the memory that holds conversation state during generation. That is the smallest of the
three footprints considered for the named model, and it is why the design chose FP8 on one node over
BF16 across two nodes or a larger 256 to 288 GB class node. No GPU count is committed today,
because no model row survived this run's live checks; Figure 6 shows the tier, what runs there and the
boundary drawn around it.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The latency budget is set by decision cadence, not by milliseconds, and no sub-microsecond requirement
exists anywhere in the design; that is why hardware time synchronization was set aside for a software
time class over existing GNSS-disciplined sources, with per-source offsets kept. Three cadences govern.
Condition watching keeps pace with the event stream, so a drifting traction converter is caught while the
trainset can still be re-diagrammed. Agent drafting and the command center conversation stay inside a
fleet engineer's working session, which makes the KV cache ceiling the real constraint on concurrency.
The month-end availability pack is computed on schedule, and the stakes there are external as well as
internal: federal regulation makes railroad service metrics a legal reporting requirement in the United
States (ECFR n.d.), and the regulator's own industry sub-group has shown that metrics members cannot
usefully collect get pruned (STB 2023). The availability figures the new maintenance-included contract will
be measured against must be computable cleanly on the operator's own numbers before anyone outside
asks for them. Because the work surface is a single node class, queueing under load is the pressure
point, and the serving layer is sized against measured load once events per day are counted in phase
one.

7.3 The Boundary and Its Failure Modes

Nothing about the trains crosses the network boundary: fleet and passenger data never leave the
operator's network, the design calls no third party model service, and it writes to nothing outside its own
stores. The inbound paths are confined to the read adapters to the builders' documented APIs and the
systems of record. Updates arrive as artifacts pulled through the Harbor registry inside the boundary, so a
failed update path leaves the platform serving the versions it already holds while the registry remains the
single write path for new ones. When the link to a moving asset drops, ingestion queues rather than
blocks: the event backbone buffers and replays in order, the design's rule for moving assets, whose
connectivity is intermittent by nature. When power fails at the depot tier, a UPS-backed clean shutdown
path protects recordings and indexes so they resynchronize on return; desert heat set the enclosure
thermal budget before any camera was chosen, on the 230/400 V supply the depots run. The two failures
that touch the reasoning tier itself are procurement and approval: the 141 GB class node is ordered at
engagement start so delivery is confirmed before the quarter begins, and the significance decision is filed
under the safety management system before any contract-facing output goes live.

9.4 Lessons

Prove the join before building the agents. The whole design stands on the claim that a door has one
history across two builders' vocabularies, so the first gate spends itself on exactly that: real extracts, real
joins, a fleet engineer reading one history of one door. Everything downstream, the agents, the drafts, the
command center, is built only on that proof. Write the baselines at signature. A repeat-fault count and an
availability figure only mean something against a population and a baseline fixed before watching begins,
which is why the baseline item sits in phase one rather than in a later retelling. Order the hardware when
the engagement starts. The serving node's lead time into the country is the one dependency that can idle
every workstream at once, so the 141 GB class node is ordered at start and its delivery confirmed before
the quarter begins. Treat the data terms as a gate, not paperwork. The builders' license terms decide
whether a diagnostic event may be retained and reused at all, so the signature sits in the approvals
register beside the technical gates it outranks.

and the personal data in the passenger incident log is minimized at ingestion under the national data
protection law. Ownership is demonstrated rather than asserted, because a rehearsed export of ontology
and memory is a phase one deliverable: the operator can walk away carrying everything. Rail safety
researchers have argued that transparency and published data are themselves measures of a national

lenses, the patterns and the equipment the reasoning runs on.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask was a sovereign AI reference architecture for passenger rail fleet condition monitoring, written in
the operator's voice and stating its own constraints: open weight models on the operator's own hardware
in the country, reading the builders' platforms and the operator's systems of record, with nothing about the
trains leaving the country or reaching a foreign model service. Praxis assigned the family Physical AI and
the industry Rail and Transportation; the pin was the FDE's own decision on this project, not a reasoned
match, and the brief was still read as reasoning input. What Praxis read was the corpus shelf of each
lens, nothing ranked or filtered by keyword, and every precedent, rule and equipment class cited in this
paper comes from that reading.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

One pattern was adopted, system of context, as the primary architecture: the FDE pinned it, and the
requirement demands its exact shape, one governed ontology joining two builders' vocabularies, agents
that draft while people decide, memory without training, and a command center the operator owns

outright. The pattern commits three layers in a fixed order, with the systems of record below, never
replaced, never modified, never loaded; the ontology as a projection over those systems, never a shadow
copy; one small grammar in which nouns become objects, facts become properties, relationships become
typed links and actions change them; and a kinetic loop that closes on the model, so the fleet's twin stays
living rather than cached. No pattern was set aside: the reasoning adopted one and found none it needed
to reject.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on four equipment classes: GLM 5.3 Node Count By GPU Class and 141 GB HBM
GPU Class, which together fix the serving footprint; Frontier Model GPU Footprint Sizing Rule (vLLM,
SGLang), which governs how that footprint is derived when a verified model stands in the register; and
Rugged Enclosure Mounting Power UPS NUT SABER, which fixes the enclosure, power and conformity
ground for the offered depot camera tier. Every one of those landings traces to recorded reading, and
nothing in this paper is inferred beyond what was read.

title: Sovereign AI Architecture for a Freight Corridor and Customs Clearance in Saudi Arabia
text:
V E R T I C A L - D R I V E N A R C H I T E C T U R E S · S U P P LY C H A I N & L O G I S T I C S · D E S I G N E D W I T H P R A X I S · N O V E M B E R
2026

Sovereign AI Architecture for a Freight
Corridor and Customs Clearance in
Saudi Arabia
Corridor Command: Industrial AI for the Whole Consignment Story

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the corridor and customs lead, the corridor planners and yard controllers in the loop, and the platform, data and
reliability engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

Where a Box Is Should Not Take Six Systems to Answer
A sovereign AI architecture for a freight corridor in Saudi Arabia starts from the one question the operation
needs answered continuously: where is this consignment, and when will it clear. It cannot be answered
today because the answer lives in six systems of record carrying six identifiers, and it is assembled by
hand by a planner whenever a consignee asks. Corridors of more than two thousand kilometers mix rail
legs with road legs run by contracted hauliers, each consignment crossing the port terminal, the customs
authority's clearance system, the operator's rail yard, a haulier, the dry port and the consignee, while the
authority's single declaration transit with pre clearance and smart inspection now runs on some lanes of a
national truck fleet of around half a million vehicles. Dwell at the dry port grows when a declaration stalls,
and the stall is learned from the consignee rather than from the systems; a late road leg is visible in
telematics but never joined to the train it will miss.

The design is a sovereign corridor and customs system built for a national freight and logistics operator in
Saudi Arabia: seven read-only source systems, two adapter families covering integration and telemetry,

fifteen objects in one governed object model, seven services covering governance, baselines, the
ontology, agents and approvals, the sovereign platform, memory and the command center, and three
surfaces consisting of the command center, the connection view and the answer queue. Every part runs
on the owner's own central node in its in-country data center, on open weights the owner holds, with no
edge inference and no third party model service, so cargo, consignee and declaration data never leave
the country. The model register carries no committed weights on this plan: no open weight model survived
this run's live verification, so the choice of weights is recorded open work with its sizing line, the inference
cluster class (GPU nodes for 300B to 1T parameter open weight models), held ready rather than fixed.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure across the six systems, the constraints and the
scoping decisions they force, the layered stack and the fifteen-object model of the consignment story, the
adapter tier and event backbone that feed it, the placement of all reasoning on the owner's central node,
the model register and the licenses that decide what the owner can own, the three phases with their item
counts and gates, and who owns the intelligence the system produces, closing with the chapter on how
Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.

 Figure 1. Corridor Command on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes,
                                            and the person who decides.

Contents

         Sources                                                                     Reference

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Industrial AI Starts with the Consignment, Not the
Systems

The corridor's cost is not a missing system but a missing object: the consignment no single
system holds, in a country whose customs programs and new corridors are moving faster
than the operators' ability to see one box end to end.

The abstract put the whole sovereign AI architecture on one page: seven sources of record, two adapter
families, fifteen objects, seven services and three surfaces, all inside the owner's own hardware in the
country. This chapter begins where industrial AI has to begin, with the question the operation cannot

answer today, the documented cost of that silence, and the scenario the design must fit without replacing
anything.

1.1 The Question, the Data and the Regimes

The question the operation needs answered is narrow and constant: where is this container, and when
will it clear? The answer requires one key and every story told about it. The container number carries the
whole join, and around it sit the vessel, gate and terminal events that open the consignment's story; the
declaration with its lane, broker and clearance state; the train, its wagons and the handover slot; the road
leg with its haulier and its ETA; the yard state at the destination dry port; and the case log of questions
already asked and answered. The question must also be answered inside four regimes at once. The
customs authority now offers single declaration transit with pre clearance and smart inspection on some
lanes, which the design reads but never acts in. The national data protection regime fixes residency,
cross-border transfer bases and the data protection officer's records of processing duties. The national AI
authority's ethics risk tiers govern how the reasoning tier is classified. The road transport law of 2025 links
the haulier fleet to the authority's electronic platform, which decides which telematics can be relied upon.

1.2 The Documented Cost

The cost of not answering lands in three places: planner hours spent assembling an answer by hand from
six identifiers, dwell hours that grow at the dry port while a stalled declaration goes unnoticed, and the
same questions answered week after week for the authority and for cargo owners. The exposure is
documented at industry scale. Cross-border data transfers are integral to international supply chains,
which depend on information moving across borders for sourcing, finance, logistics and risk management
(Globaldataalliance n.d.), and third-party breaches doubled as a share of all security incidents in the most
recent year, with regulators across Europe and the United States now holding leadership personally
accountable for vendor risk (Cybelangel 2026). When an operator's data flows stop, the physical
operation stops with them: a ransomware attack on a logistics company in October 2025 encrypted its
data and caused a large-scale service stoppage, with leakage of the information it held confirmed by the
company's own investigation (Askullogist 2025). An operator that cannot see one consignment across its
systems cannot even rank which flows it depends on.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The owner runs inland corridors linking seaports to dry ports and freight yards by rail and road, with
corridors of more than two thousand kilometers mixing rail legs with road legs run by contracted hauliers,
and new corridors opened in 2026. The national truck fleet it draws on is around half a million vehicles.
Each consignment crosses several hands: the port terminal, the customs clearance system, the rail yard,
a haulier, the dry port and the consignee. Three roles sit in the loop by name: corridor planners who own
train and slot decisions on shift, yard controllers who hold re booking authority at the dry ports, and
service desk agents who work the case queues. The physical environments are the seaport terminals, the
rail corridors, the yards and dry ports inland, and the road network between them. The regulatory ground

is the national data protection regime, the AI authority's ethics tiers, the road transport law of 2025 and
the customs authority's clearance programs. The estate holds seven named systems of record, three
named roles and four classes of place, and every system is read, never replaced.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Six Identifiers Hide One Consignment From Every
Planner

Each system of record sees one slice of the consignment's story and none can answer the
question they collectively hold, which is why dwell grows silently and knowledge of stalling
lanes, brokers and hours lives only in experienced planners' heads.

Chapter 1 stated the question and the scenario that cannot answer it. This chapter walks each of the
seven systems of record in turn, because the shape of the design follows directly from what each one
sees and what each one misses.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The rail operations and yard management system owns trains, wagons, yard slots and the handover, the
moment the whole corridor story turns on; it cannot see the declaration state behind a wagon's box, so it
schedules a train that clearance will hold. The transport management system owns the road legs and the
haulier assignments; it cannot see the train each leg feeds, so a late truck is late in isolation. The customs
authority's declaration and clearance interfaces own declaration state, the stall signal and the single
declaration transit lanes; they cannot see the physical position of the box a declaration covers, or the slot
its delay consumes. The port community system feeds own the vessel, gate and terminal events that start
the story; they go quiet at the gate. The haulier telematics feeds provide road leg position and ETA; they
carry no commodity, no declaration and no yard state. The container tracking system owns the container
number that joins every system to one consignment; it is a register rather than a story, holding no state
any other system owns. The customer service case log holds the questions asked and the answers sent;
it records what was said about a consignment, not what was true of it. Figure 2 sets these seven slices
side by side, and the register at the end of this chapter states each system's sees and misses in one line.

    Figure 2. Seven systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

What no system holds is the consignment as one object with one identifier and a continuous state, and
the costs follow directly. Dwell at the dry port grows while a declaration stalls, and the operation learns of
the stall from the consignee rather than from any system. A road leg that runs late is visible in telematics
but never joined to the train it will miss, so the handover slot is lost rather than re booked. Experienced
planners know which lane, which broker and which hour of the day stall most often, and none of that is
written anywhere, so it leaves with the shift. The same questions about the same consignments arrive
week after week, because the answer is assembled by hand each time. The join failure is therefore not a
reporting gap but a structural one: the data exists, in seven systems, and no identifier in any one of them
reaches across all six others.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereignty and Six Systems Shape Everything
Downstream

Four constraints, in-country residency under the national data protection regime, ownership
of the weights, projection over the existing systems of record, and a named person behind
every action, decide the architecture before any component is chosen.

Chapter 2 ended with the join failure: one consignment, six identifiers, and knowledge of stalling lanes,
brokers and hours living only in planners' heads. This chapter sets the four constraints that decide the
architecture before any component is chosen, then records what the design bought, what it refused and
what sits outside scope altogether.

3.1 Residency Under the National Data Protection Regime

The first constraint is that cargo, declaration and case data stay on the owner's own hardware in the
country, with nothing reaching a foreign model service. This is hard in this industry because supply chains
are inherently cross-border: their information flows underpin sourcing, finance, logistics and risk
management across jurisdictions (Globaldataalliance n.d.), and haulier telematics in particular may transit
a foreign cloud before they reach the estate, which is a covenant and contract question settled at phase
zero with egress monitoring at the boundary. The regime's transfer bases, the data protection officer's
records of processing duties and the residency rules are carried as phase-zero approvals, not as
assumptions the build outlives.

3.2 Ownership of the Weights

The second constraint is that the reasoning tier runs open weights the owner holds on its own hardware
in the country. This is hard for two reasons the industry cannot negotiate away. The GPU class the sizing
rule names faces export licensing whose timeline sits outside anyone's control, so the license
determination is a phase-zero checkpoint before purchase. And model licenses carry triggers, including
one that fires for a corporate group running a Model as a Service business above 10 billion USD, which is
checked against the owner's group at phase zero, with an MIT-licensed fallback standing behind it.

3.3 A Projection Over the Systems of Record

The third constraint is that the one model of the corridor is a projection over the seven systems, never a
migration and never a shadow copy. A projection differs from the industrial ontology examples a reader
may know: it owns no copy of any record, only the crossing mappings that answer the questions no single
system can. This is hard because each system is a system of record with its own identifier and the join
runs on the container number alone, so the design carries a weekly join-success gate at 95 per cent with
failures triaged by source system, on the grounds that a join failing silently is worse than no join at all.

3.4 A Named Person Behind Every Action

The fourth constraint is that no agent files, amends, re books or cancels anything without a named
approval, and approval authority is an explicit property of the actor objects in the model. This is hard
precisely because the value of the design lies in the actions it proposes: drafted answers with citations, re
booking proposals, stall alerts. The design resolves the tension by agreeing a per-shift alert budget before
thresholds are set and making the action rate a phase gate, so the surface earns attention rather than
demanding it and quietly losing it.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Three scoping decisions follow from the four constraints, and each buys something at a stated cost,
recorded in Table 1: the ontology as a projection rather than a migration, the phase-one corridor only with
extension by measured gates, and memory loops instead of weight changes. Each decision is revisited
only at a gate and never mid-phase, because a constraint traded quietly mid-build is a constraint that was
never held. The gates themselves spend the quarter's measured evidence of dwell, stalls, missed
connections and answered questions against the recorded baseline.

3.6 What the Design Chose Against

Table 2 records where the design made a choice and what it refused in each place, from the serving

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From Records to Reasoning In-Country

The design puts the systems of record below, one governed object model in the middle, and
services and surfaces above, all on the owner's own central node with an event backbone
holding the tiers together.

Chapter 3 fixed the four constraints that shape everything downstream: sovereignty over data and
weights, no replacement of the systems of record, a named person on every decision, and a first gate that
can stop the work cheaply. This chapter lays out the stack that satisfies them, and it is the shape a
sovereign AI architecture in this trade arrives at: records below, one governed model in the middle, agents
and surfaces above.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

Three layers in a fixed order. Below sit the seven systems of record, read only, never replaced, never
modified, never loaded. In the middle sits one governed object model of the corridor, a projection over
those systems rather than a copy of them, so the model can be rebuilt from the sources at any time and
never becomes a second book of truth. Above sit the applications and agents that draft answers,
rebookings and exception chases, all of which become real only when a named person approves them.
Figure 3 shows the layered stack with its counts: seven sources, two adapter families, fifteen objects,
seven services and three surfaces.

The pattern fits because the owner's problem is a join failure, not a data shortage. Every fact the
consignment story needs already exists inside the estate; what is missing is one place where the facts
are already joined. International supply chains ordinarily depend on information moving across borders

(Globaldataalliance n.d.), and this design inverts that habit for the operator's cargo, customer and
declaration data, which stay in the country on the owner's own central node; there is no edge tier, and the
one piece of equipment the design adds is that node, planned at about ten kilowatts of rack power and
cooling in the owner's data center. An event backbone, Apache Kafka 4.3 in KRaft mode, holds the tiers
together by carrying every change the adapters emit, in order. Table 7, printed by the platform from the
plan, gives the layer by layer register of components and choices with the reason for each.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The reusable shape is the whole middle of this design: read-only systems of record below, a projection
ontology joined by typed links, an event backbone carrying changes in order, adapters that guarantee
lineage and staleness flags, and above it all agents that draft while people approve. A team carrying a
similar brief keeps that shape and swaps the contents: their own source systems, their own object list
grown from the nouns and relationships of their operation, their own thresholds, baselines and approval
authorities, and their own hardware class once a model stands in their register. What they should not
swap is the discipline. Sources are never written to, the model is never a second book of truth, and no
action is real until a named person makes it so.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Fifteen Objects Turn Corridor Data Into One Story

The object model makes the consignment the focal object and joins container, declaration,
train, wagon, road leg, haulier, terminal, dry port, handover slot, exception, case and the
three human roles through typed links a document store cannot traverse.

Chapter 4 laid the stack from records to surfaces. This chapter opens the middle layer, the corridor
ontology, where fifteen objects and their typed links turn seven fragmented records into one story a
planner can read.

5.1 Fifteen Objects, One Story

The model holds fifteen objects: Consignment, Container, Declaration, Train, Wagon, Road Leg, Haulier,
Terminal, Dry Port, Handover Slot, Exception, Customer Case, and the three human roles, Corridor
Planner, Yard Controller and Service Desk Agent. The consignment is the focal object, anchored in the
container tracking system, with a status vocabulary that runs from Booked through At port, Cleared, In
transit rail and At dry port to Handed over, with Exception as the turning point. Every other object attaches
through typed links: the declaration joins the container by container number, the train carries its wagon list
and each wagon carries the container in its slot, the road leg names its container and its haulier, the
handover slot books its train, and the exception and the customer case name the consignment they
concern. Figure 4 shows every object and every link.

What the links buy is traversal. Ask for consignments whose declaration has sat Queried past the lane's
normal time, and the model returns a path, not a list: declaration to container to consignment, to the train
and the handover slot it will miss, to the road leg and haulier downstream of that miss, to the open
customer case asking about the same box, and to the corridor planner who holds approval authority over
that train. A document store keyed on consignment cannot make that traverse, because the joins are not
in the documents; they are in the typed links, so the traversal is a query rather than a project. Many
industrial ontology examples stop at naming entities, and this model earns its keep one level up, in the
links between them. Table 8, printed by the platform from the plan, gives each object with the system it is
anchored in and its typed links.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in three places: the corridor planner holds approval authority, the yard controller
holds rebooking authority over handover slots, and the service desk agent works the answer queue. The
single write path is a named approval; no agent files, amends or cancels a declaration on its own, and
agents draft while people decide. The hosting posture keeps everything on the owner's own hardware in
the country. Identity and access run on Keycloak with permissions scoped to the three human roles,
which matters because logistics data leaks from inside as well as from outside: at one parcel operator a
former employee moved more than 26,000 customer records to outside firms, one of which used them for
sales (Nikkei 2025). The estate makes no external model calls; there is no third party model service, and
the boundary holds cargo, customer and declaration data in the country. Memory runs through a kept
record of decisions and outcomes that the next decision reads, so each decision reads the record of
earlier ones before it acts, and nothing is trained into weights.

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Two adapter families, integration and telemetry, put seven named source systems behind
one guarantee of lineage, ordering and staleness flags, so a stall is detected when the data
says so rather than when the consignee calls.

Chapter 5 showed what the object model holds. This chapter shows how data gets into it: through two
adapter families, never directly, so that lineage, ordering and staleness are guaranteed before any agent
reasons over a single fact.

6.1 Seven Sources, All Read

Figure 5 maps the seven named source systems and their adapter paths. The rail operations and yard
management system owns trains, wagons, yard slots and the handover the whole corridor story turns on.
The transport management system owns the road legs and haulier assignments the connection watch
reasons over. The customs authority's declaration and clearance interfaces own declaration state and
clearance events, the stall signal and the single declaration transit lanes. The port community system
feeds own the vessel, gate and terminal events that start the consignment's story. The haulier telematics
feeds provide the road leg position and ETA the connection watch depends on. The container tracking
system owns the container number that joins every system to one consignment. The customer service
case log holds the questions the answer queue drafts against and the record of answers sent. Every
source carries the operator's own provenance class: each fact enters already owned by the operation,
read inbound over agreed channels, with nothing scraped or purchased, and all seven are read only.

       Figure 5. The 7 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

Two families stand between the sources and the backbone. The integration adapter, built on Debezium
with Apache Camel, brings the systems of record in as change events; the telemetry adapter brings the
haulier feeds in as positions and ETAs. Together they guarantee three things. Lineage: every property on
every object traces to a source record and a timestamp, so an answer can cite where each fact came
from. Ordering: clocks across the estate are disciplined by Chrony, so a gate event and a clearance event
on the same consignment can be sequenced. Staleness flags: each interface's cadence is published in
the command center, so a declaration that has not moved reads as no news rather than as cleared, and a
stall is detected when the data says so. One audited seam also has a security value, because logistics
estates are breached through shared infrastructure and third parties: personal data left one provider
through a shared network station (Warehousetotaal 2026), and third-party breaches doubled as a share
of incidents in the most recent year (Cybelangel 2026).

6.3 The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka 4.3 in KRaft mode carries every change the adapters emit. Ordering is per partition keyed
on the container number, so each consignment's story is sequenced within its own lane even when the
whole estate streams concurrently. Delivery is at least once with idempotent handlers keyed on source
record ids, so a replayed event cannot double-write a state change. Buffering is the retained log: when an
interface drops or a scheduled file delivery slips, events wait, and the object model marks the gap rather
than guessing. Replication stays in country, across the owner's own data center racks, and nothing
replicates outside the boundary. Replay is also the recovery path, because a ransomware event stopped
a logistics operator's services outright and encrypted the data it held (Askullogist 2025); the backbone's
retained logs let the object model be rebuilt from the sources without ever writing back to them.

All Reasoning Runs on the Operator's Own Node

There is no edge tier in this design: the central node in the owner's in-country data center
serves every agent and surface, the latency budget is set by the corridor's decision cadence,
and the boundary admits only inbound reads.

Chapter 6 described how seven source systems enter through two adapter families and never directly.
This chapter fixes where the reasoning over that joined data runs, and the answer is short by design:
industrial AI on this corridor does not need an edge tier, because the decisions the system supports run
on a cadence of minutes and hours rather than milliseconds, and the sovereignty the owner demands is
easiest to hold in one place.

7.1 One Tier: the Central Node in Country

There is one inference tier, the owner's central node in the in-country data center, and it serves every
agent and every surface. The design commits no cameras, no roadside compute, no edge orchestration
of containers and no edge model serving, because the corridor is watched through records and telematics
rather than through instruments, and haulier telematics already provide position and ETA. The plan sizes
the estate for the phase-one corridor with this single node, with any scaling decided at the extension
gates rather than assumed at the start.

The memory arithmetic comes from the sizing rule the register records, and it is stated here as that rule
rather than as a committed model row, a distinction Chapter 8 carries in full. GLM 5.3, the model the
requirement names, occupies about 756 GB of weights at FP8 precision, taken as 753B parameters. One
node of the inference cluster class (GPU nodes for 300B to 1T parameter open weight models), with eight
GPUs and about 1,038 GB of usable memory, holds those weights and leaves about 280 GB of KV cache
ceiling, the working memory that determines how much concurrent context the node can serve. The node
is planned at about ten kilowatts of rack power, which is ordinary data-center power and cooling rather
than a field engineering problem. Figure 6 sets the placement out: one node, seven read-only source
systems below it, three surfaces above it, and no second tier anywhere in the picture.

         Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget Is the Decision Cadence

Each decision the system supports has its own clock, and the budget is set by that clock rather than by a
target written in milliseconds. Stall detection watches declarations against lane normal-time baselines,
and it must fire while the stall still costs hours of a nominal 96 hour dry port dwell rather than after the
consignee calls, so its budget is the interval between a declaration's last movement time and the moment
a planner could still act. The connection watch joins a road leg's telematics ETA to the handover slot
window, and its budget is the gap between the ETA update and the window start, because an answer that
arrives after the train has departed is a record rather than a decision. The answer queue drafts replies
with citations and a named service desk agent sends them, so its budget is a working shift and
completeness of citation matters more than a second saved. Scheduled file drops make some interfaces
staler than others, so the command center publishes a per-interface cadence and flags staleness rather
than pretending to a real time it does not have.

7.3 The Boundary Admits Only Inbound Reads

What crosses the network boundary is inbound reads, nothing else: seven interfaces over agreed
channels, each read-only, with the systems of record never replaced, modified or loaded, and the single
write path in the design running from the adapter tier into the object model. Cargo, consignee and
declaration data stay on the owner's hardware in the country, and no third party model service is ever
called. The boundary is drawn against the grain of the industry, since cross-border data transfers are
integral to how supply chains ordinarily run (Globaldataalliance n.d.), and the owner's requirement inverts
that default deliberately. It is also drawn against rising third-party exposure: third-party breaches doubled
as a share of all security incidents in the most recent year (Cybelangel 2026), which is why egress
monitoring sits at the boundary and why the telematics question is asked at phase zero, because haulier
feeds may transit a foreign cloud before they reach the estate.

Each failure path has a stated behavior. When the link fails, staleness flags rise on the affected interfaces,
the object model holds last known state, and exceptions recorded on the feed's return carry their true
detected-at time rather than a smoothed one. When power fails, the node rides the data center's existing
protections, and its about ten kilowatts sit within ordinary rack capacity. When the update path is
exercised, weights and artifacts enter only through the air-gapped artifact registry, verified before anything
is served, so an update can never become an unexamined ingress.

8.1 What the Requirement Names, and What the License Allows

GLM 5.3 is the model the requirement itself names: class open weights, self hosted for sovereignty, of the
frontier class the plan records. Its role is the conversational command center the requirement asks for, the
interface that answers questions about a consignment with citations back into the object model, and it
runs on the single central node of Chapter 7. The sizing arithmetic already stated, 753B parameters at
FP8, about 756 GB of weights on one 141 GB class node with about 280 GB of KV ceiling, is the rule that
fixes its footprint. Its license carries a trigger: it bites a corporate group running a Model as a Service
business above 10 billion USD, so the owner's corporate group is checked at phase zero, and GLM 5.2

under MIT stands as the fallback if the trigger is met. Open weights are what make the ownership real,
because the owner holds the weights on its own hardware and no third party model service ever sees
cargo, consignee or declaration data.

What the register does not do is commit that row. No open weight model survived this run's live checks:
each catalog entry the design cites was verified by a person on the date it carries and was not rechecked
live for this build. That verification is outstanding work before any weights are committed, and the register
records it as open work rather than naming weights it cannot stand behind. The honest position is that the
design runs on weights the owner holds, so which weights is part of what is being bought, and a design
file that invented certainty here would spend the owner's money on it.

9.1 The Phases and Their Gates

The rollout carries three phases and seventeen items, shown with their workstreams and gates in Figure
8. Phase 0 holds two items in two workstreams, governance and residency together with baseline and
gates: residency and data protection compliance, and the phase-one baseline measurement. Nothing
moves until the residency approvals close and the baseline is recorded, because a savings claim without

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

The primary measure is dwell at the dry port, in hours, against a nominal of 96, with a breach when dwell
runs above it; the fault the design watches for is a declaration stall at the seaport, because a stalled
declaration is what turns a scheduled handover into yard congestion the design learns about from the
consignee. Around that headline the quarter counts three more things: stalled declarations by lane, broker
and hour of the day; missed connections, where a road leg running late in telematics is joined to the train
it will miss; and answered questions, the cases the service desk closes with citations from the system
rather than by a planner assembling six identifiers by hand. Two guard measures sit underneath. A weekly
join-success gate at 95 per cent, with failures triaged by source system, protects the container number
join the whole argument rests on. An action rate, the share of drafted answers and re-bookings the
planners actually act on, is itself a gate, because a command center nobody acts on is a screensaver.

9.4 Lessons

Bind the join before the agents. The ontology is a projection over seven systems of record, and the
container number is the one key that crosses all of them; an agent reasoning over a broken join produces
confident nonsense, which is why the source system bindings and lineage gate stands before any agent
triggers and why the join-success gate runs weekly forever after. Publish the cadence of every interface.
A declaration event that arrives on a scheduled file drop is stale by construction, and a stall detector built
on stale events reports yesterday's problem this morning; the command center therefore carries staleness
flags and a per-interface cadence so a planner can see how old every signal is before acting on it. Agree
the alert budget before the thresholds. Thresholds chosen in a vacuum either flood the shift or whisper;
the per-shift alert budget is negotiated with the planners who will receive the alerts, and the action rate
gate holds the design to the bargain. Check licenses and covenants at phase zero, not at purchase. The
GLM 5.3 license trigger, the telematics cloud path and the GPU export license are all contract and
regulatory questions, and each is cheap to ask before anything is bought and expensive to discover after.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Four questions remain open, and each one changes the plan when it settles. The export license
determination for the 141 GB HBM class, against the control categories that govern advanced computing
items, is a phase-zero checkpoint before purchase; settling it sets the order date and the phase-one
hardware timeline, and an unfavourable answer moves the footprint to a different GPU class and a
different node count. The register holds no open-weight model verified live on this run: each catalog entry
was verified by a person on the date it carries and was not rechecked for this build, which is outstanding
work before any weights are committed; settling it fills the serving layer and turns the unsized work
surface footprint into a node count. The telematics covenant question, whether any haulier feed transits a
foreign cloud before reaching the estate, decides whether egress monitoring closes a real gap or guards
an empty one; a logistics peer in the region absorbed a ransomware attack that encrypted data and
stopped services at scale (Askullogist 2025), and an insider leak of more than twenty-six thousand
records at another carrier shows the boundary faces people as well as networks (Nikkei 2025). Finally,
whether chrony's time synchronisation proves sufficient for event ordering decides whether a GNSS
grandmaster class is added at the central site; settling it either confirms the software-only answer or adds
one hardware class to the register.

10.1 What the Operator Owns

The owner owns the object model. Fifteen objects, their status vocabularies and their typed links form a
projection over the seven systems of record, never a copy of them, and the crossing mappings that
answer questions no single system can are the owner's asset; the model survives any change of tooling
beneath it because it is the argument, not the storage. The owner owns the weights and any fine-tunes, if
ever made: the design commits open weights running on the owner's own hardware in the country, so
whatever model the register settles on, the weights sit inside the estate, and under system of context
nothing is trained into them, which means the improvement path never creates a derivative the owner
does not hold outright. The owner owns the decision record: every exception with its confirmed cause,
every approval by a named planner, every re-booking by a named yard controller, and every case

answered with citations, held so the next decision reads what the last one learned about which lane,
which broker and which hour stalls most often. That memory was earned on the owner's corridors and
should compound inside its estate, not inside a vendor's. The owner owns the boundary: cargo,
consignee and declaration data stay on its hardware in the country, no third-party model service is called,
and the egress monitoring at the boundary exists to keep that covenant true rather than to assert it.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja designed this system on Praxis, its platform for designing physical AI systems, and the design
maps directly onto what CodeNinja builds: the object model that projects seven systems of record into
one corridor argument is Hyper Ontology; the command center and the work surface where the owner's
own people build and adjust agents is Hyper Pragma; the kept record of decisions and outcomes that
each next decision reads, which improves the operation without touching model weights, is Hyper
Engram; the posture of open-weight models on the owner's own hardware, inside the country, with the
export-license and residency questions carried as phase-zero checkpoints, is Sovereign Infrastructure.
The design is the argument that these pieces belong together, and the ownership chapter is where the
argument lands: everything the quarter measures, and everything the memory learns from it, stays with
