One Projection, One Memory, One Answer, Held
Sovereignly
The design is one projection over six systems of record that never replaces or modifies them: an object
model of fifteen objects joined by typed links anchored on the container number, adapters that guarantee
lineage for every event, all reasoning on the owner's own in-country node under open weights, a memory
of decisions and outcomes that improves the corridor without training any model, and a command center
where a named planner, yard controller or service desk agent approves every action and every answer
carries citations. The first measured quarter gates every extension beyond the phase-one corridor, so the
system grows only on evidence the operation itself produced.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes three things the operation must already hold: systems of
record whose identifiers can be resolved to one anchoring key, an in-country place for the node and its
power, and named people willing to own each decision the agents draft. Swap the object vocabulary for
the local corridor's nouns, rebind the adapters to the local source systems, re-run the export license and
residency checks for the destination country, and the same fixed order of layers, the same rule of
projection rather than migration and the same gated phases carry a different corridor to the same
sovereign answer.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

One pattern was adopted, as primary: System of context. Its three layers sit in a fixed order, with the
systems of record below, never replaced, never modified, never loaded; the ontology in the middle as a
projection over them rather than a shadow copy, its crossing mappings answering the questions no single
system can; and the applications and agents above. Its grammar is small and it is the reason the object
model reads as it does: nouns become objects, facts become properties, relationships become typed
links, and actions change status along a controlled vocabulary. Its kinetic loop closes on the model,
sense, decide, act, learn, with the return edge making the model living rather than a diagram. Nothing
was set aside, and no precedent on the shelf was rejected: the proven-solutions shelf was not searched
before the record closes, and that absence is carried as honest open work rather than dressed up as a
choice.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on three equipment classes: the inference cluster class (GPU nodes for 300B to 1T
parameter open weight models), the model GPU footprint sizing rule for the vLLM and SGLang serving
runtimes, and the GLM 5.3 node count by GPU class. Together they fix the footprint at one central node in
the owner's own data center, about ten kilowatts of rack power and cooling, with no edge tier, no cameras
and no new field sensing anywhere in the design, because the corridor is read through records and
telematics rather than instruments. Every figure in this chapter, from the records read to the citations per
lens to the memory arithmetic, was recorded reading, and nothing is inferred: what the reasoning did not
reach is stated as open work, and what it settled is traceable to the record that settled it.

title: Sovereign AI Architecture for Distribution Loss and Theft Reduction in Pakistan
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · ENERGY & UTILITIES · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

Sovereign AI Architecture for
Distribution Loss and Theft Reduction in
Pakistan
Energy & Utilities Watch: One Living Picture of the Operation

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the leaders accountable for energy & utilities operations, their supervisors, and the data and platform engineers
who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

The Answer Already Exists in the Systems the Operation
Runs
A sovereign AI architecture for loss and theft reduction at an electricity distribution company in Pakistan:
open weight models on the operator's own hardware in the country, reading its systems of record, with
nothing about its customers leaving the country or reaching a foreign model service.

The design reads 7 source systems through 1 adapter family into one object model of 15 objects, runs 8
services over it and opens 5 surfaces to the people who decide, with 3 models placed where the data is.
A sovereign, operator-owned platform that joins seven systems of record into one governed ontology of
the network and its customers, computes each transformer's energy in against energy billed, and lets a
loss agent, a tamper agent and a billing agent draft ranked causes, case files and corrections that
subdivision engineers, inspection officers and revenue officers approve, with every confirmed outcome
kept as a decision record that improves the next ranking, and every theft case ending in a court-ready
Grade 17 complaint. Phase one runs one circle of feeders for one quarter against a measured baseline

with unchanged control feeders, on GLM 5.3 self hosted in an in-country data center, gated on four
numbers before any other circle is touched.

The paper covers the operation and the problem its systems cannot answer, the constraints, the stack,
the object model, ingestion, inference placement, the models and their licenses, the rollout and its proof,
ownership, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.

     Figure 1. Energy & Utilities Watch on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it
                                         computes, and the person who decides.

Contents

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

A Daily Question Goes Unanswered in the Systems That
Hold the Data

The operation holds every fact the question needs and no system answers it.

The abstract posed the question and promised a sovereign AI architecture that answers it inside the
operator's boundary. This chapter states the question precisely, prices the cost of leaving it unanswered,
and fixes the scenario the design must serve.

1.1 The Question and the Data It Requires

The operation needs one question answered every day for every transformer: why does the energy that
entered leave a gap between what was measured in and what was billed downstream, and what should
the inspection team do about it today. The data that answers it sits in four places at once. The energy
entering each transformer comes from the feeder-head and transformer metering; the energy billed to
every service connection downstream sits in the billing system; the topology that ties a meter to a
transformer to a feeder sits in the geographic information system; and the human record of tamper
events, inspections and closed cases sits in three further systems. The answer must also satisfy several
regimes at once: the national program replacing every conventional meter by the end of 2026, a

government-ordered technical audit of billing systems now under way, privatisation preparations that
place every process under external scrutiny, and theft prosecutions brought under the Penal Code section
for electricity theft, filed as a Grade 17 complaint before the Electricity Utilities Court. Those regimes
constrain the means as well as the ends, because the operator's requirement is explicit that nothing about
its consumers may leave the country or reach a foreign model service.

1.2 The Documented Cost of the Problem

The direct cost is stated in the operator's own requirement: companies of this class lose a large share of
the energy they buy to technical losses, theft and unbilled supply, and the sector's distribution losses ran
to hundreds of billions of rupees in the last financial year. The cost of mishandling the data that would fix it
is documented publicly. A utility in North America paid a 2.7 million dollar penalty after a vendor exposed
its data (Natlawreview 2018), and a Japanese utility was issued business improvement recommendations
by its market surveillance commission after consumer information obtained through a third party was
leaked and accessed (Chuden 2023). Energy sector operators are explicit targets of state-sponsored
cyber actors (CISA 2022), and a regulator elsewhere has opened a board inquiry into a cybersecurity
incident at a power company (Nserbt 2025). Any architecture that sends consumption records abroad to a
hosted model service carries exactly this class of exposure, which is why the boundary is a cost line here
and not a slogan.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is an electricity distribution company in Pakistan, described by class only. It distributes
power through hundreds of grid stations and thousands of feeders to several million consumers, and it
knows its losses by feeder a month late and by transformer almost never. The people in the loop are
subdivision engineers who own feeders, inspection officers and field teams who visit meters and
transformers, revenue officers who own billing corrections, and the Grade 17 officer who signs each theft
complaint; the loss reduction team works from a command center, and all compute runs in an in-country
data center or colocation on the operator's own hardware. The physical environments are the field, where
inspections happen and photographs are taken, and that data center, where every model runs. The
regulatory ground combines the meter replacement program, the billing audit, privatisation conditions and
the Penal Code theft route through the Electricity Utilities Court. The design counts seven named systems
of record, the roles listed above, and places counted as grid stations, feeders, transformers, circles,
subdivisions and courts; phase one runs one circle of feeders for one quarter before any other circle is
touched.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System Sees One Slice of the Operation

Each system of record sees its own part of the answer and none sees the whole.

Chapter 1 fixed the question and the regimes it must satisfy. This chapter walks the seven systems of
record one by one and shows that each holds one slice of the answer and none holds the whole.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The consumer information and billing system sees every account with its billed units, tariff and arrears,
but it cannot say which transformer feeds the premises or whether the billed units match the energy that
reached it. The meter data management system sees interval load and tamper events for every smart
meter, but not the billing history of the account behind that meter or what an inspection later found there.
The energy audit records hold the loss percent per feeder each month and almost never per transformer,
and they carry no tamper events, no inspections and no case outcomes. The geographic information
system holds the topology from meter to transformer to feeder to grid station, which is the skeleton of
every energy balance, but it holds no measurement at all. The outage and complaint system records
outages and complaints with times and places, which is what separates a supply problem from theft, yet it
cannot join either to the meters and accounts affected. The meter reading and inspection app holds field
findings and photographs, but the team using it arrives without the tamper alarms or the billing history that
would tell it where to look. The theft case register holds case numbers, penal sections and recovery
amounts, while the evidence that would have made each case defensible was never joined to it. Figure 2
sets these seven views side by side, converging on the question none of them can answer alone.

   Figure 2. Seven systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

No system joins energy in against energy billed at transformer level with the tamper record, the inspection
record and the topology in one argument, and that join is the whole answer. In practice a feeder losing a
third of its energy has hundreds of possible causes: a tampered meter, an illegal connection, an
overloaded transformer, a wrong meter multiplier, a reading never taken. Because no system ranks those
causes, field teams are sent on hunches, tampering events reported by the meters are never joined to
billing history or the inspection record, and case files are assembled by hand and fall apart on paperwork.
The engineers who know which neighbourhoods and which hours the losses come from are retiring or
leaving ahead of privatisation, so the tacit knowledge that once substituted for the join is walking out of
the building.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Four Constraints Shape Everything Downstream

The goals, the scoping decisions and the exclusions were fixed before any component was
chosen.

Chapter 2 showed the join failure: seven systems, seven slices, no shared argument. This chapter fixes
the goals and the exclusions that every component choice downstream had to satisfy.

3.1 Sovereignty Is a Boundary, Not a Preference

The first goal is that the operator owns the intelligence it produces: open-weight models served on its own
hardware inside the country, reading its systems of record, with nothing about its consumers leaving the
country or reaching a foreign model service. This is hard in this industry because the hardware itself is
governed: export controls turn on total processing performance, so the GPU class a frontier model needs
requires a license determination before any card is committed for Pakistan, with a non-US accelerator
class held open as the alternative. Hosted model services are ruled out twice over, by the operator's own
requirement and by the documented cost of utility data exposure abroad (Natlawreview 2018).

3.2 One Governed Model of the Network and Its Consumers

The second goal is a single governed ontology joining all seven systems of record, so that a query can
walk from a feeder through its transformers to a meter, its readings, its tamper events and its closed
cases. This is hard because no packaged connector set exists for the seven systems of a distribution
company of this class: each connector is built as real work, and billing and network records change on
their own cycles, so the design must choose carefully which systems are worth streaming and which are
worth batching.

3.3 Every Decision Carries a Name, and Every Outcome Feeds the Next Ranking

The third goal is that agents draft and people decide: subdivision engineers, inspection officers and
revenue officers approve every ranked cause, case file and correction, and every confirmed outcome is
kept as a decision record that the next ranking reads, without training a model on the fly. This is hard
because approvals degrade into rubber-stamping as trust builds, and rubber-stamped approvals logged
as ground truth poison what the next ranking learns from; the design therefore polices its own approvers
with known-answer probes and steps an agent class back to shadow mode when the upheld rate falls.

3.4 Proof Before Scale

The fourth goal is a measured claim before expansion: phase one runs one circle of feeders for one
quarter against a measured baseline, with unchanged control feeders, and gates any extension on four
numbers. This is hard because privatisation pressure rewards fast numbers, while only untouched control
feeders make the numbers defensible before the billing audit; the discipline of not touching the other
circles is the price of a causal claim.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Three decisions fixed the design's shape before any component was chosen, and each bought something
at a stated cost. Table 1 records them.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From the Systems of Record to the
Surfaces

Systems of record below, one object model in the middle, services and surfaces above.

Chapter 3 fixed the constraints: the country's boundary around every byte, the join before the analytics, a
named officer behind every action, and a measured gate before any extension. This chapter turns those
constraints into a stack of named components, each of which the operator can hold, inspect and replace.

4.1 Why the Pattern Fits

The pattern is the three layers with one direction of dependence that a sovereign AI architecture for a
utility converges on. Below sit the seven systems of record exactly as they run today, named in full in
Table 3: the billing, meter data, energy audit, geographic network, outage, field inspection and theft case
systems. None is replaced and none is bypassed. In the middle sits one object model, fifteen objects with
typed links, each anchored in exactly one system of record, holding the join no single system can make.
Above it sit the applications and agents: eight services that compute each transformer's energy in against
energy billed, rank causes, draft case files and corrections and record approvals, and five surfaces that
put those drafts in front of the subdivision engineers, inspection officers and revenue officers who decide.

The pattern fits because the operator's problem is a join failure, not a sensing failure: the meters already
report tampering and the registers already record cases, but no system can answer which transformer,
which cause, which case in one question. A middle layer that owns the join lets every system keep its role
while the intelligence compounds above it, and because the agents only draft and the officers approve,
nothing above the object model ever writes to a system of record directly. Figure 3 shows the layered
stack with its counts: seven sources, one adapter family, fifteen objects, three models, eight services and

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Fifteen Objects Turn Operational Data Into One
Argument

The object model is the join the systems never made.

Chapter 4 placed one object model at the center of the stack and gave every other layer its reason: the
adapters feed it, the services read it, the surfaces show it. This chapter opens the model itself, object by
object and link by link.

5.1 Every Object and Its Typed Links

The model holds fifteen objects: the grid station as its one site; the feeder, the distribution transformer, the
service connection and the meter as assets; the interval load as its one measure; the reading, the billing
account, the tariff, the theft case and the recovery as records; the inspection, the tamper event and the
approval as events; and the agent draft as the document the whole loop turns on. Each is anchored in
exactly one system of record, so provenance sits on every object's face: the transformer's energy in and
energy billed come from the energy audit records, the meter's seal state from the meter data
management system, the theft case's court and PPC section from the theft case register.

The typed links are what make the model an argument rather than a filing system. A grid station supplies
feeders; a feeder is metered at its head and carries transformers; each transformer serves service
connections; each connection carries a meter and is billed under a tariff; a meter reports interval load,
yields readings and raises tamper events; an inspection visits a meter; a tamper event opens a theft case;
a theft case yields a recovery; and an approval settles an agent draft. Figure 4 shows every object and
every link, with the transformer at the center in navy.

One traversal across those links answers the question field teams actually ask: every transformer on a
feeder whose monthly loss percent crossed its threshold, the tamper events its meters raised in the same
window, what was billed to the connections it serves, and which inspections already visited. That question
crosses four systems of record, and a document store can answer it only if the words co-occur in one
document, which they never do, because the tamper event lives in one system, the billing history in
another and the inspection findings in a third. Table 8, printed by the platform, records each object with
the system it is anchored in and its typed links.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The loop lives inside the model, not around it. Every agent draft is an object carrying its draft type, ranked
causes, evidence citations, model version and confidence, and its status moves through drafted,
approved, amended, rejected and expired; every approval is an object carrying the approver role, the
officer grade, the timestamp, the artifact hash and the written reason, and the hash ties the approval to
the exact draft text it settled. The surfaces are where the loop is worked: the command center where the
loss reduction team sees feeders and transformers by loss, the approval queue, the case file queue, the
correction queue and the printable complaint pack.

The hosting posture follows the requirement. The model and every service above it run in an in-country
sovereign data center or colocation on the operator's own hardware; identity is held by Keycloak inside
the boundary; there are no external links; and no consumer record leaves the country or reaches a
foreign model service. The single write path out of the platform is the approved correction: reading and
multiplier corrections land in the customer information and billing system, and approved theft cases land
in the theft case register, each through the adapter tier and each traceable to the approval object that
authorized it.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Nothing reaches the object model except through an adapter that owns its contract.

Chapter 5 described what the object model holds. This chapter describes how data gets into it: seven
sources, one adapter family, and a backbone that keeps every event ordered, buffered and inside the
country.

6.1 Seven Sources and Their Provenance

All seven sources are the operator's own commercial systems of record, provenance class operator, read
direction only: the customer information and billing system, the meter data management system, the
energy audit records per feeder and transformer, the geographic information system of the network, the
outage and complaint system, the meter reading and inspection app and the theft case register. Each
earns its place: billed units and tariffs are half of every transformer's energy balance, interval load and
tamper events are the live sensing, the audit records are what the computed balances are validated
against, the geographic system ties meters to transformers to feeders to stations, outage and complaint
context separates supply problems from theft in the rankings, the field app is where approved inspections
land and findings and photographs return as evidence, and closed cases are what the next ranking learns
from.

The transport is split deliberately, as Figure 5 shows. The meter data management system is read
through a Kafka subscription, because interval load and tamper events lose their value if they wait for a
batch; billing, energy audit, geographic and outage records arrive as scheduled batch extracts, because
they change on their own cycles and streaming them would add connector risk without improving a
monthly transformer balance; and the field app and the theft case register are reached through mapped
connectors built for their interfaces, because no packaged connector set for a distribution operator's
records exists on any shelf.

          Figure 5. The 7 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

The adapter tier owns every contract, and the guarantee is absolute: no service reads a source directly,
and no source is written except through an approved correction path. Each adapter maps the source's
schema onto the object model, normalizes units and timestamps, and carries the meter multiplier through
untouched, because a wrong multiplier is itself one of the ranked causes, not something to silently
correct. Every extract is minimized to the agreed fields, stamped with its provenance, and written
idempotently so a re-handed over event collapses rather than duplicates. Each feed carries a freshness
window with stale and flatline detection: a stale feed flags its drafts and holds them, and the staleness is
visible on the command center, so no ranking rides on data nobody noticed had stopped.

Minimization is defense, not courtesy. A leak of consumer information through an operational system drew
business improvement recommendations from a market surveillance commission in another utility
(Chuden 2023), and a vendor data exposure cost a utility a seven-figure penalty (Natlawreview 2018);
both were records leaving through a path nobody owned. Here every path is owned by one adapter, every
extract stays inside the country, and every field in it is agreed.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka is the backbone. Interval load and tamper events travel on topics partitioned by meter
number, so ordering holds per meter, which is the ordering a balance and a tamper join need; delivery is
at least once, and the adapters' idempotent writes make re-delivery harmless. Buffering absorbs the
bursts a head end produces after an outage, and replication inside the in-country data center means a
broker loss does not lose a tamper event. Updates arrive the same way everything else does, as
versioned images through the Harbor registry and never over an open link; Chrony keeps the clocks
aligned so an event joins to the right billing period; and Prometheus watches consumer lag, so a feed
falling behind is seen before it goes stale.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Inference Belongs Where the Data Is

Each tier runs what its data and its link can carry.

Chapter 6 described how seven systems of record enter through one adapter family, as event streams for
the meter data and as scheduled batch extracts for the billing, audit, geographic, outage and case
records. This chapter fixes where the inference over that data runs, and what the arithmetic of that
placement obliges.

7.1 Each Tier and Its Arithmetic

All inference runs in one place: an in-country sovereign data center or colocation, on hardware the
operator owns. There is no edge tier, because the smart meters and their head end already exist and the
platform reads them from the data center rather than adding compute beside them; there is no hosted tier,
because the operator's own requirement is that nothing about its consumers leaves the country or
reaches a foreign model service. What the design carries instead is three serving classes inside that one
boundary, and Figure 6 shows each tier, what runs on it and what crosses the boundary to reach it: a
frontier node for the work surface model, and a dual-socket server with a 48 GB PCIe inference GPU that
hosts the embedder and the forecaster together.

The frontier tier carries GLM 5.3, whose filed parameter count is 753 billion. At FP8, one byte per
parameter, that is 753 GB of weights; the 1.2 planning factor for KV cache and activations lifts what the
GPUs must hold to 904 GB. One node of eight GPUs of the 141 GB class provides 1,128 GB, which
holds the weights with 375 GB left beside them against the 151 GB the planning factor reserves, so the
KV cache ceiling is comfortable rather than marginal. The FP8 choice is the reason one node suffices: at
BF16 the same model is roughly 1.5 TB of weights, which demands a second node and doubles the
export-control exposure for an accuracy gain the ranking and drafting tasks have not been shown to
need. Export control is itself a placement constraint, not just a procurement one: US ECCN 3A090 and
4A090 controls turn on total processing performance, so a license determination precedes any card
commitment for Pakistan, and a non-US accelerator class stays open as the alternative. That
determination may change which accelerator the node carries; it never changes which country the node
sits in.

The second tier is deliberately small. The embedding model at FP16 occupies about 1.1 GB and the
forecaster at FP32 about 0.48 GB, so both fit on the 48 GB card with two orders of magnitude of
headroom, which is why the design gives them one server rather than two.

           Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The design has no control loop, and nothing in it is allowed to touch one, so its latency budget buys
interaction rather than reaction. The outer bound is set by the work itself: a transformer's monthly energy
balance is computed on the billing cycle, and a feeder's loss percent moves monthly. Inside that outer
bound the budget tightens in three steps. Tamper events must be joined to billing history and drafted as
case files within a working day, so an inspection officer opens a queue that is already populated. The loss
boards must refresh on the cadence of their feeds, not on the cadence of anyone remembering to run a
report. And the command center's conversational interface must answer with citations at reading pace,
which local serving on the operator's own hardware holds without any inference call leaving the network.
Every hop, from Kafka through the object model to the surfaces, stays inside the operator's boundary,
which is what makes the budget credible: there is no wide-area round trip in any path an officer waits on.

7.3 The Boundary and Its Failures

What crosses the network boundary is reads, and reads only. The meter data management system is
read through a Kafka subscription; billing, energy audit, geographic information, outage and case records
arrive as scheduled batch extracts. The single inbound crossing is the artifact path: model weights and
container images enter through the Harbor registry as versioned artifacts, never as a call to a foreign
service. This posture answers documented threats rather than hypothetical ones. State-sponsored actors
have been indicted for targeting the energy sector specifically (CISA 2022), and a vendor data exposure
at a utility drew a seven-figure reliability penalty (Natlawreview 2018), so a design that keeps consumer
data off every external path is answering the sector's recorded history, not a general caution.

Each failure path has a stated behavior. If the link to a system of record fails, Kafka buffers the meter
event stream and the batch extracts simply wait for their next schedule; per-feed freshness windows with
stale and flatline detection flag any feed whose age exceeds its window, drafts built on stale feeds are
held rather than sent, and staleness is visible on the command center so no one acts on a silent gap. If
power fails, the data center's own resilience carries the platform and Kafka's replication preserves
undelivered events for replay. If the update path fails, the artifact registry means the running versions
continue to serve; a failed weight or image update leaves the previous version in place rather than leaving
the platform down, and the retry is another artifact pull inside the same controlled path.

The License Decides What the Operator Can Own

Every model was chosen against its license before its accuracy.

Chapter 7 placed three serving classes inside one in-country data center and showed the arithmetic that
fits them there. This chapter names the three models that occupy those classes, and shows why each

one's license was weighed before its accuracy: a license decides whether the operator can hold the
weights at all. The model stack is small by design, and Figure 7 shows it whole: one frontier model for the
work surface, one embedding model for cited retrieval, one forecaster for the energy balances that trigger

parameter count is 753 billion, served at FP8, which is about 756 GB of weights and roughly 1.5 TB if
served at BF16; it runs on one node of eight GPUs of the 141 GB class, in the central tier. Its role is the
agentic work surface and ontology maintenance: the command center's conversational interface, the
drafting of ranked causes, case files and corrections, and the upkeep of the governed object model all run
on it. Its license is the GLM-5.3 bespoke license, whose terms permit commercial use, fine-tuning and
redistribution, and those three permissions are exactly what an operator-owned system needs: the
operator can hold the weights, serve them for its own commercial purpose, and keep serving them
regardless of any vendor's fortunes.

8.1 Three Models, Three Licenses

BGE-M3 is the embedding model. It occupies about 2.27 GB at float32 as published, about 1.1 GB at the
FP16 serving precision chosen here, and about 0.6 GB at 8 bit, and it runs on the 48 GB PCIe inference
GPU beside the forecaster. Its role is retrieval embedding for cited answers: the command center
answers with citations, which means tariff codes, meter numbers, PPC sections and inspection findings
must survive retrieval exactly, and BGE-M3 provides dense, sparse and multi-vector retrieval in a single
pass over an 8,192-token window, long enough to embed a full inspection finding rather than a truncated
one. It is MIT licensed. It was chosen over multilingual E5, whose 512-token window cannot hold a long
finding, and over Nomic v2, whose Matryoshka truncation this design has no use for.

Chronos-2 is the forecaster. It occupies about 0.48 GB at 32 bit, about 0.24 GB at 16 bit, and runs at
FP32 on the same 48 GB card. Its role is transformer and feeder energy balance forecasting: it forecasts
multivariate series with covariates zero-shot, so the residual between each transformer's forecast and its
measured balance is the anomaly signal, with no training run anywhere in the loop. That last clause is a

requirement, not a convenience: the operator asked that the next ranking be better without training a
model on the fly, so improvement runs on the kept record of confirmed causes and closed cases, never
on the weights. Chronos-2 is Apache-2.0 licensed, and it was chosen over TimesFM 3.0 and Moirai 2.0,
whose non-commercial terms cannot ship in an operator-owned system no matter how well they forecast.

The license test is the same for all three, and it is the chapter's argument. A non-commercial or service-
only term would convert a sovereign system into a rented one, and a utility that leaked consumer
information through a third party has already shown what such dependencies cost in regulatory response
(Chuden 2023). Every model here is held as weights inside the country, on the operator's own hardware,
under terms that let the operator keep them.

Shadow Mode Comes Before Any Flag Is Trusted

The rollout earns each phase at a gate the operator can read.

Chapter 8 fixed the model stack and the licenses that let the operator hold every weight it runs. This

9.1 Phases, Workstreams and Gates

The rollout is two phases, and neither is a schedule: each phase is a set of items with an exit gate, and
the gate, not a date, moves the work forward. Phase 1, one circle and one quarter, carries 15 items
across six workstreams: the network and customer ontology, loss analytics, the loss and theft agents,
approvals and audit, the sovereign platform, and measurement. Its items include the governed network
and customer ontology, the meter and tamper event stream ingest, and the billing and network record
batch extracts. Its exit gate is the billing agent drafting corrections: reading and multiplier corrections that
a subdivision engineer approves and that land back in the customer information and billing system only
through the recorded approval path. The phase runs on GLM 5.3 self hosted in an in-country data center,
across one circle of feeders measured against a baseline, with control feeders left unchanged so the
comparison stays honest. Phase 2, extending to the other circles, is a single item in the measurement
workstream: the circle extension gate and the rollout plan. No other circle is touched until the four
numbers that gate reads are met. Requirement coverage holds the design to the same discipline: 29
requirements trace through the two phases, so an item that serves no requirement does not enter the
plan, and a requirement with no item is visible as a gap rather than silent. Figure 8 sets the phases, their
item counts, their workstreams, their gates and the requirement coverage on one page.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

Phase 1 measures against a baseline the operator already trusts, and the control feeders carry the
counterfactual. The computed transformer balances, energy in against energy billed, are validated against
the existing energy audit records per feeder and transformer before any agent ranking is read. Beyond
the balances, the phase measures the confirmation rate of agent-ranked causes at inspection, the
acceptance rate of case files at the Grade 17 gate, and the outcome of billing corrections in the system of
record itself. It measures the meters actually delivering interval load and tamper events, reported
separately from meters installed, because the two populations diverge exactly when the rollout outruns
the interface. It measures approval quality through known-answer probes in the normal queue, and feed
health through per-feed freshness windows. These measurements feed the four numbers the circle
extension gate reads, and the gate is the single path from one circle to the next.

9.4 Lessons

Shadow the agents before anyone approves them. The trust that matters is the approvers', not the
platform's, and trust built without measurement becomes rubber-stamping. The probe mechanism exists
because an approval queue that is never tested cannot show that it has stopped judging, and a poisoned
record of confirmed causes cannot be un-poisoned later. Report meters delivering data, not meters
installed. An installed meter that has dropped out of smart mode is indistinguishable from a conventional
one at the data center, and a loss ranking built on the installed count silently overstates its own coverage.
The delivery count is the honest denominator for every coverage claim the command center makes. Treat
the export license as a design input, not a procurement step. The controls turn on total processing
performance, so the determination changes which accelerator class the sizing arithmetic runs on. Making
it a checkpoint before any card is committed keeps the design portable between US and non-US classes
instead of re-planned after a refusal.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Four questions stay open, and each has a named consequence. The measured interval rate is not yet
stated, so the time series store is committed at design against that rate rather than now; settling it fixes
the store and the retention arithmetic. The export license determination may move the node between
accelerator classes without moving it out of the country; settling it fixes the hardware class and the node
count. Interface charges levied by the operator's own vendors on the seven systems of record are
payable by the operator; settling them fixes the connector cost line. The blind spot on conventional meters
and unmetered taps closes only as the national program completes; until then the design bounds that
loss without attributing it.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Three patterns were adopted. The asset to alert to work order pattern shapes the whole object model: a
crossing threshold or a tamper alarm becomes a tamper event or an agent draft linked to the exact meter
or transformer, and it is resolved by an inspection or an approval, never by editing a status field. The
energy-balance pattern drives the analytics: each transformer's energy in against energy billed, forecast
by Chronos-2 so the residual against the transformer's own baseline is the anomaly signal with no training
run. The recorded-approval pattern guards every write: the single path into a system of record is an
approval carrying an artifact hash and a written reason. Three were set aside. Fine-tuning on historical
case labels was rejected because the labels are biased by where inspections happened to be sent on
hunches, and because the requirement forbids training on the fly. Streaming all seven systems of record
was rejected in favour of event streams for meter data and batch extracts for billing, energy audit, GIS
and outage records, since billing and network records change on their own cycles and streaming them
adds connector risk without improving a monthly balance. BF16 serving on two nodes was rejected in

favour of FP8 on one node of the 141 GB class, because the accuracy gain has not been shown to be
needed and the doubling carries export-license exposure.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on four equipment classes and their sizing rules: the frontier inference cluster class
(GPU nodes for 300B to 1T parameter open weight models) for the frontier work surface model, sized
from its filed parameter count at FP8 with the planning factor for KV cache and activations; the frontier
model GPU footprint sizing rule under vLLM; the GLM 5.3 node count by GPU class, one node of eight
GPUs holding the weights with room beside them; and the on site inference server class hosting the
embedder and the forecaster in the same sovereign data center. Every choice traced in this chapter, and
every figure in it, was recorded reading: what the lenses saw, what the shelf held and what the operator's
own requirement stated. Nothing is inferred, and nothing enters the design that the reading did not
contain.

title: Physical AI System Design for Composite Part Inspection in an Aviation MRO in Saudi Arabia
text:
V E R T I C A L - D R I V E N A R C H I T E C T U R E S · AV I AT I O N & A E R O S PA C E M A N U FA C T U R I N G · D E S I G N E D W I T H P R A X I S ·
NOVEMBER 2026

Physical AI System Design for
Composite Part Inspection in an Aviation
MRO in Saudi Arabia
Damage Draft: Sovereign AI Reference Architectures for Composite Repair in Aviation and
Aerospace Manufacturing

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the shop's accountable engineering leader, the certifying and design engineers who approve and sign, and the
platform, data and edge engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

Physical AI System Design Begins at the Inspection
Bench
A physical AI system design for an aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul provider in Saudi Arabia that
repairs radomes, flight control surfaces, nacelle panels and fan cowls for commercial single aisle and
wide body fleets starts from one question at the bench: does this damage on this part fall inside the
allowable limit, and what has this part type suffered in the same place before? Today that question is
assembled by hand from photographs stapled to a paper traveller, scan files stranded on the scanner's
own computer and a findings log joined to nothing, so the same disbond on the same panel type is
assessed from scratch every time, and no query the shop would recognize as simple can be run at all; the
physical AI system design that would fix this must keep customer records, scan images and licensed
manual content inside the shop's own network, on the operator's own hardware.

The design is a sovereign system of context built over the shop's existing systems of record: seven
sources enter through two adapter families into a governed ontology of sixteen objects, five services run
over that model, and eight surfaces carry the work to the people who sign; six models serve the whole,
with zero-shot and anomaly vision models on sealed fanless edge units at one inspection bench and one
scan station, a dense multimodal reader and a retrieval embedding model on a 48 GB-class site inference
card, and a 753B-parameter frontier model served at FP8 on one node of eight 141 GB-class GPUs
inside the shop network; three named agents draft damage maps, repair schemes and release paperwork
while certifying engineers decide and sign, and every confirmed outcome is kept as memory the next
decision reads rather than trained into weights.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure in the shop's systems, the constraints that
shape the design, the stack and the object model, ingestion through adapters, the placement of inference,
the models and their licenses, the rollout in two phases with their item counts and gates, and who owns
what the design builds, before closing with how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design from
recorded reading.

 Figure 1. Damage Draft on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes, and

Contents

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Damage Assessment Is the Slowest Step Nobody Can
Query

The most skilled step in a composite repair shop produces evidence that cannot be searched
the next time the same part type arrives, which is why turnaround time suffers and training
stalls.

The abstract promised a physical AI system design that drafts damage maps, repair schemes and release
paperwork while certifying engineers decide and sign. This chapter starts at the bench, with the question

the shop actually needs answered, the evidence it already holds but cannot reach, and the regulatory
ground any answer must stand on.

1.1 The Question and the Data It Requires

When a fan cowl arrives with a disbond near a hinge fitting, the certifying engineer needs two answers at
once: does the measured extent fall inside the allowable limits for that part number at that location, and
what happened the previous times this part type showed the same damage in the same place. The first
answer requires the scan file, the serialized part's identity, the licensed structural repair manual and the
inspection record all resolved to one location on the part. The second requires every confirmed damage
map, finding and release for that part type over the last year, and today that evidence lives in photographs
stapled to a paper traveller, so the question cannot be asked at all. The regulatory ground is layered: the
national civil aviation regulations govern the repair quality system, the qualification of certifying staff and
the release of parts to service; the personal data protection law governs records that name technicians
and inspectors; and the structural repair manuals are held under license whose terms constrain what may
be extracted from them. A system that answers the question must satisfy all three at once, which rules out
most of what the market sells as an inspection assistant.

1.2 The Documented Cost

The cost of fragmented maintenance evidence is documented publicly, and it is not specific to one shop.
One aerospace structures and precision components manufacturer with 85 million dollars in revenue and
340 employees found its data trapped in 7 disconnected systems, so the shop described here is in
recognized company (RYSHE n.d.). The American Society for Nondestructive Testing states that
standards are vital to the ability of different digital systems to exchange data in maintenance, repair and
overhaul, which is precisely the exchange this shop cannot perform today (ASNT n.d.). IATA's TechOps
group has published a white paper proposing a more efficient maintenance data standard and a lifelong
digital maintenance record for aviation assets, an industry-level admission that the record, not the tooling,
is the bottleneck (Aircraftit n.d.). And when an accident occurs, maintenance evidence is read closely by
investigators, as the maintenance group factual report following a freighter accident shows (NTSB 2025).
Inside this shop the fragmentation costs three things the airlines measure: turnaround time on damage
assessment, the scarce hours of the few senior engineers who approve schemes, and the pace at which
engineers in training can be shown precedent.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is an aircraft maintenance, repair and overhaul provider in Saudi Arabia serving commercial
single aisle and wide body fleets, with a composite repair shop expanding under the national program to
localise aviation maintenance. The shop repairs radomes, flight control surfaces, nacelle panels, fan
cowls and cabin monuments, removed from aircraft in its own hangars and sent in by airlines. Shops of
this class handle hundreds of parts a year, and the number is rising with the fleets based in the country.
Each part arrives with a work order, is inspected visually and with tap testing, ultrasonic scanning and

thermography, has its damage mapped against the manufacturer's structural repair manual, is repaired by
laminating technicians under a certifying engineer, is inspected again and released to service. The people
in the loop are the laminating technicians, the inspectors who perform and record each inspection, the
certifying engineers who confirm damage maps and decide whether a standard repair applies, the design
engineers who approve repair schemes or take the question to the manufacturer, and the certifying staff
who sign the release. The physical environments are the hangars, the shop floor with its rack, the
inspection bench, the scan station and the material store with its freezer. The systems of record number
six: the maintenance information system holding work orders and task cards, the scan equipment's own
image files, the airlines' technical records, the structural repair manuals under license, the material and
shelf life stock system, and the quality findings log.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Six Systems Hold the Evidence, None the Argument

Every system of record sees one slice of the part, and the question that matters needs all of
them joined, which none of them can do today.

Chapter 1 named the question and the six systems that hold its evidence. This chapter walks those
systems one at a time, because the design's whole case rests on what each sees and, more precisely,
what each misses.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The maintenance information system sees the spine of the work: which part serial arrived, for which
airline, under which task cards, and when it is due back. It sees workflow and not damage; a disbond
reaches it only as a task description, and the scan that defines the disbond's extent is a file on another
computer. The scan equipment's image files hold the subsurface truth, ultrasonic and thermography
images with their method and scanner identity, and they miss everything around the scan: which work
order it belongs to, which allowable limit it must be measured against, and what the previous scan of the
same part type showed. The airlines' technical records hold serialized part identity and history, isolated
per airline because records of different carriers mix in one shop, and they miss the shop's own inspection
evidence entirely. The structural repair manuals hold the allowable damage limits and the standard repair
schemes by part number and location on part, and they miss the actual damage on the bench; their
license terms also constrain extraction. The material and shelf life stock system holds lots, cure dates,
shelf life ends and accumulated out-time, and cannot see which repair scheme will need which kit. The
quality findings log holds findings joined to part serials, and misses the scans and confirmed maps that
would explain them.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

The question that matters crosses all six: how many fan cowls of one part number showed a disbond at
the same hinge fitting in the last year, and did a standard repair apply each time. Answering it means
traversing from part number to serialized part, to work order, to inspection, to scan, to damage, to
damage class, to allowable limit, a path along which no system holds more than one hop, and the middle
hops exist only as photographs on a traveller. Figure 2 sets the six systems side by side and shows the
same convergence. The cost in practice is the one the operator stated: the same disbond on the same
panel type is assessed from scratch each time, because the precedent is unreachable; repair scheme
approval queues on a few senior engineers, because the precedent that would let others judge is
unreachable too; engineers in training cannot be shown the shop's own history of a damage class; and
turnaround time, the measure the airlines use, stretches exactly at the most skilled step. Investigators
have shown the same reach matters after an event, when a maintenance data computer's records must
be reconstructed by hand (NTSB 2013).

      Figure 2. Six systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereignty and the Signature Constrain Every Layer

Licensed manuals, a regulator-approved quality system, personal data law and a hard
network boundary shape the design before any model is chosen.

Chapter 2 showed the join failure: six systems of record, each holding one slice, with no traversable path
between them. This chapter states the goals any design must satisfy before a single component is
chosen, because in this industry the constraints, not the models, decide the architecture.

3.1 Everything Stays Inside the Shop Network

The first goal is that records, scan images and manual content never leave the shop network, on the
operator's own hardware, with no data center or colocation entertained. This is hard in this industry
because the reasoning the shop needs, drafting schemes against manual limits with citations, is frontier-
class work, and the easy way to obtain it is an external model API that carries the evidence out with every
request. Meeting the goal self hosted means the design stands on sovereign infrastructure of its own: one
GPU node of the 141 GB class inside the shop network running the work surface, and edge units at the
bench and scan station, with no third boundary ever crossed.

3.2 The Signature Stays with Named People

The second goal is that agents map and draft while certifying engineers decide and sign, with no
autonomous damage classification and no autonomous release. This is hard because the quality system
under the national civil aviation regulations assigns release responsibility to named certifying staff, and
any system output that holds a required record is a change to that system, which must be filed and
approved before it carries weight. Guidance for software management programs during aircraft
maintenance exists and shows the shape of that approval path (FAA 2023). Until the change lands, every
agent draft runs advisory beside the existing process, and the design accepts that a draft is never a
decision.

3.3 Nothing Is Trained on the Shop's Records

The third goal is that every confirmed damage map and every approved scheme is kept so the next
assessment of the same part type is faster, without training a model on the fly. This is hard because the
obvious artificial intelligence play in a damage inspection shop is fine-tuning vision models on
accumulated damage images, and that would bake licensed manual content and airline records into
weights, crossing both the license and the boundary. The design instead holds memory of confirmed
outcomes as retrievable records read before each run, which costs retrieval engineering and buys
compounding speed with no retraining pipeline at all.

3.4 Two Laws Gate the Records

The fourth goal is to satisfy the personal data protection law and the manual license before anything
holds a record. A personal data assessment covers records naming technicians, inspectors and certifying
staff; it is filed in the first phase, before the system holds such a record. The manual license is harder: the
whole classification comparison depends on extracting allowable limits as queryable objects, and the

license terms may not permit it, so written confirmation is required first, with the fallback of citing the
manual revision in each draft rather than holding limit objects.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Scope is a constraint like the rest, and Table 1 records the three decisions that bound the first phase,
each with what it buys and what it costs.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From Records to the Bench

The design keeps the systems of record below, one governed object model in the middle,
and applications and agents above, all inside the shop network.

Chapter 3 fixed the four constraints that shape everything downstream: no data leaves the shop network,
no system of record is replaced, every required record keeps a named human signature, and nothing is
trusted before it is shadowed. This chapter lays the stack that satisfies those constraints, stage by stage,
from the records the shop already trusts to the surfaces its engineers already work at.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

The design uses one architectural pattern end to end: systems of record below, one governed object
model in the middle, applications and agents above, all inside the shop network. The pattern fits this
industry because the records below are already certified, licensed and audited, and the design has no
authority to change them; an aerospace structures manufacturer of comparable scale reports its data
trapped in disconnected systems, which is the condition this pattern exists to remove (RYSHE n.d.).
Nothing in the design writes back to a maintenance information system, a stock system or a licensed
manual; every one of them is read, joined and reasoned over, never modified. The middle layer, a single
object model of the shop, is where the join happens, and because it is governed, every draft an agent
produces can be traced to the record and the scan it came from. Above it sit the five services and the
eight surfaces, and the agents that draft while certifying engineers decide and sign. Figure 3 shows the
layered stack with the count at each layer: six named systems of record below, two adapter families as
the sole path in, one object model of sixteen objects, five services, eight surfaces and six models across
three inference tiers. The Federal Aviation Administration's guidance on managing software used during
maintenance treats the integrity of such tooling as part of the maintenance process itself, not as an
accessory to it, and the stack is built to that standard (FAA 2023). Table 7, printed by the platform from the
plan, carries the layer by layer technology choices with the reason each was picked, from Apache Kafka
in KRaft mode to Keycloak for on-site identity.

Each stage has one responsibility and named components that carry it, so that a fault, an upgrade or an

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

A team carrying a similar brief can reuse the whole shape: records read and never replaced below, two
adapter families as the sole entry path, one governed object model in the middle, agents that draft and
named people who confirm and sign above, and a shadow period before any draft carries weight. What
they swap is the content: their own named systems of record in the sources stage, their own object set
and typed links, their own detection vocabulary at the bench, and models sized to their own hardware.
What they keep regardless of industry is the part that carries the constraints: the adapter-only entry, the
single write path through human confirmation, hosting inside their own boundary, and the assurance
workstream that files the quality system change before anything holds a required record.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Sixteen Objects Turn Shop Data Into One Argument

Sixteen typed objects with governed links turn work orders, scans, damage, schemes and
releases into one queryable argument that no document store can hold.

Chapter 4 described the stack that carries the design from records to surfaces. This chapter describes
what the middle of that stack holds: the sixteen governed objects and their typed links that turn the shop's
scattered records into one queryable argument.

5.1 Sixteen Objects and the Links Between Them

The object model holds sixteen objects: Customer, Aircraft, Part Number, Part (serialized), Work Order,
Task Card, Inspection, Scan, Damage, Damage Class, Allowable Limit, Repair Scheme, Material Lot,
Technician Qualification, Finding and Release. Each is anchored in a system of record the shop already
runs, and each carries a status vocabulary that mirrors the shop's real states, so a serialized part moves
through Received, In assessment, Awaiting scheme approval, In repair, Final inspection, Released or
Scrapped exactly as it does on the floor. Figure 4 shows every object and its typed links, with the Damage
object in the focal position because it is where the slowest and most skilled step happens. The links are
typed, which is what makes the model an argument rather than a pile of documents: a damage event
points to the serialized part it sits on, the damage class it is measured against, and the scan that
evidences it, while the part number points to the allowable limits that govern the comparison. The
question the shop cannot ask today, how many fan cowls of one part number showed a disbond at the
same hinge fitting in the last year, is answered by walking four links: from the part number to its serialized
instances, to the damage events confirmed on them, to the scans and hinge fitting locations that evidence
each one, and out to the findings log. A document store holds each of those facts somewhere, but it holds
no path between them, and the industry's own work on a lifelong digital maintenance record argues for
exactly this joined form (Aircraftit n.d.). Investigations reconstruct maintenance history from whatever
fragments systems happened to keep, which is the failure a governed model prevents (NTSB 2013).

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in the status vocabularies and in three of the eight surfaces: the confirmation queue
where a certifying engineer confirms, amends or rejects an agent's damage map draft, the scheme
approval queue where a design engineer approves or supersedes a drafted repair scheme, and the
release queue where certifying staff sign the release paperwork. An agent never moves an object past its
drafted status; only a named person's confirmation does, and that confirmation is the single write path into
the model for anything that becomes a required record. The hosting posture follows the boundary
constraint: the ontology, the memory of confirmed outcomes and the model node all run on the operator's
own hardware inside the shop network, in Saudi Arabia, with identity handled by Keycloak on site. No
external links leave the boundary except the one-way update path through a hardware data diode, which
lets artifacts in and nothing out, and the personal data protection assessment is filed before any record is

held. Per-airline isolation of technical records is a property of the model itself, because records of different
airlines mix in one shop and must not mix in one query.

5.3 One Object in Its Recorded Form

The Customer record below shows the identifier, label, kind, properties, status vocabulary and links the
platform prints for every object; the Damage object, the one every assessment turns on, is recorded the
same way.

  { "id": "customer", "label": "Customer", "kind": "actor", "anchored_in": "The technical
  records of each customer's parts", "properties": [ "Customer code", "Fleet types", "Bilateral
  recognition basis", "Release certificate format" ], "status_vocabulary": [], "links": [ {
  "to": "release", "label": "receives" } ] }

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter

Seven sources of record enter through two adapter families, so no source system is modified
and no data path bypasses the governed model.

Chapter 5 described what the object model holds and how its links carry an argument. This chapter
describes how data gets into it: seven sources, two adapter families, and an event backbone that keeps
every arrival ordered, buffered and traceable.

6.1 Seven Sources and Their Provenance

Seven sources feed the model: the six named systems of record plus the camera stream from the bench
and scan station. The maintenance information system, which holds work orders and task cards and
exposes a live API, is read through the integration adapter and is the spine every scan, damage map and
scheme resolves to. The scan equipment image files, the subsurface half of every damage map, are lifted
from the scanner's own computer by the file and document adapter together with whatever metadata
each scan carries. The airline technical records supply serialized part identity and history, with per-airline
isolation enforced at the ontology. The structural repair manuals, held as licensed digital manuals
confirmed parseable at intake, supply the allowable limits and standard repair schemes, with license
permission to extract confirmed in writing before go live. The material and shelf life stock system feeds
material lots with cure dates, shelf life ends and accumulated out-time. The quality findings log supplies
the findings that make the repeat-finding question answerable. Figure 5 shows each named system, its
provenance class and its adapter path; all six systems of record carry operator provenance and read-only
direction. The nondestructive testing community's own position is that shared standards are what let

different digital systems exchange inspection data at all, which is the gap the adapter tier is built to close
(ASNT n.d.).

       Figure 5. The 7 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

The adapter tier guarantees four things. First, no source system is modified: every connection is read-
only, so the certified systems of record stay exactly as their auditors last saw them, in line with guidance
that treats software touching maintenance data as part of the managed process (FAA 2023). Second,
provenance is recorded on arrival: every work order, scan file and manual clause enters carrying the
system, the timestamp and the extraction method it came from, and where a scanner's export lacks the
calibration reference the evidence chain needs, the gap is recorded and shown rather than hidden. Third,
per-airline isolation is applied as data lands, so records of one airline never enter a query path for
another. Fourth, ingestion is idempotent, so a re-read of the same work order or the same scan file
produces the same objects rather than duplicates, which is what lets the pipeline be replayed after any
interruption without corrupting the model.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka in KRaft mode carries every arrival from the adapters to the object model and every
downstream service. Ordering is keyed by work order, so all events for one part arrive in the order the
shop generated them, which matters when a damage confirmation must not overtake the inspection that
precedes it. Delivery is at least once, paired with the idempotent consumers above, so a repeated event
is recognized and dropped rather than double-counted. Buffering absorbs the shop's natural bursts: a
scanner export, a batch of task card updates and a camera clip set can arrive together without loss,
because Kafka retains them until every consumer has acknowledged. Replication keeps a copy of the
stream inside the shop network, so a node restart does not lose an in-flight damage map, and Chrony

time synchronization with an OCP Time Card grandmaster keeps sensor and system clocks aligned,
which is what makes the evidence chain's timestamps mean the same thing everywhere. Updates to the
running system itself arrive the same one way, through the data diode, so the backbone never opens an
outbound path.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Vision Runs at the Bench, Reasoning In-Country

Zero-shot and anomaly vision run on edge units at the bench and scan station, multimodal
reading runs on a site card, and the frontier model runs on one GPU node inside the shop.

Chapter 6 showed every source entering through one of two adapter families and landing in the object
model as typed, provenance-carrying records. This chapter fixes where inference runs, because in a shop
whose records, scan images and licensed manual content must never leave its network, placement is a
boundary decision before it is a performance one: the same weights that are cheap to serve from a data
center are impossible to serve there once the evidence they read cannot follow them.

7.1 Three Tiers and Their Memory Arithmetic

Figure 6 places the work on three tiers. At the edge sit two units of the on-device class the design carries:
an octa-core SoC with a 6 TOPS neural processing unit in a fanless sealed housing, one at the inspection
bench and one at the scan station. They run the vision models, whose weights are small enough to state
exactly: OWLv2 at about 310 MB for the base checkpoint and about 875 MB for the large at 16 bit, SAM
2.1 at about 78 MB for tiny and about 449 MB for large at 16 bit, and an Anomalib model whose size is
model dependent, typically tens to hundreds of MB at 32 bit, with memory bank methods such as
PatchCore also growing with the number of reference images. Capacity is therefore not the open question
at this tier; rate is, because loads on the neural processing unit are unmeasured, and measurement with
the actual models on a development board is the phase one gate before any unit is committed, with the
ONNX Runtime CPU provider and a small GPU at the bench as the stated fallbacks.

The site tier is a single card of the 48 GB PCIe inference GPU class on a server inside the shop. It holds
the multimodal reader, a 27 billion parameter dense vision-language model at about 28 GB of weights at
8 bit, which leaves the rest of the card for the key-value cache and the visual tokens that scan reading
generates. Beside it sits the retrieval embedding model at about 1.1 GB at FP16, small enough that it
never competes with the reader for the card.

The central tier is one node of 8 GPUs of the 141 GB class, self-hosted inside the shop network with no
data center and no colocation, because the boundary constraint keeps records, scans and manual
content on site. The arithmetic comes from the frontier model's filed parameter count: 753 billion
parameters at FP8, at one byte per parameter, give 753 GB of weights; multiplying by 1.2 for the key-

value cache and activations gives 904 GB the GPUs must hold; and the node offers 8 times 141 GB, or
1,128 GB, which holds it with headroom for the cache ceiling that long drafting sessions push toward.

         Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget is set by the shop's work rather than by any model's benchmark, and each tier has its own
clock. At the bench, detection runs on selected frames rather than every frame, so the constraint is that
an indication surfaces while the part is still under the technician's hands and the lighting and framing that
produced it can be repeated. At the scan station, anomaly mapping of an exported file must finish inside
the same inspection slot the scan already occupies, or the operator will read the raw image first and the
draft becomes a check rather than a head start. The multimodal reader must turn one scan into a
structured damage draft while the work order is still open, and the frontier model's draft must be waiting in
the confirmation queue by the time the certifying engineer opens it, because a draft that arrives after the
decision has been made is worth less than none. Every tier is therefore sized so that the slowest step a
person waits on is the person's own judgement, which is the step the design protects rather than
compresses.

7.3 What Crosses the Boundary, and What Fails

Nothing crosses outward. The technical records of the airlines' parts, the scan images and the manual
content stay on the shop network, and the single write path, a named person's confirmation or signature,
lands in the object model and never in a system of record. What crosses inward is the update stream:
container images and model weights arrive through a one-way transfer, Lidi over a hardware data diode,
into the on-site registry installed from Harbor's offline installer, and the diode's direction is what
guarantees that shop data cannot follow an update back out.

The failure paths follow from that shape. If the link between an edge unit and the site server fails, the
edge units keep detecting and segmenting against the models they already hold, drafts queue locally, and
the queues resynchronize when the link returns; the shop's existing process is unaffected because every
draft is advisory until an engineer signs it. If power fails, the NUT-managed UPS carries the edge units
and the site server through the interruption, and the systems of record are the shop's own in any case. If
the update path fails, the units run the versions already in the on-site registry, and the absence of a new
version is a condition the system health surface shows rather than hides, alongside agent draft
acceptance and the weekly count of engineer disagreement reports.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 8

The License Decides What the Shop Can Own

Six models under permissive or bespoke terms let the operator hold every weight it runs, on
hardware whose export path is settled before any order.

Chapter 7 placed the three tiers and sized their memory from the models' filed weights. This chapter
states what runs at each tier and on what terms, because the license behind a model, not its benchmark,
decides whether the operator can hold the weights its inspection process comes to depend on.

                               Figure 7. The six models, their placement, and the work each one does.

8.1 Six Models the Shop Holds Outright

Figure 7 stacks the six models against the three tiers. At the center sits GLM 5.3, a frontier-class model
with about 753 billion filed parameters served at FP8 on the one GPU node. Its role is the agentic work
surface and ontology maintenance, and the reasoning behind every agent draft. It carries a bespoke
GLM-5.3 license whose terms permit commercial use, fine tuning and redistribution, which is what lets the
operator hold and change the weights it runs rather than rent them, and it was chosen because the
command center the requirement names, with parts in work, open assessments, approvals waiting and a
conversational interface that answers with citations, needs reasoning weight that smaller models cannot
supply.

At the site tier, Qwen3.8-27B dense multimodal reads scan images and bench photographs into
structured damage for the mapping agent. It is a 27 billion parameter dense vision-language model under
Apache-2.0, at about 28 GB of weights at 8 bit on the 48 GB card, and it was chosen to keep the reading
of images beside the data while the frontier reasoning stays on its own node.

Three vision models run at the edge. OWLv2 is a zero-shot, text-conditioned detector under Apache-2.0,
at about 310 MB for the base checkpoint and about 875 MB for the large at 16 bit; it was chosen because
it needs no training for this shop, so the bench unit detects the damage vocabulary the shop already
uses, from disbond indication to hinge fitting, without any labelled local damage data, and it runs on
selected frames rather than every frame. SAM 2.1 is promptable segmentation under Apache-2.0 on
checkpoints, inference and training code with no field of use restriction, at about 78 MB for tiny and about
449 MB for large at 16 bit; the damage map needs masks and extents rather than boxes, and it is driven
by the detector's boxes or an operator click. Anomalib, under Apache-2.0, maps subsurface anomalies on
ultrasonic and thermography scan images, flagging where a scan of a fan cowl deviates from reference
panels; its size is model dependent, typically tens to hundreds of MB at 32 bit, and memory bank
methods grow with the reference set, so it is sized on the chosen model.

BGE-M3, under MIT, is the retrieval embedding over the licensed manuals, records and confirmed maps.
Its dense, sparse and multi-vector output from a single pass keeps part numbers and clause references
retrievable as exact strings, with an 8,192-token window, at about 1.1 GB at FP16 on the site card. The
two accelerator purchases carry their own term: the 141 GB class node and the 48 GB site card are US-
origin accelerators whose export to the operator needs a license determination before any order, with in-
country sourcing weighed as the alternative.

8.2 The Model and Equipment Register

Table 4 gathers every choice this chapter and the last rest on: each model, the hardware classes and
sizing rules the tiers are built from, the sensing that feeds them, the patterns the design stands on, and
the ground the whole system runs on. Read together, the rows show that the intelligence in this design is
held, not borrowed: every weight runs on the operator's own hardware inside the shop network, under
licenses that permit it, on equipment whose export path is settled before anything is ordered.
