PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 9

Shadow Mode Comes Before Any Draft Is Trusted

A measured first phase on fan cowls and nacelle panels runs a baseline and then shadow
mode before any draft carries weight, with the quality system change filed in parallel.

Chapter 8 settled the model stack and the licenses that let the shop hold every weight it runs. This
chapter sets out how the design arrives in the shop: two phases, what each carries, what the rollout
measures, and the gates that stop the work cheaply when a premise fails.

9.1 Phases, Items and Gates

Phase one carries 17 items across five workstreams: One model of the shop, Physical AI at the bench,
Named agents and memory, Command center, and Assurance and acceptance. The first workstream
builds the shop ontology from the systems of record, and its items include the maintenance information
system read integration and the scanner file export integration; the last workstream carries the assurance
work that must land before anything holds a required record. Phase one runs on fan cowls and nacelle
panels only. Its exit gate is the bench and scan station edge units: a dev-board run with the actual vision
models, because whether they fit the 6 TOPS NPU class at a usable rate decides whether the edge tier is
viable at all. Phase two carries a single item, the extension design to flight control surfaces and the
remaining part families, under the Assurance and acceptance workstream, and it begins only when the
phase one gate has been passed.

Within phase one the order is fixed by what the shop must trust first: the baseline before the drafts,
shadow mode before any draft carries weight, and a capability demonstration on reference panels before
the quality system change is relied on. The quality system change under the national civil aviation
regulations and the personal data protection assessment are filed in phase one, in parallel with the build,
because the approval path and not the technology sets the schedule; a precedent recorded in the plan's
own risk register makes exactly that point. Figure 8 shows both phases with their item counts,
workstreams and gates, and carries the coverage of the 22 requirements, each traced to a workstream
and a gate rather than left as a claim.

               Figure 8. The two phases and their gates, and coverage of the 22 requirements across them.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

The rollout measures the shop, not the models. The baseline comes first: how long an assessment takes
today from received part to confirmed damage map, how often the certifying engineer escalates to the
manufacturer, and how many assessments start from scratch for a part type the shop has seen before.
Shadow mode comes second, with agent drafts running beside the existing process and no draft holding
a required record. Its measures are how often a draft is confirmed without amendment, how often the
engineer amends the location, the extent or the class, and how often a draft is rejected outright.

Alongside these the rollout tracks the time from scan ingested to map confirmed, the count of out-time
alerts acted on before a material lot expires, and whether the repeat-finding question the shop cannot ask
today, how many fan cowls of one type showed a disbond at the same hinge, becomes answerable from
confirmed maps joined to part serials.

9.3 Failure Modes

Table 5 lists what the design accepts can fail and what it does about each. Every row is a recorded risk
with a named answer, and the first two are gates in their own right.

9.4 Lessons From the Build

Shadow the drafts before anyone trusts them. A draft that reaches a certifying engineer before its
agreement rate is known transfers risk to the signature, which is the one place the design cannot afford it.
Shadow mode on fan cowls and nacelle panels buys the evidence, and the reference panels buy the
demonstration, without either touching a required record.

Build the disagreement path before the agreement path. The instructive signal in advisory drafting is
where the engineer and the agent diverge, because each divergence is either a model finding or an
engineer precedent the memory should hold. Publishing the count of engineer reports each week turns
quiet non-use into a visible finding instead of a slow failure that reads as a technology problem.

File the paperwork with the build. The quality system change and the data protection assessment run
in parallel with the engineering from the first item of phase one, because the recorded precedent in the
plan's risk register is that the approval path, not the technology, sets the schedule.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Four questions remain open, and settling each changes something concrete. The manual license
permission, once confirmed in writing, decides whether allowable limit objects exist in the ontology or
every draft cites a manual revision instead. The export license determination decides the sourcing route
for the 141 GB HBM class node and the 48 GB site card, and an in-country answer would change the
hardware plan rather than the design. The scanner survey decides which provenance fields the evidence
chain can rely on and where the gaps will sit. The survey of PoE ports and switch budget at the bench
and scan station decides whether the edge units land where the design places them or the shop's existing
network constrains the placement.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 1 0

The Intelligence Stays with the Shop

The object model, the weights, the memory of confirmed outcomes and the boundary all
belong to the shop, and nothing that compounds ever leaves it.

Chapter 9 ended on the open questions the rollout must settle. This chapter settles the question
underneath all of them: who owns what the design builds, and what never leaves the shop that produced
it.

10.1 What the Shop Owns

The object model is the shop's outright. Its 16 objects are anchored in systems of record the shop already
holds: the work order spine in the maintenance information system, the serialized part identity in the per-
airline technical records, the allowable limits in the licensed manuals, the material lots in the stock
system. Because the ontology is governed and self-contained, it can be exported, audited and rebuilt
inside the shop's boundary without any vendor's continuing presence, and the per-airline isolation of
technical records is a property of the model itself, since records of different airlines mix in one shop.

The weights are the shop's too. GLM 5.3 runs under a license that permits commercial use, fine tuning
and redistribution, so the operator may hold, tune and even redistribute the weights it serves on its own
node; the vision and embedding models carry Apache-2.0 and MIT terms with no field of use restriction.
Nothing in the stack rents intelligence from outside the boundary.

The decision record, every confirmed damage map, approved scheme and signed release with its
signature method and retention expiry, belongs to the shop as evidence. The memory of confirmed
outcomes is a record the next decision reads, and nothing in it updates model weights. The boundary
itself is owned and enforced: records, scans and manual content never leave the shop network, updates
arrive one way over a hardware data diode, and the reasoning node sits inside the shop, self-hosted. This
is the shape a physical AI system design takes in practice when the operator owns it, and the shop that
produced the intelligence keeps all of it.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja designed this system on Praxis, its platform for designing physical AI systems, and each
element of it maps to the offer behind the design. The bench and scan station sensing, the cameras and
the zero-shot and anomaly detection of physical damage, are Adaptive Operations. The confirmation,
scheme approval and release queues, where ranking and drafting end in a named person's decision, are
Decision Systems. The governed object model of 16 objects is Hyper Ontology, and the command center
where certifying engineers, design engineers and certifying staff act on agent drafts is Hyper Pragma, the
work surface where the shop's own people build and run their agents. The whole footing, own hardware in

the shop, open-weight licenses, in-country self-hosted serving with a data diode at the edge, is Sovereign
Infrastructure.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Shop Owns the Argument It Produces
In one view the design is a single governed argument built from records the shop already holds: a part
arrives, its scans and photographs join its serialized history and the licensed manual limits, agents draft
the damage map, the scheme and the release papers over that joined context, and a named engineer
signs each one, with every confirmed outcome kept so the next assessment of the same part type starts
from evidence instead of from zero.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes the same four things it took here: systems of record that can
be read without being replaced, a boundary the data never crosses and hardware the operator holds
inside it, licenses that let the operator keep every weight it runs, and a regulator-approved path in which
agents draft and people sign; any operation with serialized assets, a skilled assessment bottleneck and a
hard sovereignty constraint can swap its objects, sources and damage vocabulary for its own and keep
the shape.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every choice in this design traces to recorded reading, from the ask and its family to the eight
lenses and the patterns they returned.

Chapter 10 established that everything the design builds stays with the shop. This chapter turns the
design around and shows how it was produced, so any choice in it can be traced back to what justified it.
Every design in this series is produced on Praxis, the design team platform for designing physical AI
systems, and this chapter lets a reader follow the reasoning the way the platform recorded it. Figure 9
shows the path from the ask to the equipment classes: the ask and its assigned family and industry, what
it read, the eight lenses and what each returned, the patterns adopted and set aside, and the ground the
design runs on.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask, in the operator's own words, was a physical AI system design for composite part inspection in a
composite repair shop: radomes, flight control surfaces, nacelle panels, fan cowls and cabin monuments,
assessed visually and with tap testing, ultrasonic scanning and thermography against allowable limits in
licensed manuals. Praxis assigned the family system of context and the industry Aviation and Aerospace

Manufacturing, which pinned the architecture before any component was chosen: a governed ontology
over the systems of record, agents that draft while certifying engineers decide and sign, and memory of
confirmed outcomes instead of any training into weights. What Praxis read was the operator's
requirement, written in its own voice and dated 7 November 2026, together with the corpus shelf of each
lens, and nothing beyond the published sources cited in this paper's register was consulted.

 Figure 9. From the ask to the design: the family and industry Praxis assigned, the eight lenses and what each cited, the
                        patterns adopted and set aside, and the equipment the design lands on.

11.2 The Lenses

Table 6 shows all eight lenses, what each could see, what it cited and what it contributed to the design.
One lens returned nothing the others had not already carried, and it is shown as a gap rather than folded
into a neighbour.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Four patterns were adopted. Agents draft and engineers sign, because the signature is the airworthiness
instrument and the design protects it. Every source enters through an adapter, never directly, so the
systems of record stay untouched and provenance is a property of the connection rather than a promise.
Vision runs at the edge and reasoning runs on one in-country node, because scan images and bench

photographs should never cross the network boundary to be read. Memory of confirmed outcomes
substitutes for training, so the shop compounds experience without ever touching weights.

Three patterns were set aside with reasons. Object tracking and trajectory forecasting were rejected
because parts are static on the bench and the scan station, and the design maps damage extent on a
stationary fan cowl. A labelling and retraining pipeline was rejected because nothing in the architecture
trains into weights; the reference panels serve capability demonstration instead. A new network segment
was rejected because the shop network already exists and the constraint is that nothing leaves it.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on equipment classes rather than named hardware where no shelf entry supported a
specific part: the octa-core 6 TOPS NPU SoC class in a fanless sealed housing at the bench and scan
station, the 48 GB PCIe inference GPU class for the multimodal reader, the 141 GB HBM class node of
eight GPUs for GLM 5.3 sized from its filed 753B parameters at FP8, the OCP Time Card grandmaster
class for time synchronisation, and the non-destructive testing equipment classes already in the shop.
Every figure in this paper, from the 17 items of phase one to the eight lenses of this table, traces to
recorded reading, and nothing in it is inferred beyond that record.

title: A Self-Improving AI System for OT Vulnerability Management at a Utility in the United States
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · ENERGY & UTILITIES · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

A Self-Improving AI System for OT
Vulnerability Management at a Utility in
the United States
Energy & Utilities Watch: One Living Picture of the Operation

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the leaders accountable for energy & utilities operations, their supervisors, and the data and platform engineers
who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

The Answer Already Exists in the Systems the Operation
Runs
A self-improving AI system for OT vulnerability management at an electric utility in the United States: open
weight models of United States origin on the utility's own hardware, reading its systems of record, that
gets better at the patch cycle every cycle from its engineers' confirmed decisions, without training a model
on the fly and without anything about its assets leaving its network.

The design reads 8 source systems through 2 adapter families into one object model of 16 objects, runs 7
services over it and opens 5 surfaces to the people who decide, with 2 models placed where the data is.
This engagement builds the utility a self-improving, utility-owned system for the OT patch cycle: a
governed fleet ontology projected over its seven systems of record, three named agents that draft
applicability, disposition and evidence while named people decide, and memory that compounds every
confirmed call, all served on one node of the 80 GB GPU class running gpt-oss-120b inside the utility's
own network, with nothing about its assets leaving it. The first phase runs on protective relays and their
engineering workstations at one group of substations for two patch cycles, measured against the utility's

own baseline of engineer hours, window compliance, evidence completeness and auditor questions
answered from the record.

The paper covers the operation and the problem its systems cannot answer, the constraints, the stack,
the object model, ingestion, inference placement, the models and their licenses, the rollout and its proof,
ownership, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

A Daily Question Goes Unanswered in the Systems That
Hold the Data

The operation holds every fact the question needs and no system answers it.

The abstract claimed the operator already holds every fact a self-improving AI system for the patch cycle
needs, in systems it already runs. This chapter states that question exactly, prices the industry's failure to
answer it, and fixes the scenario the design must serve: the assets, the people, the regulatory ground and
the systems of record.

1.1 The Question and the Regimes Behind It

The question the operation needs answered, every time any vendor publishes any advisory, is one
sentence: which of our devices does this touch, what does the verified baseline say, do we apply the
patch or mitigate, and where is the evidence that we decided inside the window. The data it requires
spans the device inventory with firmware and software versions, the verified configuration baselines, the
vendor advisory text, the national vulnerability record with severity and exploit status, the change and
work order history, and the reasoning behind past calls on the same devices. The regulatory ground
comes in three parts. The reliability standards for critical infrastructure protection require review of every

patch for every in-scope software and firmware item within thirty five days of release, and application or a
documented mitigation plan within thirty five more; they require a verified configuration baseline for every
system; and they require a full vulnerability assessment every fifteen months. Two named standards sit
inside that family, because every change request the cycle raises carries CIP-005 and CIP-007 impact
determinations, covering the electronic security perimeter and systems security management
respectively.

1.2 What the Violations Cost

The operator's own reading is that the patch cycle is the most violated standard in the industry, and the
public record shows what violation costs. Grid authorities issued a record 10 million dollar fine to a utility
over more than 120 security violations spanning four years (Eenews 2019), a scale of penalty that turns
each missed review window into a balance sheet exposure rather than an inconvenience. The cost of
answering late is regulatory; the cost of executing carelessly is human, because 142 workers in the
United States died in 2023 from exposure to electricity or arc flash (NFPA 2023). That figure is why
outage windows, execution crews and change safety remain separate disciplines from assessment work,
and why any system that drafts changes must respect the wall between deciding and doing.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is an electric utility in the United States, running substations, control centers and generating
plants whose control systems fall under the critical infrastructure protection standards. Utilities of this
class track thousands of in-scope devices from dozens of vendors, and the scenario is drawn at that class
scale, with anything specific to the fleet treated as an assumption to confirm. The people in the loop, by
role, are the compliance manager who owns the escalation ladder, the compliance engineer who confirms
applicability and disposition drafts, the asset owners who approve changes on their devices, the OT-side
engineers who hold read-only access, and the execution crews who take the outage windows. A handful
of engineers carry the tacit knowledge of which vendors' advisories matter and which devices can take an
outage, and two of them retire next year. The physical environments are substation control houses, plant
control rooms, control centers and the corporate network behind the segregation boundary. The named
systems of record number seven: the asset inventory and configuration baseline system, the vendors'
patch and advisory feeds, the national vulnerability advisories, the change management system, the work
order system, the evidence repository for audits, and the network monitoring tool's device list. The places
are banded as one group of substations for the first phase, with the wider estate held behind the phase
gates.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System Sees One Slice of the Operation

Each system of record sees its own part of the answer and none sees the whole.

Chapter 1 set out the question. This chapter explains why no system the operation already runs can
answer it.

2.1 What Each System Sees

Asset inventory and configuration baseline system the foundation of the fleet ontology: sites, devices,
firmware and software versions, and the verified baselines every applicability call must cite.

Vendors' patch and advisory feeds the trigger of the whole cycle: a new advisory wakes the applicability
agent, and patch artifacts are verified for source identity and integrity before any change.

National vulnerability advisories the national vulnerability record joins the vendor advisory to give severity
and exploit status the disposition reasoning cites.

Change management system the disposition agent drafts apply or mitigate change requests here so the
work lands in the system the utility already governs by, never in a parallel queue.

Work order system mitigation plans become tracked work here; reading completion status is how the
design knows a documented mitigation was actually implemented.

Evidence repository for audits the evidence agent writes confirmed audit packages here, which is what
turns a closed change into a defensible answer when the auditor asks why a relay firmware patch was
mitigated rather than applied.

   Figure 2. Seven systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

Each holds one slice, and the question needs all of them in one place at once, which today is done by
hand at the cadence of whoever has the time.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Four Constraints Shape Everything Downstream

The goals, the scoping decisions and the exclusions were fixed before any component was
chosen.

Chapter 2 showed the join failure: seven systems, each holding a slice, none able to carry the argument
from advisory to evidence. This chapter fixes the four goals that shape every component chosen in Part II,
the scoping decisions bought with them, and the alternatives the design stood against.

3.1 The System Must Improve While Every Decision Stays Named

The operator asked for a self-improving system, and the compliance regime asks that every call carry a
named person. Recursive self-improvement is an active rollout priority at frontier AI companies and is
beginning to diffuse into the broader corporate sector (Stanford 2026), but in a regulated OT estate an
unattended improvement loop has no audit story. The design's answer is improvement from confirmed
calls only: three agents draft applicability, disposition and evidence, named people confirm or reject, and
memory compounds the confirmations. The difficulty is behavioral as much as architectural, because
engineers under a thirty five day clock can rubber-stamp drafts, and a confirmation nobody made is
poison to the memory; the design therefore instruments the acceptance rate both ways and samples
unflagged items independently each cycle rather than reading a falling override rate as improvement.

3.2 Nothing About the Assets May Leave the Boundary

The operator set the rule in its own words: open weight models of United States origin, on hardware it
owns, with no third party model service. This is the constraint that a self-improving AI system for a utility
has to serve, and it fixes the compute before any model is chosen: one node of the 80 GB GPU class
inside the operator's own network, a class with domestic supply and no export control complication. What
is hard in this industry is direction: the useful inbound signals, advisories and vulnerability records, arrive
from outside, while the asset facts must never travel out. The design reads inbound feeds through verified
paths and sends nothing back, and where the operator's policy demands it, OT-side data leaves the
electronic security perimeter only through a hardware-enforced one-way path with no return route and no
credentials inside the perimeter.

3.3 Every Draft Lands in a System of Record

The disposition agent drafts apply or mitigate change requests in the change management system, not in
a parallel queue, and the evidence agent writes confirmed audit packages into the evidence repository,
because the utility already governs its work through those systems and the auditor already looks there.
The difficulty is that the integrations are mixed, some APIs and some scheduled exports, so the ontology
is only as current as its slowest source. The design therefore records freshness on every record under a
per-system connector plan, and business-critical drafts refuse data older than an agreed age rather than
guessing from stale baselines.

3.4 Weights Move Only Through Change Management

Improvement is memory first: retrieval of confirmed decisions, with supersession and tombstone checks
on every retrieval so a wrong precedent cannot confirm itself. Weights change only through a separately
governed offline fine-tune lane, promoted against a frozen question set built from the first cycles'
confirmed calls, through the instruction gate, with the prior model retained in the registry for rollback, and
never inside an active cycle week. The difficulty in this industry is timing: a regression in the served model
surfaces mid-cycle, exactly when the thirty five day clock is running, so the promotion path is treated as a
change like any other.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Three scoping decisions translate the four goals into boundaries the build can hold, and each buys
something at a stated cost, set out in Table 1. The first keeps every decision named while the agents do
the drafting; the second makes the ontology a projection over the systems of record rather than a
replacement for them; the third narrows the first phase to the relay fleet so the measurement is honest
before anything widens.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From the Systems of Record to the
Surfaces

Systems of record below, one object model in the middle, services and surfaces above.

Chapter 3 fixed four constraints: open weights of United States origin on hardware the operator owns,
every decision resting with a named person, the systems of record left exactly where they are, and a first

gate that can stop the work cheaply. This chapter lays out the stack that satisfies those constraints stage
by stage, from the systems of record at the bottom to the surfaces the compliance team works in at the
top.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

The design follows one architectural pattern: systems of record below, one object model in the middle,
applications and agents above. Below sit the seven named systems of record, the asset inventory and
configuration baseline system, the vendors' patch and advisory feeds, the national vulnerability
advisories, the change management system, the work order system, the evidence repository for audits
and the network monitoring tool's device list; none is replaced, migrated or modified beyond the two draft
write paths named in Chapter 5. In the middle sits the fleet ontology, a governed projection over all seven,
so the join every applicability call needs happens once, in one place, instead of being remade by hand
each cycle. Above it, three decision agents draft applicability, disposition and evidence, and the command
center carries those drafts to named people who confirm or reject them.

The pattern fits this industry for three reasons. The failure of Chapter 2 is a join failure, and a join is
solved at exactly one layer, which keeps every other layer replaceable. Each stage can be tested against
the stage below it, so the first gate can be cheap. And energy regulators have begun publishing
expectations for how AI should be governed in the sector (OFGEM 2026), and a stack whose reasoning
layer is separable from its record layer is the shape such expectations ask for. Figure 3 shows the layered
stack with its counts: eight sources, two adapter families, sixteen objects, two models, seven services and
five surfaces.

           Figure 3. The layered stack: 8 sources, 2 adapter families, 16 objects, 7 services and 5 surfaces.

4.2 The Stack Stage by Stage

Table 3 walks the stack stage by stage, naming the component responsible in each. Two things in it
deserve note. The sensing stage is deliberately thin: the design watches advisories, baselines and
decisions rather than sensor telemetry, so the one sensing input is the read-only OT-side device list and
the clock that orders decisions. And the inference stage is deliberately centralized: gpt-oss-120b, about
120 billion parameters held in MXFP4 at roughly 61 GB of weights, runs on one node of eight 80 GB
GPUs on the operator's own hardware, alongside the Nomic Embed Text v2 MoE embedding model at
under 1 GB resident. Table 7, printed with this chapter, carries the layer by layer component choices

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The reusable shape is this: a read-only projection ontology over whatever systems of record a team
already governs, two adapter families owning the contracts, agents that draft with citations and never
decide, memory that compounds only confirmed calls, and one sovereign node inside the boundary. A
team carrying a similar brief swaps the object set, the source list and the clock, here the thirty-five day
review and thirty-five day disposition windows the standards impose, and keeps the rules that make the

shape safe: the single write path rule, drafts that must cite retrievable records, and confirmations that
carry a named person. Self-improvement is an active priority at frontier AI companies and is diffusing into
broader corporations (Stanford 2026); this design takes the safer register, memory first with a governed
offline fine-tune lane promoted only through change management. That is what turns a self-improving AI
system from a procurement posture into an engineering one: the sovereignty sits in the object model, the
write paths and the node, not in a label.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Sixteen Objects Turn Operational Data Into One
Argument

The object model is the join the systems never made.

Chapter 4 laid the stack from the systems of record to the surfaces. This chapter opens the middle layer,
the sixteen objects of the fleet ontology and the typed links between them, because that layer is where
the join the systems never made finally happens.

5.1 Sixteen Objects and Their Typed Links

The sixteen objects divide by where they anchor. Five anchor in the asset inventory and configuration
baseline system: Substation, Protective relay, Engineering workstation, Firmware and software version,
and Configuration baseline, which together carry the fleet's identity, firmware state and verified baselines.
Two anchor in the vendors' patch and advisory feeds, Vendor and Advisory; one in the national
vulnerability advisories, Vulnerability, which joins severity and exploit status to the vendor's notice. Two
anchor in the change management system, Change request and Outage window; one in the work order
system, Work order; and two in the evidence repository, Evidence item and Auditor question. Three
anchor nowhere because they are born in the system itself: Applicability decision, Disposition and Cycle
agent. These three hold the operator's own reasoning as first-class records with status vocabularies,
rather than leaving it in an email thread, which is the failure the operator named when it asked why a
mitigated relay firmware patch could not be explained to an auditor.

Figure 4 draws every object and its typed links. What the links buy is traversal. A question such as "which
relays run firmware affected by the advisory published today, at which sites, under what outage
constraints, and what did we decide the last three times this vendor's advisories touched those devices" is
one walk across the links from Advisory through Firmware and software version to Protective relay,
onward to the Substation and the Outage window, and back through prior Applicability decisions to their
Evidence items. A document store could hold every one of those facts and still fail the question, because
each answer would be a fresh manual join, and the person making it would be whoever is on the rota.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in the status vocabularies of the three unanchored objects. An Applicability decision
moves from Drafted to Confirmed or Rejected only when a named engineer acts; a Disposition moves
from Drafted through Approved and Scheduled to Closed only through the change management system;
a Cycle agent sits at Awaiting confirmation and cannot advance itself. Every confirmation carries the
person who made it and the citations the draft stood on, so the reasoning an auditor asks for is in the
record, not in a mailbox.

The hosting posture follows the constraints of Chapter 3. The object model and everything above it run on
the operator's own hardware inside its own network in the United States, and nothing about its assets
leaves that boundary. Identity is Keycloak 26.8 federated to the operator's own directory, so no person
acts anonymously. External links are inbound and verified only: vendor feeds, national advisories and
patch artifacts checked for source identity and integrity. The write paths back into any system of record
are limited to the two named in the design, draft change requests into the change management system
and confirmed evidence items into the evidence repository; every other source is read-only. Regulator
guidance on AI in the energy sector asks that decisions be explainable and attributable (OFGEM 2026),
and this posture delivers both by construction rather than by policy.

The substation record below shows the id, label, kind, anchor, properties and typed links the platform

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Nothing reaches the object model except through an adapter that owns its contract.

Chapter 5 defined what the object model holds and where the human loop lives. This chapter defines how
data reaches that model: every source enters through an adapter that owns its contract, and nothing
reaches the ontology directly.

6.1 Eight Sources and Their Provenance Classes

Figure 5 maps the integration. The design counts eight sources. Seven are named systems of record, and
each is an operator record, read-only, reached through its own API where one exists and through a
scheduled export where it does not: the asset inventory and configuration baseline system, which
grounds every object anchored in the fleet's identity; the vendors' patch and advisory feeds, whose
advisories wake the applicability agent; the national vulnerability advisories, which add severity and
exploit status; the change management system, where drafted dispositions land as change requests; the
work order system, whose completion status tells the design whether a documented mitigation was
actually implemented; the evidence repository for audits, which receives the confirmed evidence items;
and the network monitoring tool's device list, which is the reconciliation source, because devices the
monitoring tool sees that the inventory lacks are applicability gaps, and drift between the two is itself a
signal. The eighth source is the patch artifact channel, the patches themselves, which arrive from vendors
and are verified for source identity and integrity before any change can reference them. All eight are
reads; the sole writes out of the design are the two draft paths Chapter 5 named.

          Figure 5. The 8 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

Two adapter families own the contracts: the integration adapter, for the API and export sources, and the
telemetry adapter, for the OT-side device list where it crosses a hardware-enforced one-way path. The tier
guarantees five things. Each source is mapped once, into the object model, with its source system and
freshness stamped on every record, so a citation always resolves to a retrievable record with a known
age. Patch artifacts are verified for source identity and integrity before anything downstream may cite
them. No agent, service or surface ever reads a source system directly, which is what keeps the ontology
the single join. Business-critical drafts refuse data older than an agreed age rather than guessing from a
stale baseline, which answers the risk that mixed API and export integrations leave the model stale on
exactly the records an applicability call cites. And the write surface stays two paths wide, never more.

6.3 The Event Backbone

Apache Kafka 4.4 carries everything between the adapters and the ontology. Ordering is keyed on
advisory identifiers and record identifiers, so the per-advisory and per-device sequence of events holds
even when connector schedules interleave. Delivery is at least once, made safe by idempotent upserts
keyed on record identity and content hash, so a replayed export can refresh a record but can never
create a second applicability decision or a duplicate evidence item. Buffering is where the scheduled
exports land: a vendor's batch or a work order extract arrives as a burst, sits in the topic, and drains at the
connector's pace while the advisory cycle reads a watermark rather than a moment in time. Replication
runs inside the operator's own cluster on its own hardware, so no record crosses the boundary in transit.
Model and artifact updates travel the same discipline: Harbor v2.15.2 holds them as signed artifacts in the
registry, a fine-tuned model is promoted only through the instruction gate with the prior version retained
for rollback, and never inside an active cycle week, so the backbone that feeds the cycle never becomes
a side channel around its governance.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Inference Belongs Where the Data Is

Each tier runs what its data and its link can carry.

Chapter 6 described how all of the sources enter through adapters and how the event backbone orders,
buffers and replicates what they emit. This chapter decides where the reasoning on that data runs, and
what the hardware must hold for it to run there.

7.1 Two Tiers, Both Central, and the Arithmetic That Fixes Them

The design runs two inference tiers, and both sit inside the operator's own network: a reasoning tier
where the applicability, disposition and evidence agents draft their records, and an embedding tier that

turns advisories, baselines and confirmed decisions into the vectors retrieval memory reads. There is no
edge tier, because the patch cycle reasons over advisories and records rather than sensor telemetry, and
the requirement fixes compute on the operator's own hardware on its network. Figure 6 shows both tiers,
what runs on each, and what crosses the boundary to reach them.

The reasoning tier serves gpt-oss-120b, a mixture of experts model of about 120 billion parameters, on
one node of eight GPUs of the 80 GB class. The arithmetic that fixes that node: the register files 117
billion parameters, and at INT4, 0.5 bytes per parameter, the weights occupy 58.4 GB; multiplying by 1.2
to cover KV cache and activations gives 70.1 GB the GPUs must hold. The node offers 640 GB, so the
weights fit with generous headroom for concurrent agent sessions. The checkpoint itself is 60.8 GiB, 65.2
GB of root safetensors, with the mixture of experts weights in MXFP4 at 4.25 bits and the remainder at 16
bit; expanded fully to 16 bit it would need about 234 GB, which is what rules out a smaller host. KV cache
runs about 4.8 GB per session, and vLLM 0.32 serves the model from the node it sits on.

The embedding tier runs Nomic Embed Text v2 MoE, 475 million parameters at FP16, about 0.95 GB
resident and about 0.5 GB at 8 bit; the published Hub weights are float32, so the download is about 1.9
GB. All 475 million parameters stay resident, because every expert is in play at inference.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The binding clocks are regulatory rather than electronic: thirty-five days to assess every advisory and
thirty-five more to apply it or document a mitigation, with a full vulnerability assessment every fifteen
months. Inside that frame the budget is a working day: an advisory that arrives in the morning intake
should be drafted, with citations to the baseline and to retrieved precedent, before the confirming
engineer leaves. Retrieval reads are bounded by resident embeddings and a local graph query, not a
network round trip, and the conversational surface answers at conversational speed because model,

memory and ontology share one node. The design spends latency where it is free instead: cycle-day
alarms at day 25 with a named escalation ladder to the compliance manager and the asset owner, so the
genuinely slow part of the cycle, human confirmation, receives the warning rather than the drafting
receiving speed it cannot use.

7.3 The Boundary and the Failure Modes

What crosses the boundary inward is content the operator must have: vendor advisories, national
vulnerability advisories, and patch artifacts verified for source identity and integrity before any change.
What crosses outward is nothing about the operator's assets. Where policy demands it, the network
monitoring tool's device list and any OT-side data leave the electronic security perimeter through a
hardware-enforced one-way path, with no credentials and no return path inside the perimeter; a DMZ
conduit remains the lighter alternative where that policy does not apply, and OT-side engineers reach the
command center read-only over the corporate network.

When the link fails, the adapters buffer and the backbone replays in order, but business-critical drafts
refuse data older than an agreed age rather than guessing, because a mixed diet of APIs and scheduled
exports can leave exactly the records an applicability call cites out of date. When power fails, the node
rides the data center rack's existing power and cooling, and the services recover from the events the
backbone retained. When the update path fails, the air-gapped Harbor registry still holds the last
promoted model and its artifacts, promotion runs only through the instruction gate with the prior model
retained for rollback, and nothing is promoted inside an active cycle week.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 8

The License Decides What the Operator Can Own

Every model was chosen against its license before its accuracy.

Chapter 7 fixed where inference runs and what the node must hold. This chapter fixes what the operator
owns once it holds those weights, because the license, not the benchmark, decides that.

                       Figure 7. The two models, their placement, and the work each one does.

8.1 Two Models, Both Ownable

Figure 7 sets out the model stack: one reasoning model and one embedding model, both on the same
node, both under licenses that let the operator keep them. The reasoning model is gpt-oss-120b: about
120 billion parameters in a sparse mixture of experts architecture, served in MXFP4 with the dense
portions at 16 bit. Its role is the agentic work surface and ontology maintenance: it is the model behind the
command center's conversational surface that answers with citations, and behind the three agents that
draft applicability, disposition and evidence. It runs centrally on the node of the 80 GB GPU class
described in Chapter 7. Its license is Apache-2.0, a permissive license with no usage-based trigger and
no field of use restriction, which is precisely what permits the operator to hold the weights on hardware it
owns with no third-party model service in the loop. It was chosen because the requirement names open
weights of United States origin on owned hardware, and the domestic supply of this GPU class carries no
export control complication.

The embedding model is Nomic Embed Text v2 MoE: 475 million parameters, a sparse mixture of experts
embedding model at FP16, about 0.95 GB resident. Its role is embedding advisories, baselines and
confirmed decisions for retrieval memory, which is the mechanism by which the system gets better at the
cycle every cycle. It runs centrally alongside the reasoning model, under the same Apache-2.0 terms, and
it was chosen because improvement here must be retrieval of confirmed precedent first, not weight
change.

The pattern the pair stands on matters more than either name: retrieval memory of confirmed decisions,
with a governed offline fine-tune lane promoted only through change management, instead of continuous
online fine-tuning or a hosted model service that improves itself. Recursive self-improvement is already
moving from frontier laboratories into ordinary corporations (Stanford 2026), and an energy regulator has
published guidance on ethical AI use in the sector (OFGEM 2026); a design whose every improvement is
a retrieved, cited, human-confirmed record answers the governance question both raise, and does so
with weights the operator can hold outright.

8.2 The Model and Equipment Register

Table 4 gathers the choices this chapter and Chapter 7 made, so an engineer building from the design
can see each decision, what was picked, and the reason it was picked here rather than elsewhere.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 9

Shadow Mode Comes Before Any Flag Is Trusted

The rollout earns each phase at a gate the operator can read.

Chapter 8 settled which models the design holds and on what license terms the operator may hold them.
This chapter sets out how the build earns trust in stages: what each phase carries, what its exit gate
tests, what is measured while it runs, and what the design already knows can fail.

9.1 Phases, Workstreams and Gates

The rollout runs in two phases, shown with their item counts and exit gates in Figure 8. Phase 1 covers
the protective relay fleet and its engineering workstations at one group of substations, and carries 16
items across six workstreams: Fleet ontology, Advisory cycle, Command center, Decision agents, Memory
and improvement, and Phase gates. The Fleet ontology workstream builds the object model from the
systems of record; the Advisory cycle workstream brings in the vendor and national feeds and reconciles
the asset baseline against the network monitoring tool's device list; the Command center workstream
stands up the five surfaces; the Decision agents workstream brings the applicability, disposition and
evidence agents online in shadow; the Memory and improvement workstream writes confirmed calls back
as precedents; and the Phase gates workstream holds the exit test itself. The gate is read from behavior,
not from a calendar: Phase 1 exits when the disposition agent is drafting apply or mitigate
recommendations that engineers confirm on the record. Phase 2 carries a single item, the extension
gates and rollout to the other asset classes and the generating plants, and its exit gate is set from Phase
1 evidence rather than fixed in advance. Requirement coverage closes the loop: the design carries one
requirement, covered in full, with nothing partial and no gap.

             Figure 8. The two phases and their gates, and coverage of the one requirement across them.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

Phase 1 is measured across two patch cycles against the operator's own baseline, taken before anything
changes: engineer hours spent per cycle, window compliance expressed as windows taken against
windows missed, evidence completeness for closed changes, and auditor questions answered from the
record rather than from email. Alongside those, the instrumentation watches the acceptance rate in both
directions, the freshness of every record the drafts cite, and an independent sample of drafts that nobody
overrode. Window compliance and evidence completeness are measured rather than assumed because
the enforcement record gives the stakes: grid authorities have issued a record 10 million dollar fine to a
utility over more than 120 security violations spanning four years (Eenews 2019), and the violations that
fine counted were failures of documentation and follow-through of exactly the kind this cycle exists to
prevent.

9.3 Failure Modes

Table 5 states each recorded failure mode and what the design does about it. The common thread is that
the system's own improvement depends on the honesty of its inputs, so each mitigation protects either
the confirmation, the memory or the clock.

9.4 Lessons

Shadow the drafts before anyone signs them. The agents come online drafting, never deciding, and
the first cycles are run so that every draft can be compared against what the engineer would have written
alone. This is what makes the acceptance rate a real number rather than a rubber stamp, and it is why
the exit gate is a drafting gate: the system must show it can produce the work before anyone is asked to
trust a summary of it. Sample what nobody overrode. A falling override rate looks like improvement and
can simply be fatigue, so each cycle takes an independent sample of unflagged drafts and checks them
as if they had been flagged. The memory only compounds from calls that survived that check, which
keeps the precedent base worth retrieving. Treat record freshness as a gate, not a metric. A draft that

cites a baseline record past its agreed age is refused before it is written, because a confident applicability
call on stale data is worse than no call at all. Freshness is recorded on every record at ingestion, and the
refusal is visible in the command center rather than silent.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Three questions remain open. The Phase 2 exit gate is unset; settling it decides what the extension to
other asset classes must prove, and whether it is another drafting gate or a closed-loop evidence gate.
The promotion threshold for the fine-tune lane is unset; settling it decides whether the served weights
ever change or memory alone carries the improvement, and it sets the size of the frozen question set.
The boundary path is a policy choice between the hardware-enforced one-way transfer and the lighter
DMZ conduit; settling it fixes the hardware list and the exact path the network monitoring tool's device list
takes out of the electronic security perimeter.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 1 0

The Intelligence Should Stay with the Operation That
Produced It

What the design builds belongs to the operator.

Chapter 9 showed how the rollout earns each gate. This chapter settles the question the whole design
turns on: who owns what it builds, and where the intelligence lives once the cycles compound.

10.1 What the Operator Holds

Four assets change hands, and all four stay inside the operator's boundary. The first is the object model:
sixteen objects with their typed links, projected over the seven systems of record, governed as a
projection rather than a migration, so the asset inventory, change management, work order and evidence
systems remain the records while the ontology remains something the operator can rebuild from them at
any time. The second is the weights and fine-tunes: gpt-oss-120b and the embedding model both sit
under Apache-2.0, held on the operator's own node of the 80 GB class inside its own network, with no
third party model service in the path; any fine-tune is an artifact in the operator's own registry, promoted
and rolled back through its own change management. The third is the decision record: every applicability
decision, disposition, evidence item and auditor question belongs to the operator and is kept where its
auditors already look, and the memory that compounds cycle over cycle is that record, readable without
the models. The fourth is the boundary: nothing about the operator's assets leaves its network, and OT-
side data crosses only through the hardware-enforced one-way path where its policy demands it. The
design is one instance of the sovereign reference architectures this series documents: intelligence that
compounds inside the organization that produced it, on weights that organization holds.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja builds each of these elements as a named product, and the mapping is direct. The
applicability, disposition and evidence drafts that named people decide on are Decision Systems. The
object model that holds the sixteen objects and their typed links is Hyper Ontology. The command center
where the operator's compliance team and engineers act on drafts, and where they can build their own
agents on the same governed model, is Hyper Pragma. The kept record of decisions and outcomes that
every next decision reads before it acts is Hyper Engram. The operator's own hardware, the open-weight
licenses and the in-country operation that keeps every byte inside the boundary are Sovereign
Infrastructure. And the design itself, from the constraint set through the stack to the phase gates, was
produced on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for designing physical AI systems.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Pattern Repeats Wherever Systems of Record Do
Not Meet
Seen whole, the design is one object model over the systems an electric utility in the United States
already runs, with inference placed where the data is and every decision left to a named person.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes the same four things: the named systems, an object model
anchored in them, a first gate that can stop the work cheaply, and the license posture that lets the
operator own what it learns.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every choice above traces back to something Praxis recorded reading.

Chapter 10 settled where the intelligence lives: with the operator, on its hardware, inside its boundary.
This closing chapter shows how the design was reasoned, so that any choice above can be traced back
to the recorded reading that justified it (Figure 9).

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask was a self-improving system for OT vulnerability management: open-weight models of United
States origin on the operator's own hardware, reading its systems of record, and getting better at the
patch cycle every cycle from its engineers' confirmed calls, with no agent applying a patch or closing a
change without a named approval. Praxis assigned it to the Energy & Utilities family in the United States.
What Praxis read: the requirement record; the System of Context architecture record that fixed the work

surface; the stack and equipment registers behind Chapters 4 and 8; the model cards for gpt-oss-120b
and Nomic Embed Text v2 MoE; the eight lens libraries; and the six public sources in the register.

                        patterns adopted and set aside, and the equipment the design lands on.

11.2 The Lenses

Table 6 states what each of the eight lenses could see, what it cited and what it contributed to the design.
One lens returned nothing and is shown as the gap it was.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Four patterns were adopted. Improvement is memory first: confirmed calls become retrievable
precedents, and the offline fine-tune lane is a separately governed extension promoted only through
change management. Every source enters through an adapter, and the sole writes are the draft and
evidence paths named in the requirement. The ontology is a projection over the systems of record, not a
migration of them. All inference runs centrally on one node, with no edge box anywhere in the design. Set
aside, with reasons: continuous online fine-tuning and any hosted model service that improves itself, both
ruled out by the operator's constraint on owned weights and by its change discipline; SCADA and
telemetry integration, which would pull the design across the segregation boundary it is committed to
respect; and any replacement of the systems of record, which would trade a governed projection for an
ungoverned copy.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

Three equipment classes carry the whole design. The 80 GB HBM GPU class holds gpt-oss-120b, whose
checkpoint sits near 61 GB in MXFP4, on one node with generous headroom for concurrent agent
sessions. The frontier model GPU footprint sizing rule turned the filed parameter count into that one-node
answer, which is why no larger cluster is committed anywhere in the design. The data diode one-way
transfer class stands behind the boundary where the operator's policy demands it, moving the network
monitoring tool's device list out of the electronic security perimeter with no return path. Every figure,
version, license and citation above traces to recorded reading: the stack card, the model cards, the
equipment registers and the six public sources. Nothing in this paper is inferred beyond them.

title: Industrial AI Reference Architecture for Tailings Storage Facility Monitoring in the United States
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · MINING · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

Industrial AI Reference Architecture for
Tailings Storage Facility Monitoring in
the United States
Section Story: Sovereign AI Reference Architectures for Mining at One High-Consequence
Facility

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the accountable executive and the responsible tailings facility engineer, the engineer of record and the
independent review board they answer to, and the geotechnical, data and platform engineers who would build and
run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

One Section Deserves One Story Before Anyone Asks
for It
When an engineer types industrial AI reference architecture for mining into a search box, the question
underneath is the one this operation cannot answer today: what is actually happening in one section of a
high-consequence tailings embankment in the United States, and is it drifting toward a trigger? The facility
holds more readings than ever and the same two engineers reading them, because a piezometer that
rises slowly over a month lives in the historian without being joined to the deposition that moved the
beach toward it, the rain that fell, the inclinometer two hundred feet away or the radar survey from last
quarter. Thresholds in the trigger action response plan fire on single instruments, so operators learn to
expect alarms and the pattern that matters hides among them, while the daily inspection app records
what the operator saw in words nobody searches. When the engineer of record, the review board or the

regulator asks for the story of one section over a year, it is assembled by hand from six sources, and the
assembling takes the very hours the surveillance obligation is meant to spend on judgment.

The design is a sovereign system of context for one high-consequence tailings facility: a governed
ontology of 15 objects and their typed links joins 8 named source systems, the historian, satellite radar
reports, the inspection app, the trigger action response plan, the engineer of record's records, the
deposition and raise plans, the water balance model and the regulator's correspondence, through 2
adapter families, a telemetry adapter and an integration adapter, so that one embankment section has
one story. Six services, from the facility ontology and the on-site platform to the phase one gates, serve 5
surfaces, from the trend and trigger view the operators watch to the read-only review view the review
board reads. Three drafting agents, a pattern agent, a response agent and a reporting agent, run on gpt-
oss-120b, 117B parameters at INT4, 58.4 GB of weights held on one node of eight 80 GB GPUs in the
site server room, with anomaly screening on edge units at the logger network and everything on the
owner's own hardware. The system improves by memory of confirmed patterns rather than by training,
the existing TARP alarm path stays untouched, and the engineer of record holds every interpretation;
phase one covers one embankment section for two quarters against the owner's stated measures.

The paper covers the industry problem and the join failure across the existing systems, the constraints
and scoping decisions, the layered stack from sources to surfaces, the object model with its typed links,
ingestion through adapters, the placement of inference and what never crosses the boundary, the four
models and the licenses that let the owner hold their weights, the rollout in three phases with their gates
and failure modes, and who owns what the design builds, closing with the chapter on how Praxis
contextualized and reasoned the design.

Figure 1. Section Story on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes, and the
                                                 person who decides.

Contents
Each chapter is tagged for the reader it serves most directly: Executive, Team Lead, FDE, Reference.

         Abstract · One Section Deserves One Story Before Anyone Asks for It                   Executive

  PA R T I · T H E P R O B L E M

 1       An Industrial AI Reference Architecture for Mining Begins at the Embankment           Executive

 2       Every System of Record Sees One Slice of the Facility                                 Executive   Team Lead

  PA R T I I · T H E D E S I G N

 3       Sovereignty and the Engineer of Record Shape Every Constraint                         Team Lead

 4       One Stack Runs From Systems of Record to Surfaces                                     Team Lead     FDE

 5       Fifteen Objects Turn Facility Data Into One Argument                                  FDE

 6       Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly                                FDE

 7       Screening Belongs at the Loggers and Reasoning on Site                                FDE

 8       The License Decides What the Operator Can Own                                         FDE     Executive

  PA R T I I I · T H E R O L L O U T

 9       Shadow Mode Comes Before Any Draft Is Trusted                                         Team Lead     Executive

 10      The Intelligence Should Stay with the Facility That Produced It                       Executive

  PA R T I V · H O W I T WA S D E S I G N E D

         Conclusion · The Facility That Keeps Its Own Context Can Answer for It                Executive

 11      How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design                                    Team Lead     FDE

         Sources                                                                               Reference

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

An Industrial AI Reference Architecture for Mining
Begins at the Embankment

A high-consequence tailings facility under the global standard now holds more readings than
ever and the same two engineers reading them, so the pattern that matters hides among
single-instrument alarms while the story of one section is still assembled by hand.

An industrial AI reference architecture for mining succeeds or fails at the point where the story of one
section has to be assembled, so this chapter starts where the abstract left off: the question the operation
cannot answer today, the regimes any answer must satisfy, and the scenario the design has to fit. The
abstract promised one embankment section with one story, drafted by named agents on the owner's own
hardware; what follows is the ground that promise stands on.

1.1 The Question and the Regimes Behind It

The operation needs one question answered continuously: what is happening in one section of the
embankment, read as a whole rather than instrument by instrument. A piezometer that rises slowly over a
month is visible in the historian, but the reading only means something joined to the deposition that
moved the beach toward it, the rain that fell, the inclinometer two hundred feet away and the radar survey
from last quarter. The data required is data the operation already holds, spread across eight named
systems of record covering readings, surveys, inspections, thresholds, design basis, plans, water balance
and correspondence. Two regimes shape what the answer must satisfy. The global industry standard on
tailings management obliges trigger action response plans with predefined actions, prompt notification of
the engineer of record when a trigger is crossed, and approval of monitoring reports by the engineer of
record together with the responsible tailings facility engineer. State dam safety regulation counts the
facility as a water impoundment and expects an operation log and unusual event notices, so every
interpretation must trace to a named person and a timestamp.

1.2 The Documented Cost of Not Joining

The industry's own safety reporting shows why this matters beyond convenience. The International
Council on Mining and Metals publishes annual fatality and injury data for its member companies, and the
pattern in that reporting is consistent: everyday injuries keep falling while fatal and catastrophic events
remain a persistent challenge (ICMM n.d.; CIM 2026). Responses across the industry are converging on
the same diagnosis, with a national serious injuries and fatalities database being built to turn incident data
into insight (CIM 2026b). A tailings facility is where the catastrophic end of that curve lives, and an inquest
into a mineworker's death in this industry found record keeping grossly deficient (Nscafoundation 2020).
That is the failure mode this design addresses at monitoring scale: records that exist but cannot be joined
when the question arrives.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The owner is a mining company in the United States running one large tailings storage facility classified at
a high consequence level: an embankment raised in stages over decades, holding tailings behind it with a

beach and a pond, inspected daily and reviewed by an engineer of record and an independent review
board. The facility is instrumented with vibrating wire piezometers in the embankment and foundation,
inclinometers, survey prisms and monitoring stations, with satellite radar surveys of the surface several
times a year. The people in the loop, by role, are the operators who walk the facility daily, the two
engineers who read the readings, the engineer of record, the independent review board and the regulator.
The physical environments are the embankment crest and faces where the logger cabinets sit, the beach
and pond the inspections cross, and the site server room where the reasoning hardware would run, one
node of eight 80 GB GPUs. The systems of record number eight, all read-only: the instrumentation data
logger network and its historian, the satellite radar deformation reports, the daily inspection app, the
trigger action response plan, the engineer of record's reports and drawings, the deposition and raise
plans, the water balance model and the regulator's correspondence. Facilities of this class are expected
to demonstrate full conformance with the global standard this year, and the industry has already moved
from periodic inspection to continuous surveillance, which is the ground the design stands on.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System of Record Sees One Slice of the Facility

Each of the eight existing systems holds one true slice, the readings, the surveys, the walks,
the thresholds, the design basis, the plans, the water balance and the correspondence, and
none of them can join a piezometer, a deposition, a storm and a radar survey into one story.

Chapter 1 established the question the operation needs answered and the regimes that govern the
answer. This chapter shows why no single system can answer it, by walking each of the eight systems of
record through what it sees and what it misses.

2.1 What Each System Sees

The historian is the primary live source: it sees minute-level readings for every instrument tag, and it
misses which section a tag anchors, which design assumption it verifies and which deposition or storm
surrounds any given reading. The satellite radar deformation reports see surface deformation across the
facility each survey, and they miss everything between surveys and everything beneath the surface. The
daily inspection app sees what the operator saw, in words nobody searches, and misses any join
between the walk and the trends running beside it. The trigger action response plan sees thresholds per
parameter and the predefined actions attached to them, and misses the pattern that spans instruments,
because it fires on single instruments. The engineer of record's reports and drawings see the design
basis and the section definitions, and miss live behavior entirely. The deposition and raise plans see
intended events with dates and volumes, and miss the instrument response those events caused. The
water balance model sees forecast pond elevation from inflows and outflows, and misses the measured
divergence read against its context. The regulator's correspondence sees due dates, submissions and

notices, and misses the evidence trail behind each filing. Figure 2 sets these eight slices side by side,
each converging on the question none of them can answer alone.

     Figure 2. Eight systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

What no system holds is the join: one piezometer, one deposition, one storm, one inclinometer and one
radar survey, arranged as one story of one section over a year. Today that story is assembled by hand
from six sources, and the assembling takes the same two engineers away from reading the readings.
Thresholds fire on single instruments, so operators learn to expect alarms and the pattern that matters
hides among them. The cost in practice is paid twice, in attention and in traceability: when the engineer of
record, the review board or the regulator asks for the story, the answer arrives late and hand-built, and an
inquest in this industry has already found record keeping grossly deficient where records cannot speak
together (Nscafoundation 2020). The failure is not any one system's failure; it is the space between them,
and that space is where the design in Part II puts the object model.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereignty and the Engineer of Record Shape Every
Constraint

Compute stays on the owner's own hardware on site, the existing alarm path stays
untouched, nothing is trained into weights, and the engineer of record holds every
interpretation, and each of these constraints is hard in this industry for a different reason.

Chapter 2 showed eight true slices and the unoccupied space between them. This chapter states the
constraints any answer must respect, because each is hard in this industry for a different reason and
each shapes everything downstream, from where the models run to who signs a draft.

3.1 All Compute Stays on the Operator's Own Hardware

The first constraint fixes every inference tier on site: the agentic work surface runs on one node of eight
80 GB GPUs in the site server room, and the anomaly screening of readings runs at the logger network,
so nothing crosses the owner's boundary and no third-party model service is used. This is hard in mining
because the sovereign posture is an obligation rather than a preference, and it is bound to a named
scope item and confirmed with the owner's own compliance owner before design freeze, since no
integration answers it by accident. It is also hard physically: a GPU node of this class draws about 10 kW,
so the server room's power and cooling must be surveyed before any order, with an in-country colocation
room as the fallback if the site cannot host it.

3.2 The Existing Alarm Path Stays Untouched

The single-instrument thresholds in the trigger action response plan keep firing in the historian exactly as
they do today, and the design sits beside that path with pattern drafts rather than in front of it with a
replacement. This is hard because the alarm path is the one part of the monitoring estate that operators
already trust and regulators already recognize: replacing safety-critical alarming would invite scrutiny the
design does not need and would put adoption at risk on day one. The cost is a second stream to triage,
which the rollout answers with an alert budget per engineer per shift and a false-trigger gate.

3.3 Nothing Is Trained Into Weights

The system improves by memory, not by training: every confirmed pattern and its outcome is kept and
read by the next run, and no model is fine tuned on trigger history. This is hard because the industry
instinct is to retrain on new data, and because memory only compounds as fast as engineers confirm
patterns. The compensation is that every model in the stack carries a permissive Apache-2.0 license, so
the owner can hold the weights it runs, inspect them and resynchronize them on its own schedule, with no
license trigger tied to use.

3.4 The Engineer of Record Holds Every Interpretation

Agents draft and engineers decide: every pattern draft, response draft and submission carries an
approver, and the standard's approval chain, the engineer of record together with the responsible tailings
facility engineer, is recorded on each monitoring report before release. This is hard because

accountability under the global standard is named to a person, and the engineer of record's authority over
interpretations is a term of a written agreement, not a workflow setting. The design consequence is an
instruction gate before anything leaves the boundary, so no draft reaches the regulator unapproved.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From Systems of Record to Surfaces

Systems of record sit below, never replaced and never modified, one governed object model
sits in the middle, and the applications and agents sit above, all on hardware the owner
owns.

Chapter 3 fixed the constraints and the scoping they forced: read the systems of record rather than
replace them, keep every interpretation with the engineer of record, hold the compute on the owner's own
hardware, and leave the existing alarm path untouched. This chapter turns those constraints into a stack
whose layers run in a fixed order, from the records the facility already keeps to the surfaces its people
already use.

4.1 Three Layers in a Fixed Order

The design follows one pattern. The systems of record sit at the bottom, never replaced, never modified
and never loaded directly. One governed object model sits in the middle, a projection over those records
rather than a copy of them. The applications and agents sit above it and read only the model. Figure 3
shows the layered stack with its counts: eight source systems below, two adapter families above them,
fifteen objects in the middle, four models across three inference tiers, then six services and five surfaces
at the top. The pattern fits this problem because the ask is a join, not a rebuild: the owner asked to read
the loggers, the historian and the reports and join them, and a new central historian or data lake would
spend its budget moving data that already sits where it belongs. The projection rule keeps the middle
layer small, since it holds objects and typed links rather than copies of minute-level readings, while every
layer runs on hardware the owner owns, from the edge units at the logger network to the inference node
in the site server room.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The shape a team carrying a similar brief can reuse is the order itself, not any component in it: sources
below, adapters as the single door in, a projection object model in the middle, drafting agents above, and
a recorded human approval before anything leaves. Keep the invariants and swap the domain. The fifteen
objects become the nouns of whatever facility is at hand; the telemetry adapter's target becomes that
site's logger network; the model set changes with the workload, provided the licenses still let the owner
hold its own weights. What should never be swapped is the rule that nothing trains on the fly: the system
improves by memory of confirmed patterns, and that memory is something the owner keeps.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 5

Fifteen Objects Turn Facility Data Into One Argument

Fifteen objects and their typed links turn six hand-assembled sources into one queryable
argument, so a question about a section reaches its raises, instruments, readings, triggers,
inspections, depositions, surveys and submissions across links no document store can
follow.

Chapter 4 described the stack that runs from the systems of record to the surfaces. This chapter opens
the middle layer, where fifteen objects and their typed links turn six hand-assembled sources into one
queryable argument.

5.1 Every Object and Its Typed Links

The model holds fifteen objects. Two are assets: Embankment Section and Instrument. Three are events:
Raise, Trigger and Deposition Event. Two are measures: Reading and Pond Level. Four are records:
Trigger Level, Inspection Observation, Pattern Draft and Response Draft. Two are documents: Radar

Survey and Regulator Submission. One is an actor, the Engineer of Record, and one is a system, the
Water Balance Model. Figure 4 shows every object and the typed links between them. What the links buy
is reach. Take the problem the owner stated: a piezometer rising slowly over a month is visible in the
historian but joined to nothing. A query anchored on those readings walks to their instrument by tag, to the
instrument's section, to the raise stage that section is in, to the deposition events that moved the beach
toward it, to the inspection observations recorded on that section, to the radar survey that covered it, and
to the matched past episodes held in memory, then returns the whole argument with citations. A
document store holding the same six sources can return whatever mentions the instrument tag; it cannot
walk relationships nobody wrote down, which is why the story of one section over a year is today
assembled by hand. Table 8, printed with this section by the platform, lists every object with the source it
is anchored in and its typed links.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

Every object that carries a decision carries a named person. A Trigger records its confirming engineer; a
Pattern Draft moves through Drafted, Confirmed and Rejected only under a human hand; a Response
Draft names its approver; a Regulator Submission requires engineer of record approval before it can be
Filed. The engineer of record holds authority over interpretations, and the review board and the regulator
read the section stories through read-only views. The hosting posture follows the same closed shape.
Everything runs on the owner's own hardware on site, so no facility data crosses a boundary. Identity is
served on site, so credentials never leave the operation. There are no external links: the radar surveys
arrive as report files and the water balance model is read where it runs. The single write path into the
object model is the adapter tier, and the sole writes out of it are recorded human decisions, so the
systems of record are read-only by construction rather than by policy.
