Measure the silicon on the real streams before ordering it. The shelf's measured NPU loads are
forklift dashcam mixes on MIPI cameras, not RTSP substream decode plus a detector, so the dev-board
measurement on the actual estate is the gate that decides the edge unit count, and no catalog figure
substitutes for it.

Gate the cameras, not the assumption. A camera hung for human review can be adequate for its
original purpose and still fail a detector that needs pixel density, angle and frame rate at the far edge of

the robot field; the six reuse gates with recorded evidence at the worst hour convert that risk into a
bounded contingency.

Make disagreement visible while it is still cheap. A human loop that only confirms the model is worse
than no loop, because it launders the model's errors into decisions; probes, logged reasoning and drafts
that carry their own evidence keep the supervisors' judgement real, in the same spirit that investigation
guidance insists causes be established from evidence rather than assumption (HSE n.d.).

Treat the near miss log as a baseline, not a record of truth. People enter the robot field more often
than procedure allows, and the log records only what someone chose to report days later; reconciling it
against live detections turns an unknown rate into a measured one, which is the number the safety case
actually needs (CEFIC 2015).

9.5 What Is Still Open

Four questions stay open after the design. The measured NPU load on the real substreams is unknown
until the dev-board runs, and a load above headroom splits each camera group across more edge units.
The export license path for the 141 GB-class accelerator is undetermined, and a failed path moves the
reasoning tier from the site data room to the in-country fallback placement. Which camera views fail the
reuse gates is unknown until the worst hour is recorded, and each failure converts contingency budget
into one purpose-placed camera. The size of the reporting gap is unknown until reconciliation runs, and it
sets how much of the memory seeding rests on live supervisor confirmation rather than on the historic
log.

PA R T I I I · C H A P T E R 1 0

The Intelligence Stays Inside the Building

The operator owns the object model, the weights and fine tunes, the decision record and the
boundary, because intelligence produced by its floor should compound inside its own
perimeter.

Chapter 9 showed how one zone earns the whole field. This chapter settles who holds what that work
produces, because intelligence made from this floor should compound inside the operator's perimeter
rather than leave it.

10.1 What the Operator Holds

The operator holds four things, and each is designed to be holdable. The first is the object model: fifteen
objects, every one anchored in a system of record the operator already owns, the zone and the robot in
the fleet orchestration system, the order wave and the tote in the warehouse management system, the
shift and the person role in the labour management system. Because each object resolves to an identifier

the operator already controls, the model is the operator's asset and survives any change of tooling around
it.

The second is the weights and the fine-tunes. GLM 5.3 runs under a bespoke license that permits
commercial use, fine-tuning and redistribution with an attribution notice; RF-DETR and Grounding DINO
run under Apache-2.0; BGE-M3 runs under MIT; the trackers run under Apache-2.0. Every license in the
register permits the operator to hold its weights, keep serving them and keep whatever fine-tunes its own
labelled evidence produces, which is the whole basis for hosting them in the site data room.

The third is the decision record: every agent draft, every approval and rejection with its reasoning, and
every reconciliation of a detection against the near miss log. This is the record the next decision reads, it
is kept on site, and it is never used to update model weights.

The fourth is the boundary. Nothing leaves the building: frames, detections, weights and memory all stay
inside one perimeter. The one crossing is the read-only conduit from the fleet and control zone through a
firewalled DMZ, and people appear in the record as anonymous presence with a role, never as an
identity.

10.2 The Offer Behind the Design

CodeNinja builds each of these elements as part of its offer, and this design maps onto it directly:
Adaptive Operations is the edge sensing that detects people, fallen totes and blocked lanes from the
existing cameras; Decision Systems is the ranking, attribution and recommendation layer whose drafts a
named supervisor approves or rejects; Hyper Ontology is the governed object model that joins those
detections to the robots, waves and shifts they affect; Hyper Pragma is the work surface on which the
operator's own people build and run their agents; Hyper Engram is the kept record of decisions and
outcomes that each next decision reads; Sovereign Infrastructure is the posture of own hardware, open-
weight licenses and everything inside the building; and Praxis is the platform on which the design was
produced.

PA R T I V · C O N C L U S I O N

The Robot Field Becomes Observable Without
Becoming Autonomous
The design is one sovereign loop for a single robotic fulfilment center: the cameras that already cover the
robot field gates, pick station fronts, charging bays and dock crossings feed edge units that detect people,
fallen totes and blocked lanes; a governed object model of fifteen objects joins each detection to the
robots, waves and shifts it affects; three named agents draft the slowdowns, clearance tasks and
handovers; and supervisors approve and execute every one of them, with GLM 5.3 reasoning self hosted
in the site data room so that frames, weights and memory never leave the building.

Running the same shape elsewhere takes three things more than money: an existing camera estate
whose views can pass six reuse gates at the worst hour, read-only access to the fleet, control and labour
systems that hold the identifiers the ontology is anchored in, and the discipline to hold phase one to one
zone for one quarter against the operator's own baselines before the whole field is earned. Any operator
with a robotic field, a fleet feed and an incident log can carry the pattern; what each swaps is the zone
class vocabulary, the stall signatures of its own fleet and the license path for its accelerator class.

PA R T I V · C H A P T E R 11

How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design

Every design in the series is produced on Praxis, and this chapter traces each choice in the
paper back to the recorded reading, the eight lenses and the patterns that justified it.

Chapter 10 closed the argument for keeping the intelligence inside the building. This chapter opens the
record of how the design itself was reasoned, so a reader can trace any choice in the paper back to what
justified it. Every design in this series is produced on Praxis, and this chapter lets a reader audit that
production: the ask as it arrived, the family and industry Praxis assigned it, what it read, and what each of
the eight lenses contributed. Figure 9 shows the whole path, from ask to patterns to the equipment
classes the reasoning landed on.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask was a physical AI system design for a mobile robot fulfilment center at a warehousing and
intralogistics operator in Saudi Arabia, written in the operator's own voice: open the robot fleet black box,
detect people inside the field on the cameras that already exist, and do it all inside the building. Praxis
assigned the design to the system of context family and to the Warehousing and Intralogistics industry,
which fixed the shape before any component was chosen: systems of record below, one object model in
the middle, agents and surfaces above, and the work surface as part of the architecture rather than an
option. What Praxis read was the operator's requirement, the model cards and license texts for every
model in the register, the hardware shelf data for the edge system on chip and the accelerator class, and
the regulatory reading covering the national personal data protection law, the industrial truck safety
standard's zone classes and the export control position.

 Figure 9. From the ask to the design: the family and industry Praxis assigned, the eight lenses and what each cited, the
                        patterns adopted and set aside, and the equipment the design lands on.

11.2 The Eight Lenses

Table 6 records what each lens could see, what it cited and what it contributed to the design; a lens that
returned nothing would appear here as a gap, and none did.

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Four patterns were adopted. Read-only integration, with no command path ever opened into the fleet
system, keeps the safety case with the fleet's own sensors. Pretrained detectors before any training keep
Phase 1 free of a labelling program. Evidence frames with citations on every draft make each
recommendation checkable at the moment of decision. Motion-only tracking with the re-identification
branch switched off keeps the incursion record anonymous. Three were set aside. Wearable positioning
of people was rejected because the data minimization case does not need it and the cameras already
carry presence. A separate site inference server was rejected because all accelerated inference sits
either on the edge NPUs or on the GLM 5.3 node, and the site servers run ingest, the backbone, the
ontology and the embedder on CPU. A one-way transfer diode was rejected because the one boundary
crossing is a firewalled read-only conduit, not a data export, so a diode would add hardware without
adding a guarantee.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The reasoning lands on four equipment classes, and every sizing in the paper traces back to one of them:
the GLM 5.3 node count by GPU class, which fixes the reasoning tier at one node; the 141 GB HBM GPU
class, whose eight GPUs hold the 753B FP8 weights with the KV cache ceiling; reuse of the existing
CCTV estate rather than new cameras, verified through the six gates per view; and edge compute sized
from the streams, with the dev-board measurement as the gate. Everything shown in this paper was
recorded reading, and nothing is inferred.

title: Sovereign AI Reference Architectures for a Remote Mine on a Satellite Link in Pakistan
text:
VERTICAL-DRIVEN ARCHITECTURES · MINING · DESIGNED WITH PRAXIS · NOVEMBER 2026

Sovereign AI Reference Architectures for
a Remote Mine on a Satellite Link in
Pakistan
Mining Watch: One Living Picture of the Operation

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the leaders accountable for mining operations, their supervisors, and the data and platform engineers who would
build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

The Answer Already Exists in the Systems the Operation
Runs
Sovereign AI reference architectures for a remote copper and gold mine on a satellite link in Pakistan: the
operator's corporate systems live in data centers abroad and reach the site over that link, so when the link
degrades the site works blind, with permits issued on paper, equipment faults logged after the shift and a
convoy's position known when it arrives.

The design reads 8 source systems through 2 adapter families into one object model of 15 objects, runs 8
services over it and opens 4 surfaces to the people who decide, with 2 models placed where the data is.
A sovereign system of context for a remote copper and gold mine in Pakistan: one governed ontology
over read mirrors of the site's seven systems of record, three drafting agents (permits, equipment,
convoys) whose drafts named people approve, memory that survives crew rotation, and a command
center that runs fully on site through satellite outages with GLM 5.3 self hosted on one 141 GB class
node. Phase one is one construction area and its heavy fleet for one quarter, gated on the site answering

a simulated link-drop day, on which a dozer fault, a permit clash and a late convoy arrive together, entirely
from its own memory.

The paper covers the operation and the problem its systems cannot answer, the constraints, the stack,
the object model, ingestion, inference placement, the models and their licenses, the rollout and its proof,
ownership, and finally how Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design.

Figure 1. Mining Watch on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes, and the
                                                 person who decides.

Contents
Each chapter is tagged for the reader it serves most directly: Executive, Team Lead, FDE, Reference.

 PA R T I I · T H E D E S I G N

 4       One Stack Runs From the Systems of Record to the Surfaces                  Team Lead     FDE

 5       Fifteen Objects Turn Operational Data Into One Argument                    FDE

 6       Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly                     FDE

 7       Inference Belongs Where the Data Is                                        FDE

         Conclusion · The Pattern Repeats Wherever Systems of Record Do Not Meet    Executive

 11      How Praxis Contextualized and Reasoned This Design                         Team Lead     FDE

         Sources                                                                    Reference

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

A Daily Question Goes Unanswered in the Systems That
Hold the Data

The operation holds every fact the question needs and no system answers it.

The abstract promised sovereign AI reference architectures for remote mine sites: read mirrors of the
site's seven systems of record, one governed ontology over them, three drafting agents whose outputs
named people approve, and one frontier class model node inside the fence. This chapter returns to the
problem that design answers, because the problem, not the technology, fixes the shape of everything
downstream.

1.1 The Question, the Data and the Regimes

Every shift, the site's supervisors need one question answered: what work is open on each pad, which
equipment is overdue for service or down with a fault, and which convoy carries the parts that work
needs. The data the answer requires is already held: permits and isolations from the construction
management and permit to work system, fault codes and work orders from the equipment telematics and
maintenance system, convoy positions and consignments from the supply and logistics tracking system,
crew locations and authorizations from the camp and workforce management system, incident records

from the health, safety and environment system, and live power and water readings from the site's own
historian. Three regimes frame how the answer may be produced. Mining law places site authority in a
named mine manager, so no software may confirm a permit or an isolation; Pakistan's personal data
protection regime is a draft bill rather than a statute, so residency obligations for worker records rest on
board policy and contracts; and export controls on high bandwidth memory accelerator classes govern
what hardware can enter the country at all. The answer must therefore be computed on site, inside the
fence, with every approval left to a named person.

1.2 The Documented Cost of a Blind Site

When communication fails at a mine, the failure reaches people, not only screens. Communication
failures were blamed for injuries to a worker trapped in a drilling jumbo during a roof collapse at an
underground mine, in a matter investigated by a state resources regulator (Miningmonthly 2026). A loss of
communications on an autonomous haulage circuit caused an autonomous truck to reverse into a
manually operated excavator (Miningmonthly 2024). Mine accidents in the United States prompted
federal law on mine communications and tracking, after which the national regulator studied survival and
interoperability requirements for underground communications (MSHA 2006), and an industry guidelines
body has collected recommendations from operating companies on keeping open pit telecommunications
functioning (Gmggroup n.d.). On this site the failure mode is routine rather than exceptional: when the
satellite link degrades, permits are issued on paper, equipment faults are logged after the shift, and a
convoy's position is known when it arrives. The people who run the site well are the ones who carry its
state in their heads, and they rotate out every few weeks.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

A mining operator in Pakistan is developing a large open pit copper and gold mine in a remote part of the
country, with construction under way, hundreds of permanent staff and thousands of contractors on site,
and first production planned around the end of the decade. The site is many hours from the nearest city
and reached by road and air; power is its own, water is pumped from distance, and its link to the outside
world is satellite, with limited and costly bandwidth that drops in bad weather. The people in the loop are
the mine manager who holds statutory authority, area supervisors who own pads, maintenance planners
who schedule work orders, logistics coordinators who track convoys over a long road route, camp
managers who hold a camp built for thousands, environment and safety leads, and the crews whose
rotations end within weeks. The physical environments are active earthworks areas and pads, a
concentrator build, a heavy equipment fleet and workshop, a camp, a supply route measured in days, and
a site server room on the mine's own power. The systems of record number seven by name, plus
corporate systems in data centers abroad that reach the site only over the link, and one satellite egress
that all of them share.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every System Sees One Slice of the Operation

Each system of record sees its own part of the answer and none sees the whole.

Chapter 1 stated the question the operation needs answered and the regimes that frame it. This chapter
shows why no existing system answers it: each system of record holds one true slice of the operation,
and none holds the join between them.

2.1 What Each System Sees

Figure 2 sets the seven systems side by side, and the prose here walks them in the order a supervisor
would query them. The project controls system sees work packages, schedules and percent complete; it
does not see which permits cover that work, or which consignment a delayed package is waiting on. The
construction management and permit to work system sees every permit, pad and isolation with its validity
window; it does not see whether the crew named on the permit is on site today, or whether the parts that
work needs have arrived. The equipment telematics and maintenance system sees fault codes, running
hours and work orders; it does not see which convoy carries the part each work order requires, or which
pad the unit is working on. The camp and workforce management system sees every worker, camp bed
and rotation due; it sees nothing about the work those workers are authorized to perform. The health,
safety and environment system sees incidents and near misses and the permits they link back to; it does
not see the equipment or the consignments around them. The supply and logistics tracking system sees
convoys, positions and consignments against plan; it does not see the work order a consignment was
bought for or the work package it serves. The site historian for power and water sees utility tags live and
continuously; it sees nothing about the work those utilities exist to serve.

    Figure 2. Seven systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

The supervisor's question crosses all seven slices at once: open work on the pad, equipment overdue or
down, and the convoy carrying the parts for its repair. Answering it today means three queries to three
systems, over a satellite link that may be down, joined in the head of one person whose rotation ends
within weeks; when the link drops, the join disappears entirely and the answer comes from paper,
memory and arrival. That is the cost in practice: permits issued on paper during outages, faults logged
after the shift that raised them, convoys known only when they appear at the gate, and a site whose state
leaves the country every few weeks with the rotating crew. The design's single contribution is to make the
join itself a governed object, so the question can be answered by one query against one model of the site,
on site.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Four Constraints Shape Everything Downstream

The goals, the scoping decisions and the exclusions were fixed before any component was
chosen.

Chapter 2 showed the join failure: seven true slices and no system holding the join. This chapter fixes the
goals and the scoping decisions before any component is named, because in this industry the

constraints, not the tooling, decide the architecture.

3.1 The Site Must Answer with the Link Down

The first goal is that the site answers the supervisor's question with the satellite link down, at full fidelity,
for as long as the outage lasts. This is hard in mining because the link is not a reliability problem to be
engineered away but a physical condition: bandwidth is limited and costly, weather degrades it, and the
corporate systems the site depends on sit in data centers abroad. Production raises the stakes, since a
concentrator cannot wait for a satellite window, and a loss of communications at a mine is a documented
path to injury and equipment damage (Miningmonthly 2024). In this industry, sovereign AI reference
architectures earn the name only when the link-down mode is enumerated and drilled rather than
assumed, so the design treats degradation as a designed state with its own surfaces, its own staleness
stamps and its own rehearsed day.

3.2 Every Decision Stays with a Named Person

The second goal is that agents draft and people approve: no software confirms a permit, an isolation or a
work order. This is hard because mining law places site authority in a named mine manager, and the
permit to work procedure exists precisely to put a human signature between a crew and a hazard. The
cost of the goal is permanent: every agent output routes to a named approval in the owning system's
procedure, and every confirmation made in the command center is recorded against the owning system's
record and reconciled, so no second version of permit state grows beside the system of record.

3.3 Personal Data Never Leaves the Site

The third goal is that camp and workforce personal data stays on site, inside the fence, forever. This is
hard because Pakistan's data protection regime is a draft bill rather than a statute, so residency
obligations rest on board policy and contracts today and could change on enactment; the design answers
by holding the camp and workforce mirror on site with purpose tags and retention limits, and making it the
one mirror the outbound sync never touches, so enactment forces no migration.

3.4 The Operator Owns the Intelligence

The fourth goal is that the operator owns the three assets the build produces: the model weights it serves,
the governed object model over its systems, and the accumulated memory that survives crew rotation.
This is hard in this country because export controls on accelerator classes, keyed to total processing
performance, gate the hardware the frontier tier needs, and a license determination naming the end user
must precede any card commitment. The design holds an in-country colocation fallback for the frontier tier
if the license path closes, and it phases the build so a slowdown pauses spend without stranding work.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Three scoping decisions carry the goals into the build, and Table 1 states what each buys and what it
costs. The mirrors are read-only, the ontology is a projection over systems of record rather than a
replacement for them, and all serving sits on one site node. Each decision buys the supervisor's single
query at the price of an engineering obligation the design must then meet.

  Table 1 · Scoping Decisions

   Agents that draft and           Statutory authority and permit                    Slower than automation, and every
   named people who                procedures stay intact, and every                 confirmation in the command center must

   All model serving on one        The site answers through outages                  One frontier class node must be licensed

   abroad                          country                                           sized with headroom for KV cache

3.6 What the Design Chose Against

Table 2 records the alternatives the design rejected and why, ending with the scope boundary. The
rejections follow the goals: one node instead of two keeps a remote site off a multi node fabric, store and
forward instead of live replication respects a link that drops mid-stream, and self hosted open weights
instead of a hosted API keeps the site answering when the link is down, which is the mode that matters
here.

                 nodes for 300B to 1T                   node fabric adds a failure class a remote site on its own power
                 parameter open weight                  does not need; one node leaves about 280 GB of KV ceiling beside
                 models) at FP8                         the weights

   Satellite     Store and forward with                 Live bidirectional replication, because the link drops in bad weather
   sync          ordered, idempotent replay             and a replication stream that fails mid-flight would leave mirrors in
                                                        unknown order

   Data          Camp and workforce                     A compliance-only reading of the draft bill, because residency
   posture       records held on site with              currently rests on board policy and holding the data on site now

    WHERE              W H AT WA S P I C K E D      I N S T E A D O F, A N D W H Y

                       purpose tags and retention   means enactment forces no migration
                       limits

    Model              Self hosted open weights     A hosted API, which leaves the site blind exactly when the link
    placement          inside the fence             drops and places the operator's accumulated context outside the
                                                    country

    Scope              Live feeds and agreed        Bulk migration of historic records, continuous fleet condition
    boundary           opening balances only        sensing, cameras, autonomous haulage integration, corporate-side
                                                    system changes, hardware and third party license fees, estate
                                                    wide training and round the clock support, all excluded: the
                                                    operator asked for none of them and each adds cost the outage
                                                    test does not need

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From the Systems of Record to the
Surfaces

Systems of record below, one object model in the middle, services and surfaces above.

Chapter 3 fixed the four constraints: sovereignty inside the fence, full function through link loss, every
decision with a named person, and a first gate that stops spend cheaply. This chapter lays the stack that
satisfies them, stage by stage from the systems of record to the surfaces supervisors work in.

4.1 A Projection Over the Systems of Record

The pattern is three layers. Below sit the systems of record, unchanged and still authoritative: each keeps
its data, its procedure and its owner, and nothing in the design replaces any of them. In the middle sits
one governed object model, a read projection that joins them, never a second master. Above sit the
services and surfaces: drafting agents that propose, governance that routes each proposal to a named
approval, and the command center on the site network. Figure 3 shows the layered stack with its counts
per layer: eight sources, two adapter families, fifteen objects, eight services and four surfaces.

This pattern fits because the failure the operator described is a join failure that becomes an outage
failure. The corporate estate abroad is a sync target, not a dependency, so when the satellite link
degrades the middle and top layers keep running on site, and the site works from its own memory instead
of paper. Link loss in mining is a safety event, not an IT inconvenience: a loss of communications on an
autonomous circuit put a haul truck into an excavator (Miningmonthly 2024), and mine regulators began
mandating survivable communications after multiple fatality investigations (MSHA 2006). The stack treats

the outage as the normal case. Table 7, printed by the platform at the end of this chapter, carries the
same stack layer by layer with the component chosen at each layer and the reason for the choice.

              Figure 3. The layered stack: 8 sources, 2 adapter families, 15 objects, 8 services and 4 surfaces.

  Table 7 · Architecture, Layer by Layer

   L AY E R                        COMPONENT           CHOICE      WHY

   Event streaming and             by class, no        Product     Apache Kafka 4.3 (KRaft, three dedicated
   messaging                       product named                   controllers)

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The shape a team carrying a similar brief can reuse is this: read mirrors over the systems of record, one
governed ontology as the single join, agents that draft and never decide, a store and forward sync with
ordered idempotent replay, and a first phase gated on a simulated link-drop day answered entirely from
site memory. Swap the source systems, the fifteen objects and the model, sized to whatever node the
license path allows; keep the adapter-only write boundary, the single write path through named approvals
in the owning procedures, and the outage drill as the exit gate. Any remote operation on a constrained
link, in any industry, can carry this shape with those substitutions.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in the governance and approvals service: every agent draft routes to a named
person who confirms it inside the owning system's own procedure, and the site manager's authority under
the Mines Act 1923 is untouched, because the agents only draft. The hosting posture keeps everything
inside the fence on the operator's own hardware. Pakistan has no enacted data protection statute, so
residency obligations rest on board policy and contracts, and the draft personal data protection bill would
place critical personal data on servers in country; the design therefore keeps camp and workforce
personal data on site now, with purpose tags and retention limits, and the outbound sync never touches
that mirror. Identity runs on Keycloak on site, so logins survive an outage. The single external link is the
monitored satellite egress. The single write path onto the mirrors is the adapter tier, and the single write
path out of a draft is a named confirmation recorded against the owning system's record and reconciled
daily during the pilot, so no second version of permit state can grow beside the permit to work system.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 6

Every Source Enters Through an Adapter, Never Directly

Nothing reaches the object model except through an adapter that owns its contract.

Chapter 5 described what the object model holds. This chapter describes how data gets into it: through
adapters that own their contracts, never directly.

6.1 Seven Sources and Two Adapter Families

Each of the seven on-site systems of record enters the design with operator provenance: it is the
operator's own system, read through a mirror, and it keeps its ownership of every record. The project
controls system holds work packages and schedules. The construction management and permit to work
system owns permits and isolations, which is why it stays read-only to the platform. The equipment
telematics and maintenance system holds fault codes, service hours and work orders. The camp and
workforce management system holds occupancy and workforce records, and its mirror is the one the
outbound sync never touches. The health, safety and environment system holds incidents and near
misses. The supply and logistics tracking system holds convoy positions and consignments. The site
historian for power and water is the one system already on site, and its utility tags join the ontology across
the plant boundary. The eighth source is the corporate estate abroad, classed as a sync target rather than
a dependency. Figure 5 shows each system, its provenance class and its adapter path. The integration
adapter carries record extracts from the transactional systems, and the telemetry adapter carries the
historian's utility tag streams and the telematics fault code and service hour feeds.

       Figure 5. The 8 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

The tier guarantees four things. First, read-only access: no adapter writes to a system of record, and the
one flow back out is chosen operational aggregates through the sync. Second, contract ownership: each
adapter defines the extract or stream schema, the cadence, the mapping onto objects and the
provenance stamp, so a change in a source system is absorbed in one place rather than in every surface.
Third, idempotency: replaying an event twice changes nothing in the mirror, which is what makes outage
recovery safe. Fourth, stamping: every mirrored record carries a last-seen time, so the command center's
staleness banners can tell a supervisor that a convoy position is fresh and a work package figure is hours
old. Nothing bypasses the tier: no script, no agent and no person reads a production system directly.

6.3 The Event Backbone

The backbone is Apache Kafka 4.3 in KRaft mode with three dedicated controllers, running in the site
server room. Ordering is per source: each system's events land in a partition that preserves the order in
which they occurred, so a permit confirmed after it was revoked never replays the other way round.
Delivery is at least once, made safe by the adapters' idempotent application. Buffering is store and
forward: queues hold mirror refreshes and outbound aggregates through a satellite outage and replay
them in stored order when the link returns, which is why the design chose store and forward over live
bidirectional replication, since a replication session that fails midstream on a degrading link leaves both
sides uncertain. Mining already treats site communications as regulated infrastructure rather than a
convenience: United States regulators mandated wireless communication and tracking in every
underground coal mine after fatality investigations (MSHA 2006), and every such mine must now operate
such a system (VT n.d.). Industry guidance for open pit telecommunications reaches the same conclusion
for surface operations (Gmggroup n.d.), and communication failures have been blamed for injuries in an
investigated roof collapse (Miningmonthly 2026). The backbone is sized so the site never depends on the
window: refresh priority is set by data class, measured against the link's real sustained rate before
anything else is committed.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 7

Inference Belongs Where the Data Is

Each tier runs what its data and its link can carry.

Chapter 6 showed every source entering through an adapter family and flowing over the event backbone
into the object model, with nothing writing directly to a system of record. This chapter decides where the
computing happens, and one fact settles most of it: the site's only link to the outside world is satellite, it is
limited and costly, and it drops in bad weather.

7.1 The Site Server Room Is the Single Inference Tier

Two inference tiers exist and both sit in the site server room, on the mine's own power, inside the fence;
below that room the design commits no inference hardware at all. The frontier tier serves GLM 5.3, the
model the operator names for reasoning, and the memory arithmetic fixes its shape. The register files
GLM 5.3 at 753 billion parameters; at FP8 precision, one byte per parameter, the weights occupy 753 GB.
One node of the frontier inference cluster class (GPU nodes for 300B to 1T parameter open weight
models), eight cards, holds 1,128 GB, which leaves 375 GB beside the weights; the 1.2 planning factor
reserves about 151 GB of that for KV cache and activations, so the node carries the model with about
280 GB of KV ceiling to spare. The rejected alternative, two nodes of the 80 GB class, offers 589 GB
usable and cannot hold the weights at all, and it would drag a multi-node RDMA fabric into a remote site
on its own power. The embedding tier serves BGE-M3 at FP16, about 1.1 GB as published, small enough
to sit beside the frontier node on the same hardware and keep part numbers, fault codes and permit
clauses retrievable. The rugged tablets are thin operators to the command center and run nothing
themselves, which is why the stack carries no edge model serving row. Figure 6 sets the two tiers against
the boundary: everything that reasons is inside the fence, and only mirror feeds and chosen aggregates
cross it.

            Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget Is a Shift Conversation, Not a Satellite Window

The budget the design sets is simple to state: no interactive answer traverses the link. A supervisor
asking what work is open on a pad, which equipment is overdue and which convoy carries the parts for it
is answered entirely from local read mirrors, by models served on site, so the answer returns in the time a
shift conversation takes rather than the time a satellite round trip allows. The operator's own words carry
the constraint forward into production: a mill cannot wait for a satellite window. Because answers come
from mirrors, each one is stamped: the command center states when its facts were last synced, and

staleness banners carry that age into every view, so a reader always knows whether an answer is fresh or
held from the last good sync.

7.3 What Crosses the Fence, and What Happens When It Fails

Exactly two flows cross the boundary, both data-class filtered: mirror feeds come in from the corporate
systems abroad, and chosen operational aggregates go out. The camp and workforce mirror is the one
the outbound sync never touches, because personal data stays on site. When the link drops, the sync tier
does not fail mid-replication; it runs store and forward with ordered, idempotent replay, buffering outbound
aggregates and refreshing mirrors in stored order once the window returns, prioritised by data class. The
stakes of a blind site are documented in this industry: communication failures were blamed for injuries at
an underground mine, where a worker was trapped in a drilling jumbo during a roof collapse in a matter
investigated by a state resources regulator (Miningmonthly 2026), and a loss of communications on an
autonomous circuit sent an autonomous haul truck reversing into a manually operated excavator
(Miningmonthly 2024). Open pit telecommunications guidance collected from mining companies and
suppliers points the same way: the network must be planned for the degraded day, not the clear one
(Gmggroup n.d.). When power fails, the enclosure and power class orders a clean shutdown of the
sovereign node and the mirrors, so that on restoration the mirrors resynchronize rather than corrupt.
When the update path fails, nothing in the daily loop notices: artifacts and models move through Harbor,
the air gapped registry, and the site keeps serving its current verified versions until a new one arrives.

sovereign AI reference architectures of this shape the load bearing decision is not which model scores
highest but which one the operator can hold, tune and keep inside the fence. Figure 7 shows the model

                      Figure 7. The two models, their placement, and the work each one does.

8.1 Two Models, Two Licenses, One Fence

GLM 5.3 is the frontier model, and the operator names it: reasoning runs on its open weights, self hosted
on the operator's own hardware at the site. The register files 753 billion parameters, which at FP8 occupy
about 756 GB of weights and roughly 1.5 TB at BF16, so the model is served at FP8 on one node of the
141 GB class under vLLM, per the sizing in Chapter 7. Its role is the agentic work surface and ontology
maintenance: the conversational interface that answers with citations and says when its facts were last
synced, and the reasoning behind the three drafting agents whose outputs people approve. Its license is
the GLM-5.3 bespoke license, whose terms permit commercial use, fine tuning and redistribution, which is
what lets the operator hold the weights inside the fence, tune them for site vocabulary, and carry them
across the fence without renegotiating terms. It was chosen over GLM 5.2, which carries the MIT license
but was not the model the operator named, and over any hosted API, which would place the reasoning
outside the fence and fail exactly on the bad day the design exists for. BGE-M3 is the embedding model,
serving retrieval over permits, work orders, faults and maintenance histories. It performs dense, sparse
and multi-vector retrieval in one pass, which is what keeps part numbers, fault codes and permit clauses
retrievable behind the command center's cited answers. It is about 2.27 GB at float32 as published, about
1.1 GB at FP16 and about 0.6 GB at 8 bit; the design serves it at FP16 beside the frontier node, where it
is a rounding error against the KV ceiling. Its MIT license lets the operator copy it into the air gapped
registry and run it anywhere on site without terms to track, which is why it was chosen before any
comparison of embedding accuracy.

Shadow Mode Comes Before Any Flag Is Trusted

The rollout earns each phase at a gate the operator can read.

Chapter 8 fixed which models the site runs and on what license the operator holds their weights. This

9.1 Phases, Items and the Gate

The rollout is a single phase with a single gate, shaped so a pause strands no work. Phase One carries
17 items across six workstreams: Site ontology, Drafting agents, Governance and approvals, Memory and
reasoning, Command center, and the Phase one pilot itself. The items include the governed site ontology
of pads and permits, local read mirrors of the site's seven systems of record, and the outage-tolerant
satellite sync with staleness stamping that keeps those mirrors honest about their age. Requirement
coverage stands at one requirement stated, one covered in full, none partial and none open: the
operator's ask for a sovereign build that runs on site, reads the site's systems locally, syncs to the
corporate systems when the link allows and works fully when it does not. Figure 8 lays the phase, its
items, its workstreams and its gate on one page.

The gate is a simulated link-drop day, answered entirely from the site's own memory with the satellite
egress severed. The pilot area must resolve a dozer fault, carried from a raised fault code to a drafted
work order whose parts the on-site inventory can name; a permit clash between two crews on adjacent
pads, held as a conflict rather than issued; and a late convoy, read from its last known position against
plan, with the consignments it carries tied to the work packages waiting on them. The pilot covers one
construction area and its heavy fleet, and until that day is answered from local memory, nothing the build
drafts is load bearing.

9.2 What the Rollout Measures

The pilot measures before it claims. Four baselines are taken from the site's own records before any
figure is quoted, because the requirement itself states that its scale figures come from public reporting on
projects of this class and must not stand in for this site. The sustained rate and the outage statistics of the
satellite link are measured first, since they set the order in which the seven mirrors refresh by data class
and the size of the replay buffer the sync must hold. Every agent confirmation is recorded against the
owning system's record and reconciled daily during the pilot, so the permit to work system remains the

single version of permit state. Staleness stamps carry the measurement to every surface: each answer
the command center gives states when its facts were last synced.

9.4 Lessons

Rehearse the link-down day before anyone relies on site memory. The gate does not ask whether the
mirrors work; it asks whether a supervisor on a bad day gets one answer from site memory instead of

three answers from three systems, if the link is up. Treating the outage as a drill rather than an
assumption is what makes the degradation graceful in practice.

Run the license determination before the card commitment. ECCN 3A090 turns on total processing
performance, and the 141 GB class node is the class most exposed by it. Naming the end user and
settling the determination as the first checkpoint means a closed path costs a fallback decision, not a
stranded purchase.

Keep the write layer with the system of record. The permit agent drafts and the permit to work system
approves, through its own procedures and a named person. Daily reconciliation during the pilot is the
check that this boundary held.

9.5 What Is Still Open

Four questions remain open, each with a settled consequence attached. The export license outcome
either confirms the one-node frontier tier inside the fence or moves it to the in-country colocation fallback,
which changes the hosting posture and nothing in the object model. The measured sustained rate of the
satellite link fixes the refresh priority by data class and the buffer sizing for ordered replay. The enactment
of Pakistan's draft data protection bill, if it comes, lands on records already tagged by purpose and limited
by retention, so it forces no migration. And the site's own baselines, once measured, replace the public
reporting on projects of this class that the requirement itself flags as assumption.

10.1 What the Operator Owns

Four assets, each named and each held inside the fence. The first is the object model: fifteen objects and

extendable by the operator as the site moves from construction into production. The second is the

boundary: camp and workforce personal data never leaves the site, the outbound sync carries only
chosen aggregates, and the single write path to any system of record runs through that system's own

design itself was reasoned, so any choice in the preceding chapters can be traced to what justified it.
Every design in this series is produced on Praxis, and this chapter lets a reader trace any choice above
back to what justified it. Sovereign AI reference architectures cannot be lifted from a generic pattern; each
is argued from one operation's constraints, and Figure 9 shows the whole argument on one page: the

ask, the family and industry assigned, the records read, the eight lenses, the patterns and the equipment
the reasoning landed on.

11.1 Contextualizing the Ask

The ask, written in the operator's own words, is a sovereign build for a remote copper and gold mine on a
satellite link in Pakistan: open weight models on the operator's own hardware in the country, inside the
fence, reading the site's systems locally, syncing to the corporate systems when the link allows and
working fully when it does not. Praxis assigned the design to the system of context family in the Mining
industry, which fixed the architectural pattern before any tool was chosen: a governed ontology as a read
projection over systems of record, drafting agents above it, memory beside them. What Praxis read: the
case study, tooling and recency, hardware and equipment, rules and regulations, approach and history
shelves. The first principles and domain fusion reasoning drew on the brief's own doctrine.

 Figure 9. From the ask to the design: the family and industry Praxis assigned, the eight lenses and what each cited, the
                        patterns adopted and set aside, and the equipment the design lands on.

11.2 The Lenses

Praxis reasons through eight lenses, and Table 6 states what each could see, how many sources it cited,
and what it contributed to this design. A lens that returned nothing is shown as the gap it was: the history

11.3 Patterns Adopted and Set Aside

Four patterns were adopted. The ontology is a read projection over the seven systems of record, never a
replacement for them; every agent draft routes to a named approval in the owning system's procedure;
the sync is store and forward with ordered, idempotent replay, because a link that drops in bad weather
must be buffered through rather than replicated across; and the frontier tier is one node of the 141 GB
GPU class at FP8, sized by the model's filed parameter count against usable memory. Three were set
aside with reasons. Live bidirectional replication was rejected because replication that fails mid-stream on
a weather outage is worse than replay that resumes in order. Two nodes of the 80 GB class were rejected
because 753 GB of FP8 weights exceed one 80 GB class node's 589 GB of usable memory, and a multi-
node RDMA fabric at a remote site on its own power is the wrong shape. On-site training was set aside
entirely: under system of context nothing is trained, and the loop closes through memory rather than
weight updates.

11.4 Where the Reasoning Lands

The equipment classes the reasoning landed on are few and each is justified. The frontier tier is the
frontier inference cluster class (GPU nodes for 300B to 1T parameter open weight models), eight
accelerators in one node, holding 753 GB of FP8 weights on 1,128 GB and leaving 375 GB beside the
weights for KV cache and activations against the 151 GB the 1.2 planning factor reserves. Site serving
runs under vLLM on Kubernetes, with Harbor as the air-gapped artifact and model registry and Keycloak
for identity. Time authority is an OCP Time Card class GNSS grandmaster with OCXO holdover, driven by
linuxptp and chrony. The ruggedized site server class in the site server room is confirmed at design
against the export license outcome. Every one of these choices traces to a record Praxis read, and
nothing in this paper is inferred beyond what that reading recorded.

title: A Self-Improving AI System for Carrier Exception Handling in the United States
text:
V E R T I C A L - D R I V E N A R C H I T E C T U R E S · S U P P LY C H A I N & L O G I S T I C S · D E S I G N E D W I T H P R A X I S · N O V E M B E R
2026

A Self-Improving AI System for Carrier
Exception Handling in the United States
Lane Memory: A Sovereign AI Reference Architecture for Self-Improving Carrier Exception
Handling in Supply Chain and Logistics

Muhammad Umar, Cofounder, CodeNinja

For the operations vice president accountable for exception performance, the exception desk supervisors, and the
data, platform and reliability engineers who would build and run it.

Vertical-Driven Architectures is a CodeNinja series of system designs. Every design in the series is driven by a real-
world problem and scenario in a single industry, and every one is designed on Praxis, CodeNinja's platform for
designing physical AI systems. Operations are described by class, never by name.

ABSTRACT

The Exception Desk Should Get Better Every Week
A self-improving AI system for a third party logistics provider in the United States, one that manages
truckload and less than truckload freight for shippers across a network of contracted carriers, must
answer one question when an exception lands: what fixed this same exception, on this lane, with this
carrier, at this consignee, the last time it happened? The answer exists, but it is buried in years of email
and chat threads no system reads, held in the heads of coordinators whose knowledge leaves with them
through a high-turnover desk, and scattered across seven systems of record that never meet. Teams
evaluating a self-improving AI system for logistics meet exactly this shape: the data is already inside the
estate, the improvement loop is not, and shippers now measure the operator on time to resolve and on
whether they were told before they asked.

The design reads seven source systems, the transportation management system, the carrier tracking and
visibility platform, the appointment scheduling tool, the claims system, the carrier scorecards and
contracts, the customer order feeds and the email and chat threads, through one integration adapter
family into a governed ontology of sixteen objects joined by typed links, projected never migrated, with a

single gated write path into the scheduling tool behind coordinator approval. Eight services run on that
ontology: the network build, threads and memory, sovereign compute, memory and improvement, agent
drafting and approval, the command center, data governance, and pilot and extension, delivering triage,
recovery and review agents on two surfaces, the exception command center and the weekly recurring-
exception review. Three models carry the work: GLM 5.3, a 753B-parameter open-weight model served at
FP8 on one node of eight GPUs of the 141 GB class in the operator's own facility, drafting for
coordinators who confirm; a Qwen3.8 27B dense model at the site tier parsing threads and notes; and a
Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B model for retrieval over threads, notes and resolutions. Improvement runs on
recursive memory loops over confirmed outcomes, never on training or fine tuning, so nothing about a
shipper's freight leaves the operator's control and no weights change on the fly.

Part I states the industry problem and the join failure across the seven systems. Part II sets the
constraints, the layered stack, the sixteen-object model, the adapter tier and its guarantees, the inference
placement with its memory arithmetic, and the three models with the licenses that let the operator own
them. Part III lays out the two phases with their eighteen items and gates, what the rollout measures, the
failure modes and the open questions, then who owns what the system builds. Part IV closes with how
Praxis contextualized and reasoned the design, so any choice in this paper can be traced back to the
recorded reading that justified it.

Figure 1. Lane Memory on one page: the sources the operation already runs, one object model, what it computes, and the
                                                person who decides.

Contents

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 1

Exception Volume Grows While Resolution Stands Still

Tens of thousands of shipments a month throw exceptions that are still worked the way they
were ten years ago, and the knowledge that would resolve them faster walks out the door
with every departing coordinator.

The abstract argued that a self-improving AI system for the exception desk can run entirely on the
operator's own hardware, reading systems it already owns. This chapter establishes why that argument is
needed at all: the volume of exceptions has grown while the practice of resolving them has not moved in
a decade, and the knowledge that carries the desk leaves with every coordinator who departs.

1.1 The Question the Operation Needs Answered

When an exception lands, the desk needs one answered question within minutes, not hours: given this
shipment, this carrier, this consignee and this appointment, what actually works here, and who has to be
told what right now. Answering it requires data the operation already holds but holds apart: the shipment
and its stop sequence from the transportation management system, the live tracking events and
estimated arrival from the carrier visibility platform, the appointment window and its change history from
the scheduling tool, the carrier's performance history and contract terms from the scorecards, the
shipper's data terms from the order feeds, the claims record of what similar exceptions became, and the
email and chat threads where past exceptions were actually worked. The regulatory regimes frame the
answer rather than supplying it: federal hours of service rules bind which recovery options a driver can
legally execute, privacy law governs how driver and shipper data may be used, and each shipper's
contractual data terms set what may be shown to whom.

1.2 The Documented Cost of the Problem

The cost shows up first as turnover and its consequences. Exception work is high-volume, interrupt-driven
and closely supervised by performance metrics, and the pattern is documented beyond this operator: a
peer-reviewed cross-sectional study in logistics found algorithmic management of exactly this kind
associated with psychological distress, musculoskeletal pain and occupational accidents (Springer 2025).
Turnover on the desk is high, and each departure removes knowledge that was never written down: which
carriers answer at night, which consignees accept a late slot, which exceptions become claims. The
commercial cost follows directly, because shippers now measure the operator on time to resolve and on
whether they were told before they asked; every repeat exception worked from scratch taxes that
measure, and every unresolved cascade that becomes a claim converts a service failure into a financial
one recorded in the claims system.

1.3 The Operation as a Scenario

The operator is a third party logistics provider in the United States managing truckload and less than
truckload freight on behalf of shippers, moved by hundreds of contracted carriers. It plans, tenders and
tracks tens of thousands of shipments a month. The people in the loop are the exception coordinators on
shift who own each exception end to end, the shift leads who approve changes beyond a coordinator's
authority, the carrier managers who own carrier relationships, the account managers who face the
shippers, and the claims handlers who close what resolution failed to prevent. The physical environments
are unglamorous for a physical AI design: offices, a server room in the operator's own facility, and a
national road network seen only through the tracking feeds of the carriers' devices; no site is instrumented

by this design. The regulatory ground combines the trucking safety regime that governs driver hours,
privacy law confirmed with counsel, and the contractual data terms each shipper imposes. The count of
named systems is seven: the transportation management system, the carrier tracking and visibility
platform, the appointment scheduling tool, the claims system, the carrier scorecards and contracts, the
customer order feeds, and the email and chat threads.

PA R T I · C H A P T E R 2

Every Desk System Sees One Slice of the Exception

Seven systems each hold a true but partial view of the same missed pickup or late arrival,
and none of them can assemble the argument a coordinator needs in the first minutes after
an exception lands.

Chapter 1 set out the question. This chapter explains why no system the operation already runs can
answer it.

2.1 What Each System Sees

Transportation management system: the primary system of record for shipments, stops, tenders and
carrier master data; the ontology's shipment and stop objects are projections over it, kept current by
change capture.

Carrier tracking and visibility platform: the source of tracking events, ETA updates and device status,
which is how the trucks are seen and the earliest signal for a dark device or a late arrival.

Appointment scheduling tool: owns the appointment windows the cascade prediction reasons over, and
receives the approved appointment change requests, the one operational write path, gated on coordinator
approval.

Claims system: closes the loop from unmanaged exceptions to claims, feeding the claims per thousand
shipments baseline and the review agent's view of which exception types become claims.

Carrier scorecards and contracts: carrier performance history and contract terms inform which recovery
option is likely to work and which carriers answer at night.

Customer order feeds: the shipper-side origin of demand: orders link shipments to shippers and their data
terms, which set the purpose-based access rules.

    Figure 2. Seven systems, each seeing one part of the answer. The question needs all of them in one place at once.

2.2 What None of Them See Together

Each holds one slice, and the question needs all of them in one place at once, which today is done by
hand at the cadence of whoever has the time.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 3

Sovereignty and the Human Loop Shape Everything
Downstream

Four commitments, open weights on the operator's own hardware, a named person deciding
every action, improvement without training on the fly, and no replacement of the systems of
record, discipline every choice made after them.

Chapter 2 showed that the join failure is structural: seven systems each hold a slice and none holds the
argument. This chapter fixes the four commitments that any answer must satisfy, because they discipline
every choice made after them, from where the models run to how improvement compounds.

3.1 Open Weights on the Operator's Own Hardware

The operator's requirement is explicit: open weight models on its own hardware in its own facility, with
nothing about its shippers' freight leaving its control. In this industry the constraint is harder than it looks,
because freight data is not the operator's alone: every shipment carries a shipper's commodities, values
and consignees, bound by contractual data terms, so a cloud region or a colocation cage would move
hundreds of shippers' data across a boundary none of them agreed to. The commitment also rules out
managed model services entirely, which pushes the design toward a self-improving AI system in which
the weights, the memory and the decision record all sit inside one estate perimeter, served on one node
of the frontier inference cluster class, GPU nodes for 300B to 1T parameter open weight models, which
the operator's own server room takes as standard racks.

3.2 A Named Person Decides Every Action

The second commitment is that agents draft and a named coordinator decides. Exception handling fails in
this industry when automation acts unilaterally: an unapproved carrier swap strands a load, an automated
shipper notice breaches data terms, and the regulatory and safety consequences of automated action in
trucking are documented by the federal regulator's own investigations (Tanktransport 2022). The design
therefore carries one operational write path, appointment change requests into the scheduling tool, gated
on coordinator approval, and routes every carrier message and shipper notice through the same approval
gate before anything leaves the estate.

3.3 Improvement Without Training on the Fly

The operator asks for a system that gets better every week without training a model on the fly, and the
distinction matters commercially as well as technically: fine tuning on coordinator confirmations would
produce opaque weights that are hard to audit when a shipper disputes an action, and recursive self-
improvement carries governance risks now documented for enterprises (Cloudsecurityalliance 2026) and
noted as spreading through the corporate ecosystem (Stanford 2026). The design compounds
improvement in memory instead of weights: every confirmed resolution becomes a retrievable record the
next exception reads, auditable, reversible and owned outright, with no retraining run and no distillation
step.

3.4 The Systems of Record Stay Untouched

The final commitment is projection, never migration. The transportation management system, tracking
platform, scheduling tool, claims system, scorecards and order feeds remain the authoritative systems
they are, read through their own surfaces with change capture, and the ontology is built over them. This is
hard in logistics because identifiers disagree across systems: the same carrier and the same consignee
carry different identifiers in each, so entity resolution is a first-class deliverable rather than a cleanup task
performed once.

3.5 Scoping Decisions

Three scoping decisions follow from the four commitments, each buying something specific at a stated
cost, set out in Table 1.

PA R T I I · C H A P T E R 4

One Stack Runs From Records to the Command Center

Systems of record below, one governed object model in the middle, agents and two surfaces
above, all on one event backbone and all inside the operator's estate.

Chapter 3 turned the operator's constraints into scoping decisions: no training on the fly, no shipper or
carrier data leaving the estate, a named person on every action, and the systems of record left exactly
where they are. This chapter turns those decisions into a stack, so that each layer's responsibility follows
from a constraint rather than from a preference.

4.1 The Pattern and Why It Fits

The pattern is the one shape that satisfies all four constraints at once: systems of record below, one
governed object model in the middle, applications and agents above. The seven systems of record stay
untouched at the bottom, read through their own surfaces, because the ontology is a projection over them
and never a migration. In the middle, one object model of sixteen objects joins shipment to carrier to
appointment to exception, so every agent reads one governed network instead of seven disconnected
stores. Above it, the triage, recovery and review agents draft and coordinators confirm; that split is
architecture rather than courtesy, because the requirement fixes a named approver on every action, and
the published observation that recursive self-improvement is already spreading from frontier laboratories
into the wider corporate ecosystem argues for the confirmation gate and the recorded decision trail being
structural, not appended (Stanford 2026). The same reasoning keeps improvement out of the weights: the
memory service compounds only from confirmed outcomes, which is what the requirement means by
getting better every week without training a model on the fly. Figure 3 shows the layered stack with its
counts: seven sources, one adapter family, sixteen objects, three models across a central tier, a site tier
and an embedding tier, eight services and two surfaces, all inside the operator's facility.

              Figure 3. The layered stack: 7 sources, 1 adapter family, 16 objects, 8 services and 2 surfaces.

4.3 A Reusable Pattern

The reusable shape is five rules rather than a component list, and a team carrying a similar brief can lift it
wholesale. Put one event backbone under everything, so ordering and replay belong to the platform and
not to each integration. Pass every source through one adapter family that carries provenance and scope,
so no record enters the model ungoverned. Let agents read only the governed object model, never the
raw stores, so the network's joins and vocabularies form the single argument every draft rests on. Make
agents draft and named people approve, with one gated write path that nothing bypasses. Let
improvement land in memory built from confirmations rather than in weights, so the system gets better
every week without a training pipeline. What a team swaps is the domain: its sources, its sixteen objects,
its models sized to its thread volume and its write target. What it keeps is the backbone, the adapter tier,
the approval gate and the memory loop.

5.2 The Human Loop and the Hosting Posture

The human loop lives in three status vocabularies. An exception moves from New through Triaged,
Recovery drafted and Approved to Resolved or Became claim; an action moves from Drafted through
Awaiting approval and Approved to Sent, Acknowledged or Declined; a resolution moves from Proposed
through Confirmed to Promoted to standing fix. No action is sent without a named approver, and the
approver is recorded on the action object, which is the accountability the design rests on: when
automation is implicated in harm, regulators have charged both the employer and the system supplier, so
the named decision-maker is not decoration but the defense (Ohsrep 2024). The same loop answers the
human cost of algorithmic management, which a cross-sectional study in logistics has associated with
psychological distress and occupational accidents: the coordinator sees a draft labeled preliminary,
decides, and is the decision-maker rather than the managed (Springer 2025). The hosting posture follows
the constraint that shipper and carrier data never leave the operator's hardware. Everything runs on the
operator's own equipment in its own facility, identity is federated through Keycloak, no inference call
leaves the estate and no external model is called, and the one write path in the entire design is the
approved appointment change request into the scheduling tool's request surface. Retrieval is permission-
aware, returning only what the asking coordinator could already open, and every record the agents read
carries provenance and the scope of the shipper's data terms.

Seven Systems Enter Through One Adapter Tier

Every source, whatever its provenance, passes through the same adapter family that carries
ordering, provenance and scope, leaving one gated write path into the scheduling tool and no

Chapter 5 described what the object model holds. This chapter describes how data gets into it, and why

6.1 Seven Sources, One Provenance Class

Every source in this design is of provenance class operator, held by the operator and read, never written
to. The transportation management system is the primary record for shipments, stops, tenders and carrier
master data, and the shipment and stop objects are projections over it, kept current by change capture.
The carrier tracking and visibility platform supplies the tracking events, ETA updates and device status,
and carries the earliest signal for a dark device or a late arrival. The appointment scheduling tool owns
the windows the cascade prediction reasons over, and is also the target of the one gated write path, the
approved appointment change request. The claims system closes the loop from unmanaged exceptions
to claims. The carrier scorecards and contracts carry performance history and terms, including which
carriers answer at night. The customer order feeds are the origin of demand, linking shipments to
shippers and to the data terms that set purpose-based access. The email and chat threads are where
most exceptions are actually worked, across tens of thousands of shipments a month and hundreds of
carriers, and the archived years of those threads are what bootstraps the memory before the first live
exception arrives. Figure 5 sets the seven systems beside their adapter paths into the object model.

       Figure 5. The 7 named systems, the adapter path each one takes, and the object model they all map into.

6.2 What the Adapter Tier Guarantees

The adapter tier is a single integration adapter family, and its guarantee is that no record reaches the
object model except through it. Each adapter carries four things on every record. Provenance: which
system the record came from, when it was extracted, and that source's clock offset, recorded as a field
rather than silently corrected, so a causal claim about which event came first stays honest. Ordering: a
per-stream sequence number alongside the backbone offset, so the projection can detect a gap or a
replay. Scope: the shipper whose data terms govern the record, which is what the permission-aware
retrieval in Chapter 5 enforces. Conformity: the record must map to the object model's vocabulary before
it enters, so entity reconciliation, the same carrier and consignee carrying different identifiers in each
system, happens at the adapter under governance rather than in each agent's prompt. Debezium handles
change capture on the transactional systems; governed pulls handle the feeds and threads. The tier also
guarantees the negative: no agent, service or surface writes to any source directly, and the single write in
the design is the approved change request into the scheduling tool.

6.3 The Event Backbone

The backbone is Apache Kafka in KRaft mode, and it carries ordering, delivery, buffering and replication.
Ordering is carried by Kafka offsets and the per-stream sequence numbers, with each source's clock
offset as a recorded field, so the desk can argue about sequence without pretending the clocks agree.
Delivery is at least once, and the projection into the object model is idempotent, so a replayed stream
updates the same objects rather than duplicating them. Buffering is the retained log itself: a slow
consumer, a parsing backlog or a serving restart does not lose events, because the adapter replays from
the backbone without re-reading the source. Replication runs inside the facility, so a single broker failure
does not stop the desk. The write path deserves its own sentence: an approved appointment change

request crosses from the action object to the scheduling tool's request surface only after coordinator
approval, and nothing else in the design writes anywhere.

All Reasoning Stays Inside the Operator's Own Facility

Every inference call, from frontier drafting to thread parsing to embedding, lands on hardware
the operator owns, sized from the weights up, so nothing about a shipper's freight crosses
the estate boundary.

Chapter 8's licenses decide who holds the weights; this chapter decides where those weights physically
sit and what each tier of the system asks of them. The placement follows from one sentence in the
operator's requirement, our own hardware in our own facility, and every number below is arithmetic on the
filed parameter counts, not an estimate borrowed from outside the estate.

7.1 Three Tiers, Each Sized From the Weights Up

The design runs three inference tiers, and each one is sized by the same method: take the parameter
count, multiply by the bytes per parameter at the chosen precision, and check the result against usable
accelerator memory before any workload is placed. Figure 6 shows the tiers side by side with what runs
on each and what, if anything, crosses the estate boundary.

The frontier tier serves GLM 5.3 for the agentic work surface and ontology maintenance, and it is the tier
the arithmetic is tightest on. GLM 5.3 carries 753 billion parameters, filed as the register's count, and the
design serves them at FP8, where one byte per parameter gives 753 GB of weights. Applying the
planning factor of 1.2 for KV cache and activations, the GPUs must hold 904 GB. One node of the 141
GB HBM class, eight GPUs at 141 GB each, provides 1,128 GB of memory; at the 0.92 utilization the
sizing rule allows, that is about 1,038 GB usable, which holds the weights with about 280 GB of KV cache
ceiling left for concurrent coordinator sessions in the command center. Serving the same model at BF16
would demand about 1,506 GB and would force two nodes joined over an interconnect, which is why FP8
on one node was chosen and Chapter 3 records the alternative as rejected.

The site tier serves the dense Qwen3.8 27B model for high-volume thread and note parsing, because
years of archived email and chat, plus the live threads that trigger and narrate exceptions, are a
throughput workload rather than a reasoning one. At FP8 its weights occupy about 31 GB, which fits a
single card of the site inference server class with about 13 GB of KV cache ceiling, in an air-cooled PCIe
server the facility's server room already takes without modification.

The embedding tier serves Qwen3-Embedding 0.6B over threads, notes and resolutions for retrieval. Its
weights occupy about 1.2 GB at BF16, about 0.6 GB at 8 bit, so it sits beside the site-tier model on the

same server, and its activation memory is what grows with the 32K context window rather than with
anything the desk controls. The frontier node carries the room requirement the operator's facilities team
must confirm: about 15 kW of rack power per node with margin, a 10 to 35 C inlet range, and 10 RU per
node.

        Figure 6. Where each tier runs, what runs there, and the narrow set of outputs that cross the boundary.

7.2 The Latency Budget

The budget is stated in the desk's own beats rather than in milliseconds, because the desk's measures
are time to resolve and whether the shipper was told before asking. First priority is triage freshness: a live
thread event must raise the exception, match it against memory, and leave a draft waiting in the queue
before the coordinator who opens the queue reads it, and this is what the site-tier parse and embedding
pass exist to keep ahead of. Second is the conversational answer: the command center's interface
answers with citations, and an answer that loses the session has no value, so the frontier tier's
concurrency is bounded by the about 280 GB KV cache ceiling, which makes the latency budget a
memory budget as much as a time one. Third, and free to trail, is batch work: parsing archived threads
and refreshing embeddings can run behind the live queue. In every tier the coordinator is the decision-
maker, which is the deliberate answer to the finding that algorithmic management without a human
decision point is associated with psychological distress and occupational accidents in logistics work
(Springer 2025).

7.3 The Boundary and the Failure Paths

What crosses the estate boundary is only what a coordinator approves: carrier messages and shipper
notices, sent through email on the action object's approved path. All three models, the object model, the
memory and the decision record stay inside, and nothing in the design reaches the truck itself, a line
drawn with the regulator's own investigation of an autonomous trucking mishap in view (Tanktransport

2022). If the facility node fails, the manual way of working stays warm and rehearsed: a coordinator can
always work an exception by thread, phone and note, and serving restarts from pinned images in the on-
site registry, with a rollback that has been exercised once under observation. If power fails, the same
fallback holds, and the room requirements above are the operator's side of that insurance. If the update
path is the failure, the registry's pinned images mean the desk never runs on an unobserved weight
change; and if the wide-area link fails, the desk loses only the outbound notices, because no inference
call, no retrieval and no drafting ever left the building.
